caseno: Memorandum of Appeal from Original Order No. 90 of 1997.
lawyer:
Zakir Hossain, Advocate ------ For the Appellant. 
M Moniruzzaman Khan, Advocate ------ For Respondent No. 1
Saifuddin Ahmed, Advocate ------ For Respondent No.4.
parties:
Comforts Apparels (Pvt.) Ltd  ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
Vs.
Imperial Knitting Industries Ltd and others  ------ Defendant Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff/appellant is directed against the judgment and order dated 10-5-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 113 of 1997 summarily dismissing the petition under Order 39 rule 2 read with section 151 CPC with the word "filed".

2. The plaintiff/appellant who is a manufacturer and exporter of readymade garments filed the above suit praying for a declaration that they are not liable to pay US $1,40,000.00 to the defendant No. 1 against the back to back L/C No. JBD/Back) L)150/90 dated 14-5-96 unless the bills are reexamined and accepted by the defendant No. 3, stating, inter alia, that the defendant/respondent No. 3 who is a buyer of readymade garments, opened an irrevocable Master L/C No. 200 1A 259920 dated 9-4-96 for US$ 10,35,397.82 with DG Hamburg Germany in favour of the defendant/respondent No.2, a buying house and the defendant No. 2 then transferred partial value i.e. US$ 5,56,526.00 from the above noted Master L/C in favour of the plaintiff on 15-4-96, and then the plaintiff, for purchase of 57,544 KG of 100% cotton and 65/35 TC knitted fleece fabrics which were required to manufacture readymade garments for export to defendant No.3, opened against the above Master L/C the above back to back letter of credit dated 14-5-96 for US$ 3,82,556.00 in favour of the defendant No. 1 the supplier of fabrics. In above letter of credit, amongst others, it was stipulated that the defendant No. 1 will supply fabrics to the plaintiff within the time with chemical test certificate from an independent laboratory confirming that no 'AZO and' 'Diazo' Dyestuffs and no named and banned chemicals have been used to dye the delivered fabrics and such certificate will also contain the description of the chemicals used for test as well as the result of test in detail. On receipt of the fabrics from the defendant No. 1 which were however not supplied within due time, the plaintiff with the said fabrics manufactured ready made garments as per specifications and requirements of the defendant No. 3 and exported the same to the defendant No. 3 by four consignments and after due examination the defendant No. 3 accepted two consignments but refused to accept the remaining two consignments valuing US$ 69,504,80 and US$ 66,021.00 raising the ground that exported ready made garments were manufactured with unacceptable quality of fabrics. Since the earlier consignments were accepted by the defendant No. 3, no occasion arose for the plaintiff so far to doubt the laboratory chemical test certificates sent by the defendant No. 1, along with shipping documents were false and fabricated but after the defendant No. 3 took the stand of unacceptable quality of the fabrics, the plaintiff made investigation wherein the forgery was revealed. Then, to avoid auction at the Port of Hamburg, the plaintiff• had to bring back the said two consignments to Chittagong Port incurring a cost of Taka 4 lac in the same container wherein the defendant No. 1 also brought back some consignment which the defendant No. 3 also refused to accept on the self-same ground i.e. unacceptable quality of fabrics. Thereafter having no other alternative, the plaintiff took decision to re-export the above consignments with 40% discount but the authority concerned insisted that as per rule the whole quantity of goods in the container were required to be re-exported as re-export of part quantity of the container was not allowed. The defendant No. 1, who was the owner of the balance quantity of the goods in the said container, however did not agree to re-export their portion of the goods in the container in view of which the re-export with 40% discount, as arranged by the plaintiff, was delayed. However the defendant No. 5, in spite of having knowledge of the fact that false certificates were sent along with the shipping document insisted upon the defendant No. 4 to pay to them the balance US$ 1,40,550.00 against the back to back letter of credit dated 14-5-96 and the respondent No. 4 also, in spite of knowing of the above fraud and also the fact that the plaintiff/appellant was taking steps to re-export the said consignments, contemplated to release US$ 1,40,550 to the defendant No. 5 and so the plaintiff was compelled to file the above suit. On the same day of the filing of the suit, the plaintiff also filed an application praying for restraining the defendant No. 5 from encashing US$ 1,40,550.00 from the defendant No.4 until the goods are re-exported on 40% discount and/or the final bill amount is settled, but by the impugned order the above prayer was rejected on the ground that the application for temporary injunction was filed on the very date of filing of the suit which amounts to seeking consequential relief requiring payment of ad valorem court fee but the suit was filed merely for simple declaration with fixed court fee. Being affirmed, the plaintiff/appellant, apart from filing the present first miscellaneous appeal, also filed Civil Revision No. 1883 of 1997 and when the above civil revision was taken up for hearing on 29-2- 2000 they submitted that they will not press the Rule and so the Rule was discharged for non- prosecution.

3. In their application praying for vacating the order of injunction and also in their counter- affidavit, the defendant respondent No. 4 stated, inter alia, that in accordance with the conditions of the letter of credit, the defendant respondent No. 1 sent the fabrics to the plaintiff and submitted all relevant documents along with four bills of exchange with the defendant No. 5 who then sent those to the defendant No. 4 and in turn the defendant No. 4 sent those to the plaintiff and the plaintiff having accepted the bills of exchange, the defendant No. 4 by letters dated 8-9-96 and 15-9-96 informed the defendant No. 5 about the above acceptance of the bills of exchange by the plaintiff. The letter of credit dated 14-5-96 was established subject to Uniform Customs and Practice to Documentary Credit i.e UCPDC, and in terms of Article 4 of UCPDC, in credit operation all parties concerned deal with the documents and not with the good services and/or other performance to which the documents may relate and that the defendant/respondent No.5, after receipt of the acceptance letters from the respondent No. 4, purchased the bills and effected payment to the respondent No. 1 and so the defendant No.5 as the holder of the bills, are entitled to receive payment from the respondent No.4 against the bill.

4. Mr Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff/appellant, submits that since the Chemical Test certificates enclosed with the shipping documents were found to be forged so, in terms of the principles laid down in the case of Uttara Bank vs Macneil and Kilburn 33 (AD) 298 and the case of Janata Bank vs Ahmedia Garments, 40 DLR 72, the defendant No.1 having committed fraud of which the defendant No. 4 had knowledge and the proceeds of aforesaid back to back letter of credit being still lying with the defendant No. 4, necessary order of temporary injunction ought to have been granted. Mr Hossain relying on the case of Tarapore and Co, Madras vs Tractorexport. Moscow reported in AIR 1997 (SC) 247 next submits that since there was a very restrictive clause in the letter of credit regarding chemical test certificate, that clause had to be interpreted strictly and that, as has been held in the case reported in 11 DLR 103, since the plaintiff made out an arguable case, that was enough for passing the order of temporary injunction as prayed for.

5. Mr M Moniruzzaman Khan, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.5, submits that even if it is conceded that the application under Order 39 rule 2 is otherwise maintainable, even then, in view of the principle laid down in 33 DLR (AD) 298 and 40 DLR 72, the facts of which are almost similar to the present case, no order of temporary injunction can be passed and that in terms of Articles 3 and 4 of UCPDC, the bank deals with documents and not with goods and in the present case the shipping documents appeared to be in order on the face of it and the plaintiff having accepted the documents and the bills of exchange and the defendant No.5, then in good faith, having purchased the shipping documents and negotiated the bills within the validity period and no notice of fraud being sent to the defendant No. 5 before such negotiation, no order of injunction as prayed can be passed. Further, in case of pecuniary loss only, as in the present case, no order of injunction can be passed.

6. Heard the learned Advocate and perused the papers submitted by the parties.

7. As it appears that back to back letter of credit dated 14-5-96, out of which the defendant No.5 claimed US$ 1,40,559.00 was subject to UCPDC ICC publication No. 400. Article 4 of UCPDC in credit operation, all parties concerned deal with the documents and not with the goods, services and/or other performance to which the documents may relate.

8. In 33 DLR (AD) 298, on which both Mr. Hossain and Mr Khan relied, question arose as to whether the court should grant an order of injunction restraining the bank from encashing bank guarantee and the Appellate Division, after discussing many decisions, held that the bank-

"is not concerned in the least with the relations between the supplier and the customer, nor with the question whether the supplier performed his contractual obligation or not nor with the question whether the supplier is in default or not. The bank must pay according to its conditions. The only exception is when there is a clear fraud of which the bank had notice."

9. In AIR 1970 (SC) 891 which was referred in 33 DLR (AD) 298 Court of India observed as follows:

"An irrevocable letter of credit has a definite implication. It is a mechanism of great importance in international trade any interference with that mechanism is bound to have serious repercussion on the international trade of the country. Except under any exceptional circumstances the courts should not interfere with that mechanism."

10. In the above AIR 1970 (SC) 891, the Supreme Court also quoted the following passage from Halsbury's Laws of England.

"It is often made a condition of mercantile contract that the buyer shall pay for the goods by means of a confirmed credit, and it is then the duty of the buyer to procure his bank, known as the issuing or originating bank, to issue an irrevocable credit in favour of the seller by which the bank undertakes to the seller, either directly or through another bank in the seller's country known as the correspondent or negotiating bank, to accept drafts drawn upon it for the price of the goods, against tender by the seller of the shipping documents. The contractual relationship between the issuing bank and the buyer is defined by the terms of the agreement between them under which the letter opening the credit is issued, and as between the seller and the bank, the issue of the credit duly notified to the seller creates a new contractual nexus and renders the bank directly liable to the seller to pay the purchase price or to accept the bill of exchange upon tender of the document. The contract thus created between the seller and the bank is separate from, although ancillary to the original contract between the buyer and the seller, by reasons of the bank's undertaking to the seller, which is absolute, Thus, the bank is not entitled to rely upon terms of the contract between the buyer and the seller which might permit the buyer to reject the goods and to refuse payment thereof and, conversely, the buyer is not entitled to an injunction restraining the seller from dealing with the letter of credit if the goods are defective."

In 33 DLR the Appellate Division also quoted the following observation of Lord Diplock made in the case of American Cyanamid Co vs Ethicon Ltd HJ(E) 1975 AC 296.

"The object of the interlocutory injunction is to protect the plaintiff against injury by the violation of his right for which he could not be adequately compensated in damages recoverable in the action if the uncertainty were resolved in his favour at the trial, but the plaintiffs need for such protection must be weighed against the corresponding need of the defendant to be protected against injury resulting from his having been prevented from exercising his own legal right for which he could not be adequately compensated under the plaintiffs undertaking in damages if the uncertainty were resolved in the defendant's favour at the trial. The Court must weigh one need against another and determine where "the balance of convenience" lies."

The Appellate Division after discussing the above and also other decisions held as follows:

"Applying these principles the least that can be said is that the decisions show that the courts are very reluctant to interfere with commercial transactions which have been entered by the parties in business transaction through performance of guarantee or letter of guarantee which are invoked in commercial dealing. The decisions show that the court will not interfere by granting an injunction from performing or discharging the commercial obligations."

11. In the case of Janata Bank vs Ahmedia Garments reported in 40 DLR 72 referred to by both Mr Hossain and Mr Khan, the plaintiff claimed Taka 2,56,828.00, from the defendants on the ground that they have suffered total loss of Taka 24,56,818 due to the supply or wrong machinery and the defendant having refused to pay the said amount the plaintiff filed money suit for recovery of the said amount and as the defendant company had no other property moveable or immoveable in Bangladesh except the proceeds of the letter of credit which Janata Bank was to pay to the defendant, the plaintiff prayed for attachment before judgment of the aforesaid proceeds of the letter.

12. In the aforesaid case Janata Bank took the stand that the Bank of Tokyo have already paid the drafts and they are therefore the bonafide holders of those drafts and so are entitled to full payment of the aforesaid drafts with interest, etc. The trial Court allowed the above prayer for attachment before judgment and being aggrieved Janata Bank filed the FMA case No. 90 of 1997 before the High Court Division, During hearing of the appeal different provisions of UCPDC, the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 and also the decisions reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 80; AIR 1981 (SC) 426, AIR 1920(SC) 1934, AIR 1983 (Cal) 106, AIR 1986 (Cal) 56, (1958) 1 All ER 262, 1975) 1 All ER 107, (1978) 1 All ER 976, (1982) 2 All ER 720 were referred and the High Court Division after discussing the provisions of Articles 2, 3, 4, 9(h) and 16 of UCPDC held as

follows:

"The cumulative effect of all these provisions is that an authorising or negotiating Bank is bound to pay when all papers as per terms and condition of the letters of credit are presented which appears to the paying Bank to be correct on the face of it and in such International Credit operation and International Banking transaction Banks are in no way concerned or bound by the selling contract of the parties even if reference of such contract is made in the credit, Banks in such credit operations deal in documents and not with the quality of goods shipped or deal with any other performance by the seller to which the documents may be related (refer Article 4)"

So, keeping in mind the International Banking Practice as laid down in the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit arid on a particular reference to Articles 2, 3, 4 and 16, the Bank who is authorised to pay to a third party against documents which appears on their face to be in accordance with the terms and conditions of the credit, the party giving such authority shall be bound to reimburse the "Bank which effects payment".

The High Court Division further held as follows:

"It is thus seen that the authorised or negotiating bank must pay, on presentation of the papers which appears to be correct to the Bank on the face of it, and when such payment is made to a third party reimbursement shall not be stopped by a court of law."

13. In the present case, as it appears the chemical test certificates as required under letter of credit dated 14-5-96 were also deposited as part of shipping documents for negotiation against two consignments negotiated earlier and defendant No.3 the buyer accepted those without any objection but subsequently, after rejection of the subsequent consignments where similar certificates were enclosed with the shipping documents the defendant No. 3 refused to accept consignments on the ground of non acceptability of fabrics and then on investigation, according to the plaintiff all the certificates so issued were found to be false and forged.

14. On the other hand those certificates found to be correct on the face of it the plaintiff/appellant accepted the documents and the bills of exchange and the defendant No. 5 purchased the bills at discount and paid the proceeds of the bills to the defendant No. 1 long before the allegation of fraud was made to them. So being bonafide holders in due course the defendant Nos. 4 and 5 are entitled to full payment of the draft in view of the principle laid down in 40 DLR 72 wherein the Bank of Tokyo took similar stand to the effect that having paid the drafts they, being bonafide holders in due course, are entitled to full payment of the draft.

<u>15. From going through the contents of the decisions mentioned in 33 DLR (AD) 298 and 40 DLR 72 it appears that the consistent view of the courts are that only in two exceptional circumstances an issuing bank can absolve its responsibility of not honouring the obligation created by it under a letter of credited, if it is proved that there is a clear case of fraud of which it has knowledge and secondly, if the case is of such nature that there is very special circumstances which warrant an interference by the court. But we, in the present case, find no such exceptional circumstances.</u>

16. Further, in case of encashment of the proceeds of letter of credit by the defendant No.5. the plaintiff/appellant may suffer injury of pecuniary loss which can be compensated by damages and since the defendant No.1, who allegedly sent false certificates with shipping documents, carries on business in Bangladesh so the plaintiff/appellant may file suit against the defendant No. 1 claiming damages for enclosing such false certificates with the shipping documents. So in terms of the principle as laid down in American Cynamid case referred earlier the plaintiff/appellant is not entitled to the order of temporary injunction as prayed for.

<u>17. In view of the above, we are of the view that even if it is conceded that the application under Order 39, rule 2 CPC is not liable to be 'filed' on the ground that the suit for simple declaration was not maintainable as being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act plaintiff/appellant even then in view of the grounds discussed above, are not entitled to get an order of temporary injunction and so the appeal is liable to be dismissed.</u>

18. In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated. The discussions as above have been made only to decide whether the plaintiff/appellant are entitled to an order of injunction and so the same will be confirmed only for disposal of this appeal and will not in any way affect the merit of the suit.

The parties are also free to settle the court-fee matter before the trial Court.

End.

parties:
Dudu Mia and others ------- Petitioner
Vs.
Ekram Miah Chowdhury and others ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 28th July, 1996 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 343 of 1970)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J : The instant appeal by leave at the instance of defendant No. 1 is against the judgment and order of July 28, 1996 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 343 of 1970 allowing the appeal and consequently set aside the judgment and decree of August 28, 1970 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 35 of 1969 dismissing the same which was for declaration of title in respect of the land described in Schedules 1(a) and 2(a).

2. Plaintiff-respondent instituted the suit stating, inter alia, that land described in Schedule 1 belongs to him and to his two other brothers and that upon amicable settlement with the brothers, (defendant No.2) as well as with the predecessor of defendant Nos. 5-9, got in his exclusive share the land described in Schedule 1(a), that he and his two other brothers had rent receiving interest in the land of Schedule 2, that he purchased one-third of the land described in Schedule 2 in the benami of his son, defendant No. 1, and his wife Begumjan (since deceased) and the rest two-third of the land described in Schedule 2 was purchased by his two other brothers in the benami of their respective chosen persons, that at the time of purchasing the land of Schedule 2 the defendant No. 1 was a minor boy, that on attainment of majority he entrusted to the defendant No. 1 to look after his property, that sometime in 1954 his wife Begumjan died and that while he wanted to marry again the defendant No. 1 opposed that but he took 2nd wife and that he has 4 children out of 2nd marriage, that since the 2nd marriage relation between him and the defendant No. 1 was not cordial, that in the middle of Ashar, 1376 BS defendant No.1 disclosed that by alleged lease and the decree he has acquired interest in the land described in the Schedules 1(a) and 2(a) and thereupon he made enquiry to ascertain the correctness of the claim of the defendant No. 1 and got the trace of a fraudulent Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954, said to have been filed by the plaintiff and a compromise decree was passed therein. It was the case of the plaintiff that the decree that was obtained in Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954 was fraudulent since the said rent suit was not filed by him.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1, herein appellant, contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable as framed and that the same is hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The specific case of the defendant No. 1 was that plaintiff gifted the land described in Schedule 1(a) to him so that his sisters do not raise any claim on his demise and that to perfect that right the plaintiff filed Rent Suit No. 734 of 1954 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Cox's Bazar and finally, filed a compromise petition therein and the suit was decreed on the basis of the compromise petition, that defendant No. 1's mother purchased one-third land of the Schedule 2 with her own money for her own interest and also for his interest, that the plaintiff and his 2 brothers Emdad Miah and Amin Sharif had the rent receiving interest in the land of Schedule 2, that plaintiff and Emdad Miah filed Rent Suit No. 135 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif for the rent of their two-third shares against the defendant No. 1 and his mother and other purchasers, that heirs of Amin Sharif were made pro-defendants in the said rent suit, that plaintiff never sold any land to defendant No. 2 and that the plaintiff and the defendant No. 2 have no possession in the land in suit and that the defendant No. 1 is in possession of the land in suit.

4. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court on the findings (as to the relief as regard the land of schedule 1(a)). "It has been stated that defendant No. 1 took the signature of the plaintiff in two blank sheets of paper, on the allegation that they would be required to grant receipt to the Eksona tenants of the plaintiff and the defendant used those papers in the said Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954, but not a word stated by the PW 1 in his evidence with regard to those allegations. The plaintiff was a party in the said Rent Suit and also in the decree passed on the basis of the Solenama filed in the suit. The plaintiff has filed this suit for a declaration of his title to the suit land but he has not prayed for setting aside the decree passed in that suit or to get it declared null and void. The decree passed in that suit is a great obstacle in the way of getting declaration of plaintiff's title to the suit land. Without removing that obstruction the plaintiff cannot establish his title to himself, and (as regard Schedule 2(a)). "The evidence on the side of the plaintiff as regards the benami transaction is very meagre. On the other hand, we find from Exhibit D that the plaintiff and his brother defendant No.2 filed Rent Suit 135 of 1959 against the transferees of Exhibit A including the defendant No. 1 and his mother Begumjan and by impleading the heirs of Amin Sharif as pro-defendants for the rent of 1360-1362 BS. That suit was decreed vide Exhibit C. This is also another obstruction for getting a decree for declaration of plaintiff's title in Schedule 2(a) without removing that obstruction by praying for cancellation of the decree passed in that suit or by praying for a declaration that the decree passed in that suit was, void. In this suit the plaintiff has not made any such prayer. Begumjan died leaving the plaintiff as husband and other heirs. The plaintiff can get some declaration on the basis of his inheritance from Begumjan if he has been in possession of the same. But from the discussion below it will be seen that the plaintiff has not been able to prove his possession in the lands of Schedules 1 (a) and 2(a)." Exhibit A is the kabala of June 5, 1940 by which plaintiff and his two brothers are said to have purchased the land of Schedule 2 in the benami of their chosen persons. The trial Court, as to question of possession, on detailed discussion of the evidence of the parties arrived at the findings- "thus considering the evidence on both sides I find that the plaintiff has not been able to prove his possession in the suit land and, as such, the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act."

5. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff filed First Appeal as mentioned herein above and the High Court Division has allowed the appeal on the findings; "Defendant No. 1 failed to prove his allegation that the suit land was gifted to him by the plaintiff who, therefore, remained owner of the suit land in spite of the rent decrees which are admittedly collusive. With regard to the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge as to possession, we find it faulty. Those rent suits were between an old father and his son. So unless the son can prove his exclusive possession adverse to that of his father the legal presumption that the true owner is deemed to be in possession of the suit land cannot be brushed aside". It may be mentioned that the Rent Suit No. 135 of 1959 was between the plaintiff and one of his brothers on one side and on the other side the defendant No. 1 and the heirs of one of the brothers of the plaintiff.

6. In support of the appeal learned Counsel has submitted that the Court of first instance on consideration of the evidence, namely Exhibit A, the sale deed of June 5, 1940, Exhibit C, the decree in Rent Suit No. 135 of 1959, Exhibit D, the certified copy of the plaint of the Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954 and Exhibit F, the certified copy of the decree therein, having had dismissed the suit on the findings that the plaintiff did not make any prayer in the suit for setting aside the decrees passed in the rent suits, although he was a party to the said decrees and, as such, the plaintiff was not entitled to the decree for mere declaration of title to the land in suit without having those decrees set aside but the High Court Division reversed the decree of the trial Court on the view that because of the defence case itself those rent decrees being collusive the same in law need not be set aside for having a declaration by the plaintiff in his suit as framed. The learned Counsel has further submitted that the finding relating to possession of the trial Court being that plaintiff was out of possession and consequently suit being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the High Court Division was in error in interfering with the said positive finding of fact on a mere surmise that the relation between the plaintiff and the defendant being father and son the legal presumption of possession of the land in suit is in favour of true owner, the plaintiff.

7. The learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-respondent has made submissions supporting the judgment of the High Court Division. He has also submitted that plaintiff is entitled to the relief sought since the suit as has been framed is very much maintainable and that provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is in no way a bar in having the relief of declaration of title without seeking declaration as regard the decrees in rent suits.

8. Findings as to possession by the High Court Division is totally unsatisfactory and also unsustainable in that the High Court Division has reversed the finding of the trial Court as regard possession of the parties of the land in suit without discussing the evidence on record at all, but merely on assumption and hypothesis premised contrary to the materials on record. The trial Court on discussion of evidence of both sides arrived at the definite finding that plaintiff failed to prove his possession. The learned Counsel for the respondent could not point out any infirmity or legal flaw in the discussion and consideration of the evidence of the parties by the trial Court and in arriving at the definite finding that plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the land in suit. Plaintiff's suit was for mere declaration of title. Plaintiff having failed to prove his possession in the land suit, in law the suit was not maintainable. The High Court Division in reversing the finding of possession made by the Court of first instance, as already mentioned, did not at all discuss the evidence of the parties but proceeded on presumption and assumption, contrary to the materials on record. The finding of the High Court Division as to possession of the plaintiff is based on assumption in total disregard and non-consideration of the documentary as well as oral evidence. There can be no assumption or presumption in respect of a matter in issue in a suit, in the instant suit the question of possession, when the parties have led evidence relating to the said matter in issue in the suit. In a suit contention of the respective parties in respect of a matter having bearing in the ultimate decision in respect of a matter in issue in the suit, when there is evidence either documentary or oral or both the court in law is required to give its decision on the basis of the said evidence on record or, in other words, on the basis of materials either may be legal document(s) or oral evidence or both and if a decision is made in disregard of the evidence or materials on record the same is no decision in the eye of law or, in other words, is not sustainable in law. In the instant case, the High Court Division was in serious error in reversing finding of the trial Court as to possession upon assumption in disregard of the evidence on record.

9. The other moot point whether the plaintiff is required to avoid by seeking declaration against the decrees in the rent suits wherein he was party to have the relief sought in the instant suit for mere declaration of title. The Rent Suit No. 372 of 1954 relates to the land described in Schedule 1(a). Plaintiff's case in his pleading in respect of Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954 was that defendant No. 1 obtained his signature in blank sheet of papers representing that the same would be required to grant receipts to the Eksona tenants of the plaintiff and that those papers have been used for filing compromise petition by the defendant No. 1 in Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954, but in support of the said case he did not depose in court nor had led evidence by examining witness nor had placed any material on record. The case of the defendant No. 1 in respect of the Schedule l(a) that plaintiff gifted the said land to him and that to perfect the said gift plaintiff filed the rent suit and finally compromised the same with defendant No. 1.

10. The case of the plaintiff as to the land described in Schedule 2(a) is that he purchased the land of the said Schedule in the benami of his wife Begumjan and his son defendant No. 1. As against that case of the plaintiff, the case of the defendant No. 1 is that land described in Schedule 2(a) was purchased by his mother with her money for her benefit and for the benefit of her son the defendant No. 1. The plaintiff and his two brothers had rent receiving interest in the land described in the Schedule 2 and that the plaintiff and his one brother filed the Rent Suit No. 135 of 1959 impleading the defendant No. 1 and his mother and other purchasers including the heirs of plaintiff's another brother as regard the Land of Schedule 2 for realisation of the rent of the years 1360-62 BS and the same was decreed (vide Exhibit C).

11. So, it is seen that in both the rent suits plaintiff was a party and that rent suits were decreed admitting the title of the defendant No. 1 in respect of the land described in schedules 1(a) and 2(a). The trial Court dismissed the suit on the findings that in the absence of seeking declaration against the decrees in the rent suits the plaintiff cannot have the decree in the suit as framed. Admittedly, in spite of having full knowledge and particulars of the rent decrees the plaintiff has filed the instant suit without seeking any declaration as against the rent decrees wherein he was a party. The High Court Division reversed the findings of the trial Court as to that without seeking declaration against the rent decrees either null and void or cannot have the decree as sought in the suit filed by the plaintiff upon the finding that the rent decrees in question were “collusive and consequently those need not be set aside”. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that as against the decree in Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954 it was the case of the plaintiff that the defendant No. 1 obtained his signature in blank sheet of paper upon representing that those would be required for granting receipt to the Eksona lessee of the plaintiff and that later on defendant used those in the said rent suit, but in support thereof plaintiff has not deposed in court nor has led evidence of any kind. So, the question of obtaining rent decree collusively by the defendant No. 1 in Rent Suit No. 732 of 1954 was not established by the plaintiff. The other rent suit, being No. 135 of 1959 was brought by the plaintiff and one of his brothers against the defendant No. 1 and heirs of another brother of the plaintiff, in other words, against the transferees’ of kabala Exhibit. A for arrears of rent. This rent suit was decreed. So, it comes to that the plaintiff and his brother admitted the defendant No. 1, his mother Begumjan and the other transferees of the Exhibit A (kabala dated June 5, 1940) by which plaintiff and his two brothers said to have purchased the land of Schedule 2 from the tenants, in the benami of defendant No. 1, his mother and others, as the tenants of the land of Schedule 2 and consequent thereupon tenant of the land of Schedule 2(a). Defendant No. 2 has not contested the suit denying the genuineness of the rent decree in Rent Suit No. 135 of 1959.

<u>12. Learned Counsel for the appellant in support of his submissions that while admittedly plaintiff was a party in the rent decrees as such, In the absence of seeking avoidance either by way of a declaration that the rent suits were null and void or void ab initio the plaintiff in law cannot have the decree in the suit which is for mere declaration of title, has referred to the decision in the case of Sufia Khannam Chowdhury vs Faizun Nesa Chowdhury reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46 and the decision in the case of Abdul Hamid vs Dr Sadeque Ali Ahmed & ors reported in 21 DLR 507. In the case reported in 39 DLR it has been held- "Where a document has been adjudged voidable it will have to be avoided both by declaration and cancellation and if the document is adjudged void or void ab initio it need not be cancelled". In the aforesaid case respondent, whose suit was decreed, prayed for a declaration that the sale deed was void being brought about by fraud, collusive and misrepresentation. So, in a case where plaintiff is a party to a document or decree that has clouded his title to the property in suit, he is to seek declaration either of the way, i.e., that the document or decree is void or void ab initio or that for declaration as well as for cancellation. In the absence of seeking a declaration as against such document or decree he cannot have a declaration merely in respect of his title in respect of the property in suit even if he contends that his suit is not barred as per proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The plaintiff is to seek relief as against the document or decree to which he is a party. In the case reported in 21 DLR it has been observed; "there is a difference between a suit for cancellation of an instrument and a suit for declaration that the instrument is not binding upon the plaintiff, when the plaintiff seeks to establish a title to himself and cannot establish that title without removing an insuperable obstruction such as a decree to which he has been a party or a deed to which he has been a party, then quite clearly he must get that decree or deed canceled or declared void in toto and his suit is in substance a suit for the cancellation of the decree or deed, as the case may be, even though it be framed as a suit for a mere declaration". "In case of void document a person may rely on its invalidity as against himself without suing for its cancellation, and a suit by him for declaring its invalidity is not a suit for declaration with consequential relief. But in a case of document that is only voidable the case is otherwise as the party cannot impeach the arrangement effected by it without having it cancelled ... A suit for avoiding documents to which the plaintiff was a party on such grounds of fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence is a suit for declaration with consequential relief ... "</u>

13. From the aforesaid decision it is seen that a document or a decree to which one is a party and that the said document stands as a hurdle to a declaration of title as regard the property of the one to which the document or the decree relates, then one is to avoid that instrument in having declaration in respect of the property. The High Court Division was not correct, rather was in error, in observing that "decrees are collusive and consequently those need not be set aside" and that "in the language of the decision in 21 DLR 507 those decrees to be treated as non-existence". By the expression "those decrees" the learned Judges of the High Court Division have referred to the decrees in Rent Suits. The learned Judges of the said Division have incorrectly placed reliance on the decision reported in 21 DLR 507 for the proposition that collusive instrument "need not be set aside" in that instrument alleged to be collusive has to be adjudged so and that in case of an instrument wherein plaintiff is a party, then to have declaration to the property of the said instrument the plaintiff in law is required to avoid that in one of the ways i.e. declaration that the instrument is void or that declaration and cancellation.

<u>14. The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent in support of his submissions that the decrees in the rent suit having been found collusive by the High Court Division the same need not be set aside and that no declaration to adjudge the said decrees as collusive or null and void or void ab initio need be sought by the plaintiff in seeking a declaration of title in respect of the land in suit has referred to the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 46. This decision has no relevancy to the question involved in the present appeal. The learned Counsel has also referred to the decision reported in 21 DLR (SC) 365. In the reported decision, in the background of the facts of the case it has been observed; "At best, the relief claimed might be stretched to a declaration of legal character. Since the terms and conditions of the respondent's service were not regulated by any legal instrument, it could not be said that the declaration asked for by him was in relation to any legal character". The plaintiff of the reported case was an employee of a private bank and having been removed from the employment filed the suit seeking declaration that termination of his service was illegal. In that background of the facts of the case and the relief sought, it has been held in the reported decision that the relief in the suit "could not be covered by the provisions of section 42". So, this decision has no relevancy to the point or question of law involved in the instant case. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case reported in AIR 1924 (Cal) 411 and 17 DLR 119. In the case reported in AIR 1924 Cal 411 amongst others, one of the matters was what the expression "further relief" in the proviso to section 42 of Specific Relief Act, 1908 means. In the case report in 17 DLR plaintiff filed the suit (a) for declaration that certain documents were void ab initio and that the defendants have acquired no interest in the suit premises by virtue of aforesaid documents, (b) that the documents have been brought into existence by forgeries and false personation and that no consideration did pass for the said documents. The suit was filed with fixed court fee. The learned Subordinate Judge was of opinion that plaintiff was to pay ad valorem Court fee as the plaintiff in the form of declaration was seeking some other relief which was no doubt of consequential relief and thereupon directed plaintiff to pay ad valorem court fee. As against that plaintiff moved the High Court and obtained a Rule. The matter came up before a Division Bench which differed from the decision given by another Division Bench arid referred the matter to the Full Bench. Questions formulated for answers (1) in a suit for declaration that certain document was void ab initio as it was not executed by the plaintiff but executed by somebody else by falsely personifying him to be the executant and, as such, the document has not affected the right, title and interest of the plaintiff. Whether he is bound to pay court fee under section 7(iv) (c) of the Court Fees Act as a suit for declaratory decree with consequential relief or under Article 17 of Schedule II of the Court Fees Act as a suit for bare declaration, (II) whether in such a suit plaintiff is to ask for consequential relief as contemplated under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and if he has not specifically asked for such a relief, whether he should be held, by necessary implication, that there is a prayer for such a relief, because it comes under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, (III) if a suit is framed as one for declaration that certain document is void, should it be treated as one coming under section 42 of Specific Relief Act or as one coming under section 39 of the Act. The answers to the questions were as follows;</u>

<u>"1) First part- No, Second part-Yes,</u>

<u>2) No.</u>

3) It falls under both the sections. The first part of the prayer 'A' falls under section 39 and second part of the

said prayer under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act".

15. So, the facts of those cases and the questions of law decided therein were quite different and, as such, the same are also not relevant in the instant case.

16. In view of the discussion made herein above we are of the view that the plaintiff cannot have the relief sought in the suit, i.e. mere declaration of title, in the absence of seeking declaration either that the rent decrees were not binding on him being collusive or void ab initio. The plaintiff has not framed his suit in the manner as was required by law.

In the result the appeal is allowed. The judgment and the decree of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 343 of 1970 are set aside and that the judgment and the decree of the Court of Subordinate Judge in Other Class Suit No. 35 of 1969 are restored. There is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mainul Hosein with Md Shamim-ul-Alam ----- For the Petitioner. 
Abdur Rezzaque Khan, Additional Attorney-General, with Anwarul Azim Khair, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For respondent No.2.
parties:
Salahuddin Talukder (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Arayes Uddin J : Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause why section 8 of the impugned Act being Non-Cadre Class I and II Gazetted Officers (Customs, Excise and VAT) Appointment and Service Terms and Conditions Act, 2000 (Act XX of 2000) should not be declared to be ultra vires of Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, illegal and without lawful authority and why the impugned order No. 7(2) Shu: Va: Pro- 3/2000/613 dated 20-8-2000 as corrected by order dated 28-8-2000 collectively marked as Annexure-E to the writ petition issued by respondent No.3 under section 8 of the impugned Act should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Fact necessary to dispose of this Rule, in brief, is that petitioner was appointed Appraiser in the Customs House, Chittagong on 1-9-1990 under the Recruitment Rules of the Principal Appraisers and Appraisers (Customs Department) Recruitment Rules, 1984 and that in Office Memo No. 1(11) Admn. 11/83/1007 dated 26-6-1983 issued by the National Board of Revenue the organizational setup of the Collectorate of Customs, Customs House. Chittagong has been shown in lineal order wherein the organisational hierarchy has been maintained. That the post of Appraiser in that organisational heirarchy has been shown at Serial No. 16 and the post of Inspector at Serial No. 17 and that of the Office Superintendent at serial No. 18, Preventive Officer at Serial No. 20 and the Stenographer at Serial No. 23. That the duties and the Recruitment Rules of these posts are also separate. As per that organisational set.up of the Customs House, Chittagong in Memo No. 1(11) Admn. 11/83/1007 dated 26-6-1983 (Annexure-B) Government increased the scale of pay of the Preventive Officer from Taka 425-1035 to Taka 770-1135. A group of promoted Appraisers namely, Azizul Haque Sikder and others claimed seniority over the directly recruited Appraisers on the basis of the above Memo dated 26-6-1983 stating that their scales of pay as Preventive Officer has been raised and that their Pay Scale is similar to the post of Appraiser and their promotion as Appraisers were merely paper transactions and that their case went up to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and the Appellate Division by its Judgment and order dated 25-3-1997 (passed in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 1995) dismissed the appeal with the observations-

"........the appellants argument that by receiving the same scale of pay the Preventive Officer and Appraisers have become members of the same grade with effect from 26-6-1983 and therefore the Preventive Officers became senior as a Class to those who have been appointed directly as Appraisers after 26-6-1983 cannot be accepted for the simple reason that these two classes of officers are graded differently and these posts have not been treated as equivalent posts, although they are drawing the same scale of pay. Nothing has been shown to establish that the posts of Appraisers and Preventive Officers, have been amalgamated. "

3. That the Secretary of the Public Service Commission vide memo No. SR 3/2 R-50/99/345 dated 1-2-2000 informed the respondent No.2, the National Board of Revenue, that the draft law contains many contradictions and anomalies. The Commission also recommenced some changes, but at this stage the Government dropped the idea of passing any law for amalgamation of various posts in Customs but passed the impugned Act in the name of changing service terms and conditions under Article 133 of the Constitution (vide Annexure-'C' to the writ petition) that the post of Appraisers and Inspectors are distinct and separate from each other. Their nature of duty and functions are different. These posts cannot be grouped together in two categories without amalgamation as has been held by the Honourable Appellate Division of this Court in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 1995 as such, the impugned Act, specially section 8 of the Act (Act XX of 2000) is violative of the Services (Re-organisation and Conditions) Act, 1975 and also violative of Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution. That section 8 of the impugned Act is also violative of the petitioner's fundamental right to be treated equally before law as contemplated under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution inasmuch as the petitioner has been discriminated with other Government Servants by placing him to hold a post of lower grade simply in the name of transfer and that in the seniority list dated 25-5-1998 he was at Serial No. 48 and one Abdul Gani who joined the service on 4-6-1978 as a Preventive Officer and subsequently promoted to the post of Appraiser on 31-12-1991 was shown at Serial No. 53, one Mr Omar Farouk who joined the service on 11-5-1981 as Preventive Officer and was subsequently promoted to Appraiser on 31-12-1991 was shown at Serial No. 54, and one Mr Rashedul Hassan Bhuiyan who joined on 6-11-1983 as a Preventive Officer and subsequently was promoted to the post of Appraiser on 13-8-1995 was shown at Serial No. 64. But after passing of the impugned Act (Act of XX of 2000) the National Board of Revenue in his Memo No. 2(13) Shu. Va. Pro-3/84/103 dated 4-2- 2001 ordered that the seniority of some Appraisers were to be counted from the date of their joining in the service as Preventive Officers. As a result petitioner lost his seniority to a number of Appraisers who joined the service originally as Preventive Officer, long before that promotion but seniority of the petitioner has been taken away by passing the impugned Act and that Act does not empower the Government to claim that the post of Preventive Officer/Appraiser/Inspector and Intelligence Officer are of equal status, as such, the posts are not inter-transferable on the ground of mere classification of some posts as 2nd Class Gazetted having equal scales of pay. That the impugned Act XX of 2000 was passed without paying any heed to the recommendations of the Public Service Commission. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned Act XX of 2000 dated 6-7-2000 Vide Annexure-'D' and the order of transfer passed on 20-8-2000 vide Annexure-'E' to the writ petition petitioner moved this Court and obtained this present Rule.

4. Respondent No. 2 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made by the petitioner in his writ petition. In the affidavit-in-opposition respondent No. 2 has stated that the posts of Appraiser, Inspector, Preventive Officer and Intelligence Officer are now guided by the same Service Rules and the petitioner being an employee of the same grade resorted to this writ petition only to create an embargo on his transfer with other officials though the order of transfer has been made in accordance with the law and Act XX of 2000 is not violative of the Articles 133 and 136 to the Constitution. That the Appellate Division decided those cases in view of the old rules Moreover, Government has filed Review Petition No. 21 of 1997 against the judgment passed in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 1995 and that judgment should be read with the judgment passed in Review Petition No. 21 of 1997. It has been stated that petitioner has not been demoted rather he was transferred to a post of equal rank, status and pay. Respondent No. 2 by filing a supplementary affidavit in opposition stated that the notification dated 25-4-1992 published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 14-5-1992 the pest of Superintendent of Customs and Excise and that of Inspector of Customs Excise have been upgraded as Gazetted 1st Class (non cadre) and Gazetted Second Class posts respectively and by another notification dated 6th July, 1992 published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 2nd July, 1992, the post of Superintendent and Intelligence Officer of the Directorate of Customs Intelligence and Investigation have been upgraded to Gazetted post Class-I (non Cadre) and Gazetted Class-Il posts respectively. That posts of Superintendent, (Superintendent Preventive Service) and Principal Appraiser and the post of Preventive Officer and Appraiser have also been upgraded to Class-I and Class-II (non Cadre) respectively. That prior to 24-8-1992 the pay scale of Superintendent of Customs and Excise was Taka 2300-4480 which has been raised to Taka 2850-5155 and pay scale of Inspector of Customs and Excise was Taka 1725-3725 which has been raised to Taka 2300-3380 by Notification dated 24-8-1992 and in the same way the pay scale of Superintendent of Customs (Intelligence and Investigation Directorate) was Taka 2300-5155 and the pay scale of Intelligence Officer was Taka 1725- 3725 which has been raised to Taka 2300-4480 by Notification dated 4-3-1995 and by another Notification of the same date the pay scales of Superintendent, (Preventive Service) and Principal Appraiser have been raised to Taka 2850-5155 and that the Inspector, Preventive Officer and Appraiser are of equal scale of pay and there is no bar to transfer them from one post to another for better and efficient management of the Department for collection of more revenue. That the impugned Act has been made on bonafide ground for public interest to meet the exigencies of the services.

5. Mr Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the post of Inspector, Preventive Officer and Appraiser are separate and distinct. That their pay scale is also separate and distinct and they were guided by the separate service rules. He has further submitted that their nature of works are different as such, those posts cannot be grouped together and section 8 of the impugned Act is violative of Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution as mere framing of new Service Rules does not mean the amalgamation or unification of the Services. He has further submitted that section 8 of the impugned Act is also violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution and that the said Act gives the authority arbitrary power in the absence of any guideline and without Rules under section 12 for securing the purpose of the impugned Act and that the transfer of the petitioner as Inspector, in place of Appraiser is a demotion without any departmental proceeding and a violation of natural justice. He has further submitted that in the Schedule of the impugned Act (Act XX of 2000) the post of Inspector/Appraiser/Preventive Officer/Intelligence Officer have been shown as Gazetted Class II posts of the same category the learned Advocate submitted that only by enhancing the pay of the Inspector, Preventive Officer, Intelligence Officer without making any amalgamation of the services of that Department inasmuch as the services belonged to different categories they cannot be treated to be of equal rank and status. Furthermore, the promotee Officers claimed their seniority not from the date of their promotion but from the date of their joining in the service as Inspector, Preventive Officer, Intelligence Officer. The seniority list prepared by the Department earlier has been altered and that the petitioner's serial in the seniority list dated 25-5- 1998 was at Serial No. 48 and that of Mr Abdul Gazi who joined the service on 14-6-1978 as Preventive Officer was at serial No. 53 and subsequently, on 31-12-1991 was promoted to the post of Appraiser, one Mr Omar Farouk who joined the service on 11-5-1981 as Preventive Officer and subsequently on 31-12-1991 was promoted to the post of Appraiser was shown at serial No. 54; and one Mr Rashedul Hassan Bhuiyan, who joined the service on 6-11- 1983 as Preventive Officer and subsequently promoted or. 13-8-1983 to the post of Appraiser was shown at serial No. 64 and after passing the impugned Act, XX of 2000 the seniority of the prornotee Appraisers such as Abdul Gani and Omar Farouk have been counted from the date of their joining as Preventive Officer. As a result they have been shown senior to the petitioner and the seniority of the petitioner has been taken away for no fault of his own which is the violation of his fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. He has further submitted that the impugned Gazette Notification dated 2nd July, 1992 does not empower the Government to unify the posts of Preventive Officer, Appraiser, Inspector and Intelligence Officer in one service by merely changing the terms and conditions of their Services without amalgamating the same as pc. the provision of section 4 of the Services (Reorganisation and Conditions) Act, 1975. The learned Advocate has contended that mere classification of some posts at 1 st Class Gazetted or Second Class Gazetted making equal scales of pay do not make the posts inter-transferable without amalgamation and unification of the services under the Constitution. It has been submitted that the unification of the post of Inspector, Preventive Officer to that with the Appraiser by making the post Gazetted Class-II is itself illegal and failure to follow the proper law for such unification. The power law is section 4 of the Services (Re-organisation and Conditions) Act, 1975 (Act XXXII of 1975). That the impugned Act XX of 2000 was passed without paying any heed to the recommendations of the Public Service Commission vide Memo No. Ba. SKaS/SR-3/2 R- 50/99/5561 dated 22-11-1999 in which the Public Service Commission pointed out certain anomalies in the impugned proposed Act before its enactment. He has further submitted that incorporating the post of Inspector, Appraiser, Preventive Officer, Intelligence Officer in the same category in the Schedule of Act XX of 2000 respondent No.2 has been shown to be in equal rank, status and grade and his service has been made inter-transferable with other posts without making the services amalgamation which is violative of Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution. To that effect the learned Advocate has referred the case of Azizul Huq Sikder and others vs Collector of Customs. Chittagong and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 172 and submitted that their Lordships of the Appellate Division in that case held that mere raising the pay scale of the Inspector and Preventive Officer cannot be treated that they are of equal grade with the Appraisers as they have been graded separately and their nature of work with job duty are also separate. The learned Advocate has specifically referred Para-8 of that judgment in which their Lordships clearly observed that Preventive Officer-cannot claim upgradation by implementation of that rule. It must be done by an Act made by the Government and published by Gazette Notification. He has further submitted that in the present case Government do not amalgamate the services of the Inspector, Preventive Officer and Appraisers in one category by invoking the power section 4 of the Services (Reorganisation and Conditions) Act (Act XXXII of 1975).

6. Lastly, the learned Advocate submitted that the petitioner has challenged the vires of section 8 of Act XX of 2000 under which respondent No.2 has passed his transfer order as Inspector, instead of Appraiser changing his designation from Appraiser to Inspector which, in fact, is demotion and by giving retrospective effect to the seniority of the Inspector, Preventive Officer and Intelligence Officer from the date of their respective appointment in the service has reduced the seniority of the petitioner. The learned Advocate has submitted that the petitioner challenged the vires of Act XX of 2000 as such, the Administrative Tribunal is not empowered to give any relief to the petitioner though apparently it seems to be a case of the Terms and Conditions of the service of the petitioner. In this respect the learned Advocate has relied on the decision of the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111; Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha reported in 50 DLR (AD) 166 and the case of Delwar Hussain Miah vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120.

7. Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan, the Additional Attorney-General, on behalf of respondent No.2, has submitted that respondent No.2 did not violate the provisions of law and section 8 of the Act XX of 2000 is not violative of Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution. He has submitted that the scales of pay of the Inspector/Preventive Officer/Intelligence Officer of Customs have been enhanced and made equal to the scale of pay of the Appraisers to bring uniformity in their pay scales and these posts have been made of equal status and that petitioner cannot have any grievance against his seniority and transfer order which are related to the Terms and Conditions of his service. His proper remedy lies ill the Administrative Tribunal and not in the writ jurisdiction. He has further submitted that under Article 133 of the Constitution Government is empowered to regulate the appointment and conditions of services of the persons in the Service of the Republic and accordingly, by Act XX of 2000 Government has changed the Terms and Conditions of the Services of the petitioner and others for proper administration and for the better collection of revenue they have been transferred from one post to another by the authority and there is no malafide in the impugned order of transfer passed in Memo No. 7(2) Shu: Bha Pro-3/2000/613 dated 20-8-2000 vide Annexure-'E' to the writ petition. Finally, the learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that the petitioner on test basis has filed this writ petition without any merit as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

<u>8. We have perused the records, the affidavits, affidavit in-opposition, the impugned annexures and heard the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties. It is admitted that petitioner was directly appointed Appraiser on 1-9-1990 in the Customs House, Chittagong under the Recruitment Rules on 1-9-1990 under the recruitment Rules, of the Principal Appraiser and Appraiser. (Customs Department) Recruitment Rules, 1984 vide Annexure-A to the writ petition and that by memo No. 1(11) Admn 11/83/1007 dated 26-6-1983 the National Board of Revenue issued the circular changing the organisational set-up of the Collectorate of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and in the said set-up the post of Appraiser has been shown at Serial No. 16 and the post of Inspector at Serial No. 17 and the post of Superintendent as Serial No. 18 and the Preventive Officer at Serial No. 20 and the Stenographer at Serial No. 23. It is found that Inspector of the Customs Department are one grade lower to the Appraiser. As per the Organisation set-up made in Memo No. 1(11) Admn. 11/83/1007 dated 26-6-1983 (vide Annexure-'B' to the writ petition) Government enhanced the scale of pay of the Preventive Officer from Taka 425-1035 to Taka 470-1135 and a group of promoted Appraisers namely, Azizul Haque Sikder and others claimed seniority over the directly recruited Appraisers on the basis of the said Memo dated 26-6-1983 stating that while the scales of pay of Preventive Officer has been raised and made equal to the scales of pay of Appraisers their promotion as Appraiser are merely a formal paper transaction as such, they claimed seniority from the date of their appointment in the Services. They tiled writ petition claiming equal status in view of' the enhancement in their scales of pay and the matter went up to the Honourable Appellate Division which has been reported in 49 DLR (AD) 172 (Azizul Haque Sikder and others vs Collector of Customs Chittagong and others). In that case their Lordships observed:</u>

<u>"the order of the National Board of Revenue dated 26-6-1983 is only a paper transaction showing the implementation of the approved organisational set-up of the Collectorate of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong wherein Appraisers are shown in grade 16 although the scale is Taka 470-1135. In the same list Assistant, Inspector, Master (Class-I) are placed in different grades although the scale of pay of those officers are the same to that of the Appraisers and Preventive Officer, Therefore, it is apparent that by raising the scale of pay the Preventive Officers and Appraisers have become members of the same grade with effect from 26-6-1983 and therefore, the Preventive Officers became senior as Class II officer to those who have been appointed directly as Appraisers after 26-6-1983 cannot be accepted for the simple reasons that the Class-II Officers are created differently and these posts have not been treated as equivalent post, although they are drawing the same scale of pay. Nothing has been shown to us to establish that the post of Appraisers and Preventive Officers have been amalgamated. The Appraisers and Preventive Officers are not only graded separately but they are also discharging separate functions."</u>

<u>From the above observation of the Honourable Appellate Division it has been finally settled that Appraisers and Preventive Officer are not of the same grade though their scale of pay has been made equal by the Government Furtuermore, their service has not been amalgamated as per section 4 of the Service Re-organisation and Conditions Act, 1975 (Act XXXII of 1975). Without amalgamation of their services they cannot be treated to be of the same grade. In that judgment their Lordships observed that Preventive Officers cannot claim equal status by receiving the same pay without amalgamation of their Services by proper enactment. The Preventive Officer, Appraisers, Superintendent, Inspector and Intelligence Officers cannot be placed and treated in the same grade and equal status till their services are not amalgamated under section 4 of the Services (Reorganisation and Conditions) Act, 1975.</u>

<u>9. By the impugned Act XX of 2000 Government has reorganised the service conditions of the Appraisers, Inspectors and others who are out of cadre. In that Act the services of the Inspector, Preventive Officer, and Appraisers have been made inter-transferable under section 8 of the impugned Act (Act XX of 2000). From Annexure-C to the writ petition it is found that prior to the enactment of this Act Government sought opinion of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission and the Bangladesh Public Service Commission on 1-2-2000 in Memo No. SR 3/2 R-50/99/345 dated 1-2-2000 opined that without amalgamation of the services the proposed Act (i.e. Act XX of 2000) would be improper and it will create anomaly in the services of the Appraiser, Inspector and Superintendent arid the Commission suggested that before passing Act XX of 2000 the Services of the Preventive Officer, Inspector, Appraiser and Intelligence Officer should be amalgamated and the Service Rules and Recruitment Rules should be amended. We find that the opinion of Bangladesh Public Service Commission was not adhered to and ignoring that opinion the impugned Act XX of 2000 was passed and by section 8 the Services of the Appraisers, Inspectors, Preventive Officers and Intelligence Officers have been made interchangeable and in transferable. Not only that the promoted Appraisers who were lower in seniority to the directly recruited Appraisers were given seniority from the date of their appointment as a result the directly recruited Appraisers have become junior in service though they were senior to the promoted Appraisers the seniority list complied by the Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong in Nathi No. S/Estab/ 10/27/12/339(48) dated 25-5-1998 vide annexure F to the writ petition. Copy of the seniority list were also sent to the concerned officers including this petitioner to ascertain the correctness of their seniority and to file petition in case of any mistake. The learned Advocate for the petitioner vehemently challenged the seniority list prepared subsequently by the authority showing this petitioner in lower position to that of the promotees. He argued that this demotion is a violation of the fundamental rights of the petitioner guaranteed under Article 31 of the Constitution. The learned Advocate has contended that the petitioner has been demoted to his post without any Departmental proceeding and for no fault of his own. The learned Additional Attorney General, on behalf of the respondent No.2, found it very difficult to brush aside the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner since the authority published the seniority list earlier showing the petitioner senior to the Promoted Appraisers and it was notified to all concerned. Furthermore, the learned Additional Attorney-General could not overcome the decision of the Honourable Appellate Division pronounced in the case of Azizul Haque Sikder and others vs Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 172. In that case their Lordships in unequivocal language observed that Appraisers, Preventive Officers and Inspectors are of separate grade though their scales of pay may be the same and their services cannot be inter-changed in between themselves as the Appraisers are of the higher grade to that of the Inspectors and Preventive Officers and accordingly, their Lordships opined that if the Government wants to make their services at par, the Government is to amalgamate their services and to frame rules accordingly. Without amalgamating their services they cannot be treated equal and their services inter-transferable. Accordingly, section 8 of the impugned Act XX of 2000 is found to be violative to Articles 133 and 136 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>10. The last submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General was that the remedy of the petitioner lies before the Administrative Tribunal as the relief claimed is related to the Terms and Conditions of his service. In reply to that, Mr Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, placed his submission that petitioner not only challenged the transfer order and his seniority but has also challenged the vires of law i.e. section 8 of the impugned Ad which is beyond the iurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. To that effect reliance has been placed on the decisions of the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111; Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha reported in 51 DLR (AD) 166 and the case of Delwar Hussain Miah vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120. In the case of Mujibur Rahman their Lordships heid that, "A person in the Service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)." In the case of Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and in the case of Delwar Hussain Miah vs Bangladesh. the same decision has been given by the Honourable Appellate Division. From the decisions it is crystal clear that since the petitioner has challenged the vires of law i.e. section 8 of Act XX of 2000, the present writ petition is entertainable in this Court and the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to strike down section 8 of the impugned Act and, as such, the arguments and the submissions placed by the learned Additional Attorney General in view of those decisions is not acceptable in the present case. Article 133 of the Constitution provides for enactment of law relating to the appointment and service terms and conditions of person in the service of the Republic and the President is competent to make rules regulating such appointment and condition of service of such appointees till provisions are made by or under any law. In the instant case on perusal of section 8 of the Act XX of 2000 it appears that the services of different Cadres and Categories have been amalgamated and the same has nothing to do with the appointment or terms of the service as contemplated by Article 133 of the Constitution.</u>

11. Article 136 of the Constitution provides for reorganisation of service by creation, amalgamation or unification of services by enactment of law and for such purpose the Services (Reorganisation and Conditions) Act, 1975 (Act XXXII of 1975) has already been promulgated and accordingly, this amalgamation of services made as appearing in the Schedule of the Act XX of 200 under section 8 thereof can only be made under the provisions of Act XXXII of 1975. Thus, it appears to us that section 8 of Act XX of 2000 made under Act 133 of the Constitution is misconceived and cannot be maintained for want of jurisdiction. Considering all these facts and circumstances we find merit in this Writ petition.

12. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

In view of section 8 of the impugned Non- Cadre, Class I and II Gazetted Officers (Customs, Excise and VAT) Appointment and Service Terms and Conditions Act, 2000 being Act XX of 2000 is declared to be ultra vires of Article 133 of the Constitution as such, illegal and without lawful authority and the impugned order No. 7(2) Shu: Va: Pro-3/2000/613 dated 20-8-2000 as corrected by Order dated 28-8-2000 collectively marked as Annexure-E to the writ petition issued by the respondent No. 3 under section 8 of the aforesaid impugned Act are declared to have been made without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and section 13 of the aforesaid impugned Act repealing the Service Rules of the Principal Appraiser, Appraiser and others so far relates to the petitioner is hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority.

End.

lawyer:
M Saleem Ullah, Advocate ----- For the Appellant.
