parties:
Halima Akhter Khaton and others ------ Appellants
Vs
Md Salauddin Khan and Others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Afzal Hossain Ahmed J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal, at the instance of the defendant Nos. 1-5, is directed against the, order Nos. 2 and 3 both dated 13-11-2002 allowing the prayer under Order XL rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointing a receiver, order No.6 dated 26-11-2002, order No.7 dated 28-11-2002 and order No.9 dated 1-12-2002 rejecting the prayer for recalling the writ of appointment of receiver passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 174 of 2002.

2. Facts necessary to dispose of this appeal, in brief, are that, the plaintiff (respondent No. 1) brought the aforesaid suit on 6-11-2002 against the defendants for declaration of title and partition of the suit properties mentioned in the schedule "Ka" and "Kha" of the plaint. It was claimed in the plaint that the suit property as shown in the schedule "Ka" and "Kha" of the plaint belonged to the plaintiff's father Dr Mofizuddin Khan who after peacefully possessing the suit properties died leaving behind the plaintiff and the defendants No. 1 to 6 as his heirs. That the defendants live in the suit houses and also possess and manage the same. That the plaintiff having found inconveniences in joint possession and management of the suit properties has been constrained to bring the suit for declaration of title and partition of the suit properties. That the plaintiff after filing the suit on 6-1-2002 filed a petition under Order XL, rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of a receiver in respect of the suit properties on 13-11-2002 and on the same day the court below ordered for, issuing notice calling upon the defendants to show cause against that petition and on the same day the trial Court, without awaiting for return of service of notice and without giving the defendants an opportunity of being heard in the matter, arbitrarily appointed a receiver in respect of the suit properties vide order No. 2 dated 13-11-2002. Thereafter, the trial Court rejected the defendants' prayer for recalling the Writ issued to the receiver vide the subsequent impugned orders.

3. The defendant-appellants' case, in brief, is that the plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit on 6-11-2002 by suppressing facts and by impleading some untrue and concocted stories and thereafter, with ulterior motive filed a petition on 13-11-2002 under Order XL, rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of a receiver in respect of the suit properties. The trial Court upon that petition issued notice to the defendants calling upon them to show cause within 7 days as to why such appointment of a receiver as prayed by the plaintiff should not be made and the Court below, without awaiting for service of those notices upon the defendants and without giving them an opportunity of being heard in the matter, hastily passed the impugned order No. 2 appointing one Tofazzal Hossain, Sheristadar of the said court, as receiver in respect of the suit properties and on the same day on prayer of the newly appointed receiver Md Tofazzal Hossain, the court below passed the impugned order No. 3 appointing one Mr Tarun Chandra Dey, Advocate, who was previously an employee of the Judge's Court, Dhaka as receiver in place of former receiver Mr Md Tofazzal Hossain. Thereafter, the defendants filed a petition before the court below under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for recalling the writ of appointment of receiver but the court below rejected the same vide order No.6 dated 26-11-2002 and order No.7 dated 28-11-2002. Thereafter, the defendants filed a petition for staying operation of the aforesaid orders with a view to allow them an opportunity to seek for remedial measures before the higher Court against those orders but the Court below also rejected that prayer vide Order No.9 dated 1-12-2002.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid impugned orders defendant Nos. 1-5 have preferred this appeal.

5. Heard Mr M Saleem Ullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants and Mr Ismail Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents.

6. Mr M Saleem Ullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submits that all the defendant Nos. 2-6 as well as the plaintiff executed a power of attorney in favour of their mother, the defendant No. 1, giving her authority to control and manage the suit properties mentioned in schedule "Ka" and "Kha" of the plaint and admittedly, all the defendants live in the suit premises and in such circumstances, the plaintiff with a view to oust them from the possession and control of the suit properties filed the suit and obtained the impugned order No. 2 dated 13-11-2002 for appointment of receiver and the court below passed the impugned order appointing a receiver in respect of the suit properties without the consent of the defendant Nos. 1-6 who are in actual possession of the suit properties and also without giving them an opportunity of being heard in the matter and thereby the court below erred in law resulting in an error in the decision.

<u>7. Mr M Saleem Ullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, in appreciation of his submissions, has referred to the decisions in the case of Foez Ahmed Chowdhury andanother vs Bakhtiar Ahmed Chowdhury and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 97, Mahmudun Nabi Chowdhury vs Mahfuzun Nabi Chowdhury reported in 1984 BLD 268 and Md Ali Akbor Ali and others vs Shakhina Begum and others reported in 11 BLT 1. In the aforesaid decision reported in 36 DLR (AD) 97 their Lordships of the Appellate Division while deciding a case under Order XL, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure have held which runs thus:- "Appointment of a receiver in respect of the property in partition suit-Not to be ordered except by the consent of the parties or due to some special circumstance such as danger to the property.</u>

8. As a general rule, the appointment or a receiver in a partition suit has not met with the approval of the court. The existence of a dispute offers no ground whatsoever for appointing a receiver."

<u>9. Their Lordships while deciding the aforesaid case have taken into consideration the case of Gobinda Narain Rao Desai vs Vallah Rao Desai reported in AIR 1920, Bombay, 321 wherein it has been observed which runs thus:-in a partition suit between the members of a joint family the court will not appoint a receiver except by consent and specially where the family property consists of land. Special circumstances must be proved before the court will make such appointment. The plaintiff must satisfy the court that the property in possession of the defendant is in danger of being wasted."</u>

10. The reason that a plaintiff has a prima facie case does not establish the necessity for appointment of a receiver. Such appointment may be made if it is considered just and convenient. Relief by way of appointment of a receiver is discretionary with the court. Appointment of a receiver cannot be claimed as a matter or course. Without allegations of wastage or destruction or property, it requires to be proved that not merely the plaintiffs interest but also the interest of all the parties in the suit and the property concerned need be protected. The power to appoint a receiver as conferred by Order XL, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure should, therefore, be sparingly used. The provisions for the appointment of a receiver is to be considered as one of the harshest remedies for the enforcement of rights to property. But it appears to us that the court below while entertaining the impugned petition under Order XL, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the plaintiff failed to appreciate the necessary legal requirements of the aforesaid provision of law and passed the impugned order appointing a receiver in respect of the suit properties in the instant partition suit without consent of the defendants 1-6 who are in possession thereof and also without giving them an opportunity of being heard in the matter. The learned Advocate for the appellants next submits that, the defendant No. 1, the mother of the defendant Nos. 2-6 as well as of the plaintiff: aged about 65 years, has been suffering from cancer and undergoing medical treatment and the trial Court by the impugned order appointing receiver have put the defendants into devastating circumstances and in guise it is an order to dispossess the defendants from the suit properties.

11. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case as referred to above the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellants attract for regardful appreciation.

12. The Learned Advocate appearing for the respondent could not make any convincing argument to discard the submissions made by his opponent Counsel as referred to above.

<u>13. Considering all the above aspects of the matter we find no reason for appointment of a receiver in the instant case, particularly when the court below did not find any mismanagement or damage to the property in question and hold that the court below has erred in law in the decision appointing a receiver in the instant Partition Suit occasioning failure of Justice.</u>

<u>14. As such the impugned order No.2 dated 13-11-2002 and other impugned orders passed subsequently in connection with the appointment of a receiver are not sustainable in the eye of law. This view also finds support from the decisions reported in 1984 BLD 268 and 11 BLT 1 which are also based on the same principle as was decided by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Foez Ahmed Chowdhury and another vs Bakhtiar Ahmed Chowdhury and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 97 as referred to above.</u>

In the result, this appeal is allowed on contest without any order as to costs. The impugned order Nos. 2 and 3 both dated 13-11-2002, order No. 6 dated 26-11-2002, order No. 7 dated 28-11-2002 and order No. 9 dated 1-12-2002 passed by the court below in Title Suit No. 174 of 2002 are hereby set aside.

End.

lawyer:
Sadananda Rana, Advocate on behalf of Chandi Charan Paul, Advocate ------ For the Petitioners. 
No one------For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Chand Mia and others ------ Petitioners
Vs
MA Rajput Ghosh Bahadur & others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
In this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the petitioner challenges the judgment and order No. 19 dated 1-6-1994 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Nesarabad, Pirojpur in Title Suit No. 2 of  1959 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Nesarabad, District Pirojpur rejecting the petitioner's application under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Chandi Charan Paul, being unable to be present in Court due to his illness, his friend Mr Sadananda Rana, learned Advocate, sought permission to move on his behalf and I accordingly, allowed him to make submissions of behalf of the petitioners.

3. The brief facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the instant Rule are that the predecessor of the petitioners, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 2 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Pirojpur, now Assistant Judge's Court, Nesarabad, Pirojpur, praying for declaration of Title of the suit land. The plaintiff contended, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 0.01 acre appertaining to CS Khatian No. 261 and CS Plot No. 19 corresponding to RS Plot No.313 recorded in RS Khatian No. 243 and SA Khatian No. 447 of Mouza Kourikhara, PS Nesarabad, District Pirojpur was acquired by the predecessor of the plaintiffs by oral lease in the month of Baishak, 1360 BS. There was a subsequent registered dakhila dated 27-4-54. It is further stated that the RS and SA record of rights having been wrongly prepared in the name of defendant No. 1, who claimed false title to the suit land on 20th Kartick 1365 BS, the predecessor of the petitioners was constrained to file the suit for declaration of title. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 2-6-1959 by the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge and the plaintiffs title to the suit land was declared. However, the suit land, although it was described correctly in the body and the prayer portion of the plaintiffs plaint, the current Plot No. 313 was wrongly written in schedule "kha" to the plaint as plot No. 331. Hence the petitioners, as heirs of the plaintiff to the earlier suit for declaration, filed the application for correction under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 27-11-1993. The learned Senior Assistant Judge by his impugned order was pleased to reject the said application on the grounds that the plaintiff has sought correction of the plaint after 35 years from the date of the decree, which is not acceptable in law and is beyond the jurisdiction of his Court. Thus he rejected the application, which is now challenged before this Court.

<u>4. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that there is no period of limitation mentioned in section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, the finding of the learned Senior Assistant Judge that the application is not acceptable, having been filed after 35 years from the date of the decree, is itself an error of law. The learned Advocate submits that section 152 is an inherent power of the Courts to correct mistakes occurring in the judgments, decrees and orders. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Ibrahim Sk and others vs Janab Sk alias Janab Ali Sk & others reported in 29 DLR 81. It was held in that case as follows:</u>

<u>"Where a mistake has crept into the description of an item of property in the plaint schedule and the mistake has been carried over in the decree the court certainly has powers to correct the error in the decree. If the Court is satisfied that the mistake made by the parties in the pleadings is an accidental slip or omission or is due to inadvertence and it is so palpable that nobody can possibly have any doubt as to what the parties meant, I do not see why the court cannot set it right."</u>

5. The learned Advocate submits that the body of the plaint clearly shows that the plot number referred to is RS Plot No. 313, which was previously Plot No. 19. Also the plot number has been correctly stated in the prayer portion of the plaint, but in schedule "Kha" of the plaint the present plot number has been wrongly stated as No. 331 instead of 313. He submits that this is clearly a clerical error and hence amenable to correction under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. I have heard the learned Advocate and perused the materials on record. Upon close scrutiny of the petitioner's plaint, Annexure-B to this revisional application, it appears that the suit plot is referred therein as former settlement Plot No. 19 and present settlement Plot No. 313, which is the disputed land described in schedule "Kha". But schedule "Kha" states that the Plot Number is old 19 and present 331. Clearly there is an. incongruity. In my mind, there is no doubt that this is a typing or clerical error. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, in the impugned order, has rejected the application for correction because of the lapse of 35 years from the date of the decree. The learned Judge felt that he was unable to accept the application, which was beyond his jurisdiction.

7. Section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:

"Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in judgments, decrees or orders or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected by the Court either of its own motion or on the application of any of the parties."

<u>8. There is no mention within that section of any time limit for correction of any mistake occurring in the judgment, decree or order. On the contrary, it is stated that errors arising from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected. Hence the rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation cannot be sustained. In this regard reference may be made to the decision in the case of Chaganty Katamraju vs Madavarappu Paripurnanandam reported in AIR 1949 (Madras) 282. In that case the application for correction under sections 152, 153 of the Code of Civil Procedure was opposed on two grounds, firstly, the very long delay and, secondly, that the Court is not competent to grant an application for amendment of the plaint schedule after disposal of the suit. Mr Rajamanner, the Officiating Chief Justice, observed that undoubtedly there has been delay, but the mistake had evidently escaped the attention of the parties till very recently. He went on to say that it has not been shown that on account of this delay circumstances have intervened which would make it inequitable to grant the application. His Lordship further stated as follows:</u>

<u>"What is now sought in this application is not an amendment of the pleadings as such, it is really an application to correct an error which has crept into the decree. The wide language of .sections 152 and 153 would, in my opinion, cover a case like the present. The correction of an error need not always amount to an amendment of the pleading. I do not think it correct to treat this application as an application under Order VI rule 17.</u>

<u>Further assistance may be gleaned from a decision of our Appellate Division in a recent case of Sree Narayan Chandra Panda vs Md Mahbub Ali and others, reported in 9 BLT (AD) 197. In that case it transpired at the time of execution that the suit premises were wrongly shown as Plot No. 4314 instead of 4313. In that case, the application for correction was rejected by SCC Judge on the ground that the Court was functus officio. However, the Appellate Division held that:</u>

<u>"The amendment sought being of a formal nature, it falls within sections 151, 152 & 153 of the Code of Civil Procedure which the Court can correct. The High Court Division therefore, held that such correction of clerical mistake does not amount to amendment of the plaint under Order VI rule 17.</u>

<u>The Appellate Division held that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in allowing the correction to the schedule to the plaint.</u>

<u>9. In the facts of the instant case there is nothing to suggest that, after the declaration of title in favour of the plaintiff in 1959, any objection has been raised from any quarter regarding the title and possession of the plaintiff. It appears that at that time the decree was granted without contest. In view of the above discussion, I am of the view that, there being no question of limitation under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the application for correction of the mistake in the schedule of the plaint and the resulting mistake in the decree may be allowed.</u>

10. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge is hereby set aside. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Pirojpur Sadar is hereby directed to make necessary correction by substituting plot No. 313 in place of plot No. 331 in schedule "Kha" to the plaint and corresponding correction to the decree in Title Sit No.2 of 1959 as prayed for.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md Shamsul Alam, Advocate - For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Quayum with Tapash Kumar Biswas and Md Ali Reza, Advocates-For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdur Rahman Miah and another ------ Petitioners
vs
Md Zami Shah Newaz and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J : This revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code bf Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiffs-respondents is directed against the judgment and order dated 6-1-2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Bhola in Title Appeal No, 59 of 1997 allowing the application under section XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 33 of 1994 in the court. of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Bhola for specific performance of contract in respect of 'Ka' schedule land of the plaint and also for declaration that the 4 (four) deeds of sale described in 'Kha' Schedule of the plaint were null and void, collusive, inoperative and without jurisdiction.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy being in ownership and possession of the suit land by virtue of gift entered into an agreement on 25-12-1975 with the plaintiffs to sell the suit land on receipt of Taka 55,000 as advance out. of total consideration amounting to Taka. 1,30,000 and delivered possession of agriculturalland; that on subsequent occasion on 25-11-1978, Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sudari Roy received Taka 30,000 from the plaintiffs for treatment on renewal of the agreement and delivery of possession of the homestead, a garden and tank situated in the suit land, that on subsequent occasion on 15-4-1989, the executants of the agreement received further amount of Taka 35,000 for better treatment in India on renewing the agreement and handing over possession of the house standing on the suit land and that one of the executants of the agreement, namely Mohan Bashi Roy, died in India in 1990 leaving behind 4 sons, that is, defendant Nos. 1 to 4, as his legal heirs. It is further stated that the plaintiffs requested them to execute the deed of sale but Jashoda Sundari Roy and heirs of Mohan Bashi Roy were delaying to execute and register the sale deed and lastly, refused on 15th Chaitra, 1399 BS and that the father of defendant No. 7 taking the advantage of being a clerk of the sub-registry office in collusion with the sons of Jashoda Sundari Roy, namely Profullah Kumar Roy and Samar Chandra Roy, created a false, forged and antedated power of attorney being Wilfully aware about the agreement of the plaintiffs and also created 4 deeds of sale preceded by antedated and collusive agreement. Hence the suit.

4. None of the defendant Nos. 1 to 6 in the original plaint appeared in the suit, but opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 who subsequently added as defendant Nos. 7 to 12 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that by two separate powers of attorney dated 23-4-1989, Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy made Profullah Kumar Roy and Samar Chandra Roy respectively as their respective attorneys to manage and transfer the suit land; that Samar Chandra Roy entered into an agreement on 25-4-1989 with defendant Nos. 7 to 12, to sell the suit land on receipt of Taka 1,15,000 as advance out of total consideration amounting to Taka 1,25,000 and delivered possession thereof; that the executants of the agreement on subsequent occasion on 5-3-1994 executed and registered the deed of sale on receipt of the balance amount of the consideration amounting to Taka 1000 and that the plaintiffs created an antedated agreement by false personification.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, on consideration of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, as adduced by the parties decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 22-5-1997.

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court dated 22-5-1997 the opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 preferred Title Appeal No. 59 of 1997 in the court of the learned District Judge, Bhola.

7. The appeal was fixed for hearing on 7-10-1999 before the learned District Judge, Bhola and on 15-9-1997, the appellants opposite parties filed an application seeking for comparison of the signatures and thumb impressions of Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy put in the deed of agreement for sale and in the deeds of renewal of the agreement with the signature and thumb impression put in the power of attorney.

8. The learned District Judge, Bhola, after hearing, by his order dated 2-4-1998 rejected the application on the ground of being misconceived for not seeking to adduce or accept the expert report as additional evidence against which the appellants- opposite parties did not take any legal step in the higher court of competent jurisdiction.

9. The appellants-opposite parties filed another application on 4-5-1998 under Order CLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking for comparison of the signatures and thumb impressions of Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy put in the deed of agreement for sale and in the deeds of renewal of the agreement with the signature and thumb impression put in the power of attorney and for accepting the expert report as additional evidence.

10. The learned District Judge, Bhola after hearing, by his order dated 21-5-1998 directed to keep the application with the record for consideration of the same at the time of hearing of the appeal on 25-6-1998.

11. The appellants-opposite parties on 21-5-1998 filed another application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking for the self-same relief as had been sought in the application dated 4-5-1998.

12. In the meantime, the appeal was transferred to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge, Bhola for hearing and that on 4-1-2000 the appellants-opposite parties filed an application before Additional District Judge, Bhola, for hearing the application dated 21-5-1998 before hearing the appeal.

13. Against the said application dated 4-1-2000 the petitioners filed written objection stating, inter alia, that the appellants-opposite parties did not pray for comparison of the signature and thumb impression put in the disputed documents in the trial Court and that the learned trial Court decided the documents to be genuine and that on earlier occasion, an application over the self-same matter had been rejected against which the appellants- opposite parties did not file any revision and hence, the application is liable to be rejected.

14. The learned Additional District Judge, Bhola after hearing by his order dated 6-1-2000 allowed the application for comparison of the documents by handwriting expert and thumb impression expert.

15. Mr Md Shamsul Alam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that the documents sought to be examined were admitted as evidence by the learned trial Court and no step was taken by the appellants-opposite parties for comparison of the said documents in the trial Court; that the comparison of two disputed documents with one another would be of no use without comparison of the same with any admitted document but to cause unnecessary delay in disposing of the appeal and that the order dated 21-5-1998, the application dated 4-5-1998 under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure was kept in the record for consideration of the same at the time of hearing of the appeal and the said order was in force and, as such, the learned court below committed an error of law in entertaining another application on the self-same matter and hearing the same without recalling the earlier order dated 21-5-1998 and without disposing of the earlier application. He further submits that the impugned order is based on misconception of law and the learned Court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

16. The opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 by filing a counter-affidavit stated that the application for expert examination was never rejected on merit and the said application was filed and kept with the record and the transferee court, which has all the power to decide the matter rightly, allowed the expert examination upon consideration of objection raised and that the learned Court committed no mistake in passing the impugned order causing no failure of justice.

17. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1 to 6, submits that the impugned order will only enhance the cause of justice since the method of handwriting by the examination expert has developed a lot and the findings of the expert has stood in status of exactitude.

18. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1 to 6, cited the decision in the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader and others reported in 8 MLR (AD) 209 : 8 BLC (AD) 67 in support of his contention.

19. In order to analyse the conflicting submissions of the learned Advocate we must go back to the facts and circumstances of the case in which the application of the opposite parties for an expert opinion was allowed. As stated hereinbefore, the plaintiff-petitioner claims suit land on the basis of agreement dated 25-12-1995 executed by Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy.

20. On the other hand, claims of the contested defendants is that by two separate powers of attorney dated 23-4-1989, Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy made. Profulla Kumar Roy and Samar Chandra Roy respectively as their respective attorneys to manage and transfer the suit land; that Samar Chandra Roy entered into an agreement on 25-4-1989 with defendants Nos. 7 to 12 to sell the suit land on receipt of Taka 1,15,000 as advance out of total consideration amounting to Taka 1,25,000 and delivered possession thereof; that the executants of the agreement on subsequent occasion on 5-3-1994 executed and registered the deed of sale on receipt of the balance amount of the consideration amounting to Taka 1000 and that the plaintiffs created an antedated agreement on false personification.

21. During hearing of appeal, the appellants-opposite parties on application seeking for comparison of the signatures and thumb impressions of Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy put in the deed of agreement for sale and in the deeds of renewal of the agreement with the signature and thumb impression put in the power of attorney.

22. The learned District Judge, Bhola after hearing by order dated 2-4-1998 rejected the application on the ground of being misconceived for not seeking to adduce or accept the expert report as additional evidence.

23. The appellants-opposite parties filed another application on 4-5-1998 under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking for comparison of the signature and thumb impression of Mohan Bashi Roy and Jashoda Sundari Roy put in the deed of agreement for sale and in the deeds of renewal of the agreement with the signature and thumb impression put in the power of attorney and for accepting the expert report as additional 	evidence.

24; The appellants-opposite parties on 21-5-1998 filed an application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking for the self same relief as had been sought in the application dated 4-5-1998.

25. The learned Additional District Judge, Bhola after hearing, by his order dated 6-1-2000 allowed the application for comparison of the documents by the handwriting and thumb impression expert. The present revision is against that order.

26. Now the point for determination is whether the learned Additional District Judge, Bhola committed any error in passing the impugned judgment and order dated 6-1-2000 and which caused any failure .of justice.

27. Let us now see the provision of law and the decision of our apex court.

28. Section 73 of the Evidence Act, no doubt, empowers a court to compare. any questioned signature or writing with admitted or proved signature or writing in order to come to a conclusion whether or not the questioned signature or writing is genuine. The section is an enabling one. The discretion vested in the court is to be exercised on the facts and circumstances of the case. It is however, always open to the court to decide as to whether it should itself compare the questioned signature or handwriting to come to a decision or send them for an expert opinion.

29. The High Courts of the subcontinent were holding divergent views on the power of comparison by the Court, At the earliest, we find the Appellate Division had the opportunity to express its opinion about the power of the court to compare questioned signature or writing in the case of Provoth Ranjan vs Yeasin and others, 4 BCR 457 that by comparison of the questioned signatures or writing with the admitted signature or proved signature of writing even the trial Court could come to the conclusion whether, those were genuine or not:

30. In the case of Nitai Chand Shah and another vs Md Aga Khan and another, 1 BLT (AD) 46. the question was again precisely raised before the Appellate Division and a guideline was strenuously sought for at the Bar in view of divergent views in the High Courts on the power of the Court under section 73. The Appellate Division in the case of Monindra vs Mahalaxi Bank. AIR 1945 PC 325 held that: There was no hard and fast rule which prohibits such course by the judge.

31. In the case of contentious writing, signature etc, though provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act permits the court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, but the safe and best course, in our view, for the Court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature by court in all cases because such course sometimes appears to be risky or, in other words unsatisfactory and dangerous.

<u>32. Now the pertinent question for consideration is, how far in the background of the present case as well as evidence on record which method is safe. Although the court is permitted under section 73 of the Evidence Act, 1872 to compare the disputed signature or handwriting with the admitted signature or handwriting as to its genuineness of the questioned signature or writing, the apex court held such practice to be unsatisfactory and dangerous. Modem science has been developed much. Now it is better and safe to seek the expert opinion through microscopic enlargement and expert examination. Through this method, there is more possibility to get the correct opinion as to genuineness of the contentious signature or writing with the admitted signature or writing. Thus, the desired course should be to go for microscopic enlargement and expert opinion since the science of examination of signature, writing, etc for determination of similarity through microscopic enlargement has advanced enough and has reached to the stage of accuracy and certainty. To adopt this method has two-fold advantage. Firstly, the court can seek the opinion of the expert as to the genuineness of the contentious signature or writing and secondly, after getting the opinion of the expert on the questioned signatures or writing, the court can apply its judicial mind in considering same in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and material evidence on record, to arrive at a correct conclusion as to the genuineness of the contentious signature or writing. Expert examination of contentious signature or writing is an extra advantage in addition to examine the contentious signature or writing with admitted one naked eye. Though to obtain expert opinion is time consuming and expensive, yet safe and double advantageous method should be followed for ends of justice in order to arrive at a correct conclusion.</u>

<u>33. We receive support of the above view in the case of Tarak Chandra Maghi vs Atahar Ali Howlader and others 8 MLR (AD) 209 : 8 BLC (AD) 67.</u>

34. The court is to decide this matter considering the facts and circumstances of each case. In view of facts and circumstances of this case and in the light of discussion made hereinbefore, we are of the view that learned Additional District Judge, rightly allowed the application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and correctly passed the impugned judgment and order dated 6-1-2000 which does not cause any failure of justice.

35. In this connection, the learned Additional District Judge is directed to send the contentious signature or writing with the admitted signature for expert examination. With such modification, the impugned judgment and order dated 6-1-2000 of the Additional District Judge is upheld.

In the result, the Rule is disposed of with modification stated In the body of the judgment without any order as to costs. The order dated 6-1-2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Bhola in, Title Appeal, No. 59 of 1997 allowing the application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure is affirmed with above modification that the contentious signatures or writings are to, be examined with admitted signatures.

End.

lawyer:
Khijir Ahmed, Advocate------For the Petitioner. 
Surujit Bhattacharjee, Advocate------For Opposite Party Nos. 1•4.
parties:
Monju Mia and others ------ Petitioners
vs
Shiraj Mia and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J : Heirs of defendant No.1 obtained the Rule upon making a revision application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order dated 13-7-1999 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat (In-charge) at Sylhet in Title Suit No. 46 of 1998, which rejected a prayer for an expert opinion.

2. Short facts for disposal of the Rule are that on 25-9-91 opposite party Nos.1 to 4 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 62 of 1991 against defendant No.1 and others for declaration of title in the suit land. The suit was on transfer to the aforesaid Court and renumbered as Title Suit No. 46 of 1998. Petitioners made an application for an expert opinion about the signature of defendant No.1 on six rent receipts, which the plaintiffs recently filed, claiming that defendant No.1 never executed those rent receipts. Same date the application was heard and rejected by the impugned order. Hence, the Rule.

3. Mr Khijir Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in rejecting the application mainly on the ground that the court could have compared the signatures of defendant No.1 on the rent receipts with his admitted signatures in the written statement and power.

4. He also submits that the Course adopted by trial Court was risky and unsafe. In support, he cited the decision of the Appellate Division in Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader and others 8 BLC (AD) 67.

5. He further submits that learned Subordinate Judge was wrong to reject the application on the basis of laches and negligence. He took us through the record and submits that on 29-9-93 defendant No.1 submitted written statement. In paragraph 9 of the said written statement it was categorically stated that said rent receipts were forged, collusive and procured. Then, the plaintiffs submitted the rent receipts only in 1999 in order to adduce them into evidence. In view of section 103 of the Evidence Act, it was incumbent upon the petitioners to prove the receipts as forged. In support he cited the decisions in the case of Md Zaker Sukani vs Mostanser and others, PLD 1961 Dhaka 71 (s).

6. Opposing the Rule, an affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 is filed.

7. Mr Surujit Bhattacharjee, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1 to 4, submits that on 21-5-91 the plaintiffs instituted the suit. They claimed title mainly on the basis of a registered 'Kabulyat' dated 21-6-47 executed and registered by defendant No. 1 and payment of rents on rent receipts given by said defendant. At the time of presentation of plaint, the 'kabulyat' was filed in Court. Then, on 8-2-99 the plaintiffs made an application for directiorr upon said defendants to file the counterfoils of the rent receipts in question, which was allowed by an order dated 3-3-99. After such an order directing said defendants to file the counterfoils of rent receipts, the petitioners came up with the application for an expert opinion only to avoid filing the counterfoils of the rent receipts.

<u>8. Lastly, he submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the Court did not commit any error in rejecting the application for an expert opinion on the ground that the Court itself could compare the disputed signatures with the admitted signatures under section 73 of the Evidence Act, however risky or hazardous that may be. He submits the apex courts of the subcontinent are unanimous that the Court has got the power to compare any disputed writing or signature with available admitted signature or writings. He relied upon the decisions of the Appellate Division in the cases of Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs Chapala Rani Sen and others. 37 DLR (AD) 205 = 1985 BLD (AD) 172; Sree Motilal Chowdhury and others vs Sree Haripada Seal. 6 MLR (AD) 122 and Ishaque (Md) vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury and others 54 DLR (AD) 26 and submits that the decision in Tarak Chandra Majhi is flawed for being arrived at without considering the above decisions of the Appellate Division on the issue, and therefore, not binding upon this Division, being made per incuriam.</u>

<u>9. In reply, Mr Khijir Ahmed cited the case of Sree Motilal Chowdhury and others vs Sree Haripada Seal being dead his heirs Pradip Kumar Seal 6 MLR (AD) 122.</u>

10. In order to appropriate the conflicting submissions of the learned Advocates we must go back to the facts and circumstances in which the application of the petitioners for an expert opinion was rejected.

11. As stated hereinbefore, on 21-5-91 opposite party Nos.1 to 4 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 62 of 1991 for a decree of declaration of title in the suit land. On 29-9-93 defendant No.1 filed a written statement. In paragraph 9 of the written statement, the case of the plaintiffs regarding 'pattan' and payment of rents was denied. Then, the plaintiffs on 8-2-99 produced in Court six 'farog' ie rent receipts and made an application for an order directing defendant No.1 for production of the counterfoils of said rent receipts. By an order dated 3-5-99 the application was allowed and the defendant was so directed to produce the counterfoils.

12. Then, on 13-7-99 after the death of defendant, present petitioners made an application for an expert opinion about the signatures on said rent receipts claiming those were forged and created for the suit. Same date the application was heard and rejected by the impugned order on the grounds, inter alia.

“মামলাটি বর্তমানে সাক্ষ্য গ্রহণ চলিতেছে।বাদির দাখিলী ফারগ প্রমানের সুযোগ উন্মুক্ত আছে।তাছারাও অন্যান্য সাক্ষীর সাথে মিলাইয়া তর্কিত ফারগে ১ নং বিবাদির দস্তখত তুলনা করার আদালতের ক্ষমতা ব্যবহারের সুযোগ আছে।”

13. On the basis of the above decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi learned advocate for the petitioners forcefully submits that learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in not allowing the application and sending the rent receipts for an expert opinion.

<u>14. Section 73 empowers a Court to compare any questioned signature or writing with admitted or proved signature or writing in order to come to a conclusion whether or not the questioned signature or writing is genuine. The section is enabling one. The discretion vested in the Court is to be exercised on the facts and circumstances of a case. It is however always open to the Court to decide as to whether it should itself compare the questioned signature or handwriting to come to a decision or send them for an expert opinion. Only after the exercise of the discretion by the trial Court, it is for the Higher Courts to examine whether or not the discretion was exercised in accordance with established principles of law.</u>

15. The High Courts of the subcontinent were holding. divergent views on the power of comparison by the Court. The apex Court of this part of the world seems to have set the question at rest Iong ago.

<u>16. At the earliest, we find the Appellate Division had the opportunity to express its opinion about the power of the Court to compare questioned signature or writing in the case of Provoth Ranjan vs Yeasin and others. 4 BSCR 457 that by comparison of the questioned signatures or writing with the admitted signature or proved signature or writing even the trial Court could come to the conclusion whether those were genuine or not.</u>

<u>17. Then, in the case of Abdul Matin Chowdhury and Chapala Rani Sen and others, 37 DLR (AD) 205, the question was raised as an issue and the Appellate Division expressed itself, authoritatively:</u>

<u>"Comparison of writing or signature with admitted writing or signature is a question of fact and the High Court Division is not to interfere with the conclusion of the First Appellate Court on such question. It is now well settled that comparison of signatures is a perfectly legal mode of proving handwriting and however inconclusive such proof may be it cannot be considered as an error of law to base a conclusion on such proof alone, and a Court of second appeal is not competent to set aside a finding based on such comparison."</u>

<u>18. In the case of Nitai Chand Shah and another vs Md Aga Khan and another, 1 BLT (AD) 46, the question was again precisely raised before the Appellate Division and a guideline was strenuously sought for at the Bar in view of divergent views in the High Courts on the power of the Court under section 73. The Appellate Division expressed itself:</u>

<u>"There was no hard and fast rule which prohibits such course by the Judge. The Privy Council itself compared the disputed signatures with admittedly genuine signature in Monindra vs Mahalaxmi Bank AIR 1945 PC 325 and Gannamaneedi Madhavayya and another vs Gannamaneedi Achamma and another, AIR 1949 PC 325 ....</u>

<u>...... the proceeding is still pending in the Court below and sufficient guidance has been given by the long line of decisions for the Court which do not warrant any further pronouncement.</u>

<u>19. In the case of Sree Motilal Chowdhury and others vs Sree Haripada Seal being dead his heirs Pradip Kumar Seal, 6 MLR (AD) 122, Appellate Division dismissed a civil petition for leave on the view:</u>

<u>"6. The learned Counsel for the petitioners contends that unless the documents are first admitted into evidence the Court has no jurisdiction to send them for chemical examination.</u>

<u>7. The defendants have every right to cross-examine the witness of the plaintiffs and challenge the genuineness of the documents filed. In the instant case, the defendants made a prayer for chemical examination of the documents with specific allegation of eraser of the endorsement on the back of the documents. Therefore, we find no substance in this petition which is accordingly dismissed."</u>

<u>20. Lastly, in the case of Ishaque vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury 54 DLR (AD) 26, the Appellate Division was of the view:</u>

<u>"It was well settled that section 73 of the Evidence Act permits the Court to make a comparison of signature or writings and so adoption of such a method cannot be termed as hazardous or dangerous and therefore the finding as to the genuineness of Exhibit 14 cannot be questioned only on this account."</u>

21. In the case of Tarak Chadra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader, the question raised in the circumstances that the plaintiff instituted a suit for a decree of declaration that the order dated February 5, 1985 of the Land Appellate Board in Appeal Case No. 98 of 1984 was illegal, void and not binding on the plaintiff. Plaint case was mainly based on the premise that there was at no point of time an agreement between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 and that the order of the Land Appellate Board directing reconveyance of the suit land was without jurisdiction. Defence case was that by executing an 'Ekrarnama' the plaintiff agreed to reconvey the land and the Land Appellate Board rightly ordered for redemption, and a civil Court has got no jurisdiction to interfere with such decision.

22. The trial Court dismissed the suit. Appellate Court allowed the appeal of the plaintiff and decreed the suit. In setting aside the decree of the appellate Court, this Division held that the question of genuineness of the 'Ekrarnama' is a question of fact and the appellate Court having found the 'Ekrarnama' genuine committed error in setting the decree of the trial Court. On appeal therefrom, the Appellate Division set aside the decision of this Division and restored that of the first appellate Court.

23. Leave was granted amongst others, on the power of comparison of the Court under section 73 of the Evidence Act. In disposing of the question, the Appellate Division took the view:

"In the case of contentious writing, signature, etc, though provision of section 73 of Evidence Act permits the Court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, the safe and best course, in our view, for the court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature, etc and should not stake its judgment on the opinion formed or view taken upon resorting to risky or, in other words, 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' procedure. "

<u>24. In the decision, a case of Kessarbhai vs Jethabhai Jivan, AIR 1928 FC 277 was mainly relied upon and the case of Pratiq Bandhu Roy and others vs A/ok Bandhu Roy and others, 49 DLR 241 was approved.</u>

25. It is unfortunate that none of the earlier decisions of the Appellate Division nor of the Privy Council as referred to here to above was cited at the Bar. The view expressed in the latest case by the Appellate Division makes the guidance clear for the subordinate Courts including this Division to follow that, "the safe and best course, in our view, for the court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature, etc and should not stake its judgment on the opinion formed or view taken upon resorting to risky or, in other words, 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' procedure. "

26. How can we brush aside the apprehension of the Bar that the mind expressed in the decision will go down as a directive for all Courts including this Division to follow that the Court should send all such questioned writing or signature for expert opinion, as a matter of course. In other words, the judges are being discouraged, in fact denied, to exercise their statutory discretion under section 73 of the Evidence Act.

<u>27. Now, which of the decisions of the Appellate Division we should follow, earlier ones or the latest. Our dilemma is real, which of the decisions binds us. It is basic to the rule of precedent that if a later judgment of an apex Court, particularly when given without considering or noticing its earlier decisions on the same issue or point, and comes in conflict or at variance with its earlier ones, such judgment however latest in time, loses its binding element for being a judgment made per incuriam.</u>

28. We are however relieved to see that ultimate conclusion of the Appellate Division in setting aside the conclusion of the trial Court on the genuineness of the 'Ekrarnama' by way of comparison with the admitted signature rests in the light of the evidence on record.

29. In the prevalent situation obtained in the country expert opinion is always time consuming, besides expensive. After receipt of such an opinion, it would be of no use unless the expert comes before the Court and on oath, proves his opinion, which is not always so easy. Even after the opinion of an expert on the questioned handwriting or signatures is proved, it cannot be taken as conclusive. Such opinion is no doubt relevant under section 45 of the Evidence Act, which is to be considered by the Court along with other evidence on record oral or documentary to come to a conclusion in the facts and circumstances of a case. Such expert evidence is weak type of evidence.

30. Above words are never intended to say that proof of any questioned writing or signature by an expert opinion, as a mode, should be abandoned. Choice should be left with the Court to decide how it should proceed in the facts and circumstances of a case. No hard and fast rule should be prescribed since it would not advance justice, ultimately.

31. We find the learned Subordinate Judge took the view that at the time of recording of deposition the opinion was sought for. Proof of rent receipts produced by the plaintiffs was still open. Besides, the Court itself could use its power of comparison of questioned signatures on said rent receipts with the admitted signatures in the light of evidence to be adduced by the parties. Thereafter, the Court also reasoned that in order to delay the disposal of the suit, the application was made. Such reasons for rejection of the application appear to be sound and  well reasoned.

32. In the facts and circumstances, we find the Subordinate Judge committed no error in rejecting the application for expert opinion nor such order resulted in failure of justice, in any way.

33. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 10-11-99 is hereby recalled and vacated.

34. The learned Subordinate Judge is directed to proceed with the suit, expeditiously.

Communicate at once.

End.

lawyer:
HS Deb Brahman, Advocate  ----- For the Petitioner. 
MA Samad, Advocate  ----- For the Respondents
parties:
Matiur Rahman (Md)  ----- Petitioner
Vs
People's Republic of Bangladesh and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J : Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the order of transfer of the petitioner, an unskilled labour to the post of Darowan by order dated 10-11-1999, evidenced by Annexure D to the Writ Petition, should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. The petitioner was appointed as an unskilled labour by the respondent Company vide appointment letter dated 29-6-1997, evidenced by Annexure-B' to the writ petition, and while the petitioner was working to the satisfaction of his superiors his status has been changed from "unskilled Worker" to "Darowan" by order dated 10-11-1999 and the petitioner in compliance to that order joined the new post of Darowan but submitted a representation dated 14-11-1999 for his reinstatement in his previous post and position as "unskilled labour" and that such change of designation and the transfer of the petitioner has infringed his fundamental rights of Trade Union activities ensured by Article 38 of the Constitution and as well as section 3(A) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance 1969 and because of such change of status and transfer his future prospect of promotion and benefits has been curtailed in that as an unskilled labour he had opportunity to reach Grade L-6, whereas from the status and post of darwan he can go up to Grade L-3, and that the change of his status and transfer has been made arbitrarily without any notice to or consent of the petitioner and that as per terms and conditions of his appointment letter dated 29-6-1997 he could be transferred to an equivalent post only.

3. The respondent Nos. 2-4 entered appearance and contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition. In the affidavit-in- opposition it has been stated that the writ petition is not maintainable inasmuch as the petitioner could take the recourse to section 34 of the IRO 1969 and the respondent being a Private Limited Company, order passed by it is not amenable in the writ jurisdiction and that the respondent Company did not put any bar upon the petitioner to carry on his Union activities but if there is any bar under any law the respondent has nothing to do and that the post of Darowan is higher than that of the post of unskilled labour and, as such, the petitioner should not have any grievance against such transfer and that the petitioner after accepting the transfer order joined in his new post and the objection against such transfer or change of status is a belated one and on this count also the writ petition was filed is not maintainable. The petitioner filed affidavit-in-reply and the respondent filed affidavit in-opposition there against.

4. Mr Deb Brahman, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the writ petitioner was appointed as an unskilled Worker on 29-6-1997 and since then he has been working as such to the satisfaction of his superiors and that on 10-11-1999 by the impugned order the petitioner was transferred to a post of security staff changing his designation as Darowan without notice to or consent of the petitioner and that by such change not only his right to Trade Union activity has been taken away by the respondents but his future prospect as to promotion and other attending benefits have been curtailed, in that as an unskilled labour the petitioner can go up to Grade-6 level whereas as a Darowan, a security staff, the petitioner can go up to Grade-3 level at best. The learned Advocate further submitted in view of section 2 (XXVIII) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance (IRO) 1969 after joining the post of Darowan the petitioner is debarred from taking the re-course of section 34 of IRO, 1969 for any relief against his transfer and change of status through Labour Court, since as per said section 2(XXVIII) a Darowan is not a worker and the right to Trade Union activity is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution under Article 38 thereof. The learned Advocate submitted that the petitioner after joining his new post as Darowan submitted representation on 14-11-1999 for reinstating him to his previous post as an "unskilled labour" but that was not considered and hence the petitioner caused issuance of Demand of Justice Notice dated 17-8-2000, which also remained unattended and then the petitioner moved this Court and obtained this present Rule.

5. Mr MA Samad, the learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondent, submitted that the respondent Company is a private limited Company and, as such, the impugned order is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction and the petitioner being a worker under the provisions of Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 the Writ petitioner ought to have approached the Labour Court for relief complying with section 25 of the said Act. The Learned Advocate further submitted that the petitioner is still a worker and can approach the Labour Court under section 34 of the IRO 1969 and, as such, the petitioner having not taken the re course to section 34 of the IRO 1969, this writ petition is not maintainable. In support of his contention that the respondent Company being a private limited Company is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction the learned Advocate placed a decision of an unreported case of Modern Dyeing and Screen-printing Ltd vs the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and others in Writ Petition No. 2848 of 2001, disposed of by judgment and order dated 2-3- 2002 and the said judgment and order has been passed relying on the decisions in the case of Shahabuddin vs Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR 360, in the case of Abdur Rahman. vs Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR and in the case of Ziban Kumar Barmen vs M Abdul Hye, reported in 48 DLR 569. The learned Advocate in support of his contention that the writ petitioner could move the Labour Court under the provisions of both Industrial Relations Ordinances, 1969 and Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965, referred to the decisions in the case of Abdul Muquit Chowdhury vs Election Commissioner reported in 41 DLR 57 and in the case of Imtiaz Ahmed vs Golam Ali Chowdhury reported in 15 DLR (SC) 283. The learned Advocate however could not deny the statement that the petitioner as an unskilled labour can go up to Grade-6 level whereas as darowan he cannot go beyond Grade-3, level.

<u>6. We have perused the Writ petition, and the affidavits filed by the respective parties and also the annexures thereto. On the point of maintainability it appears that section 2 (XXVIII) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, (hereinafter referred to as IRO) puts a bar on a security staff to be treated as a worker and, as such, the petitioner after his transfer and change of status as a Darowan cannot be treated as a worker under IRO 1969. Therefore, he cannot avail section 34 of the IRO 1969. There is no legal bar in approaching any forum other than Labour Court under the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as the Act, 1965) to seek relief against infringement of fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. It further appears that 100% shares of the respondent Company Government. Therefore, we petition is maintainable.</u>

7. It appears from the materials placed before us and the submissions put before us that the change of status and transfer of the petitioner from "unskilled labour to "Darowan" has taken away his fundamental right to Trade Union activity and has also curtailed his future service benefits i.e. as unskilled labour he can go up to Grade-6 level whereas as Darowan he can go up to Grade-3 level only.

8. We have perused the decisions placed before us by the learned· Advocate for the respondent. We are in respectful agreement with those. The respondent Company is owned by the Government, and is not an ordinary Company limited by shares owned by ordinary people and not similarly controlled by the Joint Stock Co. of Bangladesh as in the case of ordinary Companies incorporated under the Companies Act. The decisions in the case of Modern Dyeing and Screen Limited (Writ Petition No. 2848 of 2001 disposed of by the judgment and order dated 02-03-2002 and those reported in 45 DLR and 48 DLR referred to above have no application in this case. The decisions reported in 41 DLR and 15 DLR do not bar seeking relief under writ Jurisdiction for a worker or Darwan, Considering the facts and circumstances of the case we find merit in the Rule.

Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order of transfer and posting dated 10-11-1999 so far it relates to the writ petition changing his status and transfer as Darowan is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

End.

caseno: Contempt Petition Nos. 73, 75 of 2000 and 79 of 2000.
lawyer:
Mainul Hosein with Nazmul Huda, Aminul Hoque, Md Humayun Kabir, Bulbul and Iqbal Malik, Advocates ------For the Petitioner in Contempt Petition No. 73 of 2000. 
Rafique-ul Huq with Abdur Razzak; Md Humayun Kabir Bulbul, Advocates------For the Petitioners in Contempt Petition No. 75 of 2000. 
Moudud Ahmed with Abdur Razzak, AM Mahbub Uddin and Md Humayun Kabir Bulbul, Advocates------For the Petitioners in Contempt petition No. 79 of 2000. 
Mahmudul Islam, as Attorney-General, with Mahbubey Alam, Additional Attorney-General, Bazlur Rahman Chhana, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Mainul Hosein & others  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Sheikh Hasina Wazed  ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Hoque J: These three applications namely, Contempt Petition No.73 of 2000, Contempt Petition No.75 of 2000 and Contempt Petition No.79 of 2000 have been filed for drawing up a proceeding for contempt of Court against Sheikh Hasina, the Prime Minister of Bangladesh. One application has been tiled by Mr Mainul Hosein, President, Bangladesh Supreme Court Bar Association. The second application has been filed by Mr Rafique-ul Huq and 338 Advocates of Bangladesh Supreme Court. Third application has been filed by 110 members of Bangladesh Jatiya Sangsad through Mr Moudud Ahmed.

2. In all the applications common allegation was made to the effect that on 26-07-2000 the Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina gave an interview with the correspondent of the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) where she made some objectionable and, contemptuous statement undermining the image, honour, dignity and prestige of the Courts of Bangladesh as a whole. In all the applications the alleged contemptuous statement of the Prime Minister has been shown as under in the form of question and answer:

বিবিসিঃ

এই যে আপনাদের সরকারের ৪ বছর পার হয়ে গেছে। ৪ বছরে আপনারা একবার স্বরাষ্ট্রমন্ত্রীকে পরিবর্তন করেছেন, আইন-শৃঙ্খলা পরিস্থিতির একটা অবস্থায় গিয়ে। দক্ষিণাঞ্চলে আপনারা সাফল্যের কথা বলেছেন। কিন্তু দক্ষিণাঞ্চলের ঘটছে এখনো সহিংস ঘটনা। এই যে সহিংস ঘটনা, রক্তপাত বা খুনোখুনী এই যে পরিস্থিতিটা এ বিষয়ে আপনারা আর কি করতে পারেন?

শেখ হাসিনাঃ
