Issue

24. The statements of Mrs Hasina made as the Prime Minister of the Republic in the interview with BBC (the British Broadcasting Corporation) and the reactions thereto both against her and favour generated a tremendous debate amongst the people in the country and beyond. Such concern of the people for the independence and sovereignty of the judiciary and the honour and dignity of the judges, if is not otherwise motivated, is the healthy sign for building and strengthening the justice delivery system. However, whether the Prime Minister committed contempt of court by her statements is the moot issue before us. To decide this issue other questions require to be seriously considered and addressed as well.

Law of contempt

25. All three applications were made under Article 108 of the Constitution read with section 2 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1926.

26.	Article 108 of the Constitution reads,

"The Supreme Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power subject to law, to make an order for the investigation of or punishment for any contempt of itself."

27. By the article, the Supreme Court is empowered 'subject to law' to make an order for investigation of or punishment for any contempt of itself. The law is the Contempt of Courts Act, 1926 (Act No. XII of 1926) shortly, the Act. In 1926, to remove the doubts as to which of the High courts in the then India had the power to punish a contemner the Act was enacted. The Act comprises of 3 sections only. Under section 2 of the Act, the High Court Division is empowered to exercise jurisdiction in case of contempt of this Division or of a Court subordinate to it only. Under section 3 of the Act, a contempt of court is punishable for a maximum term which may extend to six months, or with fine, which may extend to two thousand Taka or with both. The power of this Division to award punishment is therefore limited by the Act to the extent of any contempt committed either in respect of itself or of a Court subordinate to it. But what is contempt and what is the procedure to be followed have not been defined and provided in the Act. This Division has not yet adopted any rules to deal with contempt proceedings.

28. On the other hand, the Appellate Division framed the Appellate Division Rules, 1988 detailing the procedure for dealing with contempt of that Division. Order XXVII rule 1 of the Appellate Division Rules reads:

"1. The Court may take cognizance of its contempt suo mota or on a petition by any person:

Provided that where the alleged contempt consists of wilful disobedience of its judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of the Court or a breach of an undertakings given to the Court or a Judge in Chambers, the Court may take cognizance suo motu or on a petition by the aggrieved person."

<u>29. We shall have to rely on our own procedure as developed over the years and found in the precedents, and the practice which we think best for investigation of and punishment for any contempt of this Division. In practice, this Division has been following the same path charted by the Appellate Division for taking cognizance of an offence of contempt.</u>

What is contempt of court

30. Oswald defines contempt,

"to be constituted by any conduct that tends to bring the authority and administration of law into disrespect or disregard or to interfere with or prejudice parties or their witnesses during litigation."

KJ Aiyar in his treatise, "Law of Contempt of Courts", 7th Edition has described contempt,

"A contempt can assume any form, any act, any slander, any contemptuous utterance, or can be the subject-matter of any news, report or article, or it may be an act of disobedience of Court's order. Consequently, the Courts, dealing with contempt cases have, in the peculiar circumstances associated with the nature and range of the delinquency in question, not been able to define the said words exhaustively."

Contempt, Civil or Criminal

Halsbury's Laws of England, Volunme VII, paragraph 603 divides contempt of Court into two categories,

1. criminal contempt; consisting in words or acts obstructing or tending to obstruct, the administration of justice" or

2. contempt in procedure, consisting in disobedience, of orders or other process of the Court, and involving a private injury.

Criminal Contempt is again subdivided into several categories:

a. "Contempt in the face of the Court which includes the act of insulting a judge actually sitting in Court or Chambers to administer justice,

b. speeches or writings tending to defeat the ends of justice,

c. obstructing persons officially connected with Court or proceedings,

d. obstructing the parties to pending proceedings;

e.	 abusing the process of the Court; and

f.	 breach of duty by persons officially connected with Court or proceedings."

Cognizance and Jurisdiction

<u>31. This Division may suo moto or on the information received take cognizance of an offence of contempt. The jurisdiction is sui generis and has developed an independent corpus of rules which originated in the Common Law of England consists of a special set of principles as stated in Sukdev Teja Singh, AIR 1954 SC 186 and Ashfaq Ahmad Sheik vs State, PLD 1972 SC 39.</u>

<u>Nature of the proceedings</u>

<u>32. A contempt proceeding which is quasi- criminal in nature. The contemner is entitled to benefit of doubt, and since the Court is both prosecutor and judge, rule as to proof of guilt of the contemner must be strictly observed.</u>

33. It may be borne in mind that though a contempt proceeding is quasi-criminal in nature, the contemner is not like an accused in a criminal case since he may file affidavit or make statements on oath in refutation of the allegation against him. The charge must be proved to the hilt otherwise the contemner is entitled to benefit of doubt. Moazzem Hossain vs State, 35 DLR (AD) 290 and Mahbubur Rahman Sikder vs Majibur Rahman Sikder; 35 DLR (AD) 203].

Object of the proceedings

34. As the object of the proceedings for contempt is not the vindication of the character or conduct of a Judge but to protect the Court from attack and to maintain in it the confidence of the people, particularly the litigants, the true ground for initiating such proceedings is the public interest. It is for this reason that the jurisdiction to punish for contempt is considered to be a special jurisdiction governed by its own rules even where they come in conflict with some general principles of law.

35. Secondly, the prestige and the dignity of the Courts of law must be preserved. The confidence of the litigant should not be shaken by the use of contemptuous and scandalous expressions toward Court for its judgments and attempting thereby to belittle them. Stream of justice is not to be polluted by shaking the confidence in the administration of justice by conduct exhibited and words used. It is stated in Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd edition, 9, that,

"Scandalous attacks upon judges are punished upon the principle that they are, as against the public, not the judge, and obstruction to public justice; and a libel on a judge, in order to constitute a contempt of court, must have been calculated to cause such obstruction. Temperate criticism in good faith is immune. The punishment is inflicted, not for the purpose of the protecting either the court as a whole or the individual judges of the court from a repetition of the attack, but of protecting the public, and especially those who either voluntarily or by compulsion are subject to the jurisdiction of the court, from the mischief they will incur if the authority of the tribunal is undermined or impaired."

In Morris vs Crown Office [l970] 2 QB 114, 129 Salmon LJ observed:

"The sole purpose of proceedings for contempt is to give our courts the power effectively to protect the rights of the public by ensuring that the administration of justice shall not be obstructed or prevented."

India

36. In India, in 1971, the Contempt of Courts Act, (Act 70 of 1971) 1911 was adopted as a comprehensive law. The High Courts in India have also adopted their own rules to exercise their powers to carry out the purpose of the Act. In the Act what is contempt and what is not contempt have been defined. The exceptions or the defences to the contempt of Court have also been enumerated.

Pakistan

In 1976, following the Article 204 of the Constitution, the Contempt of Courts Act, 1976 (Act No. LXIV of 1976) was enacted. Like the Indian Act, the Act of 1976 has defined what is contempt and what is not contempt. The law has also laid down the procedure to deal with a contempt proceeding.

England and USA

37. To be brief, I refrained from discussing the laws on contempt of England, USA or other developed countries. There, the law is .comprehensive and developed. The courts there never faced such a case as we are facing.

More recently Lord Diplock in Attorney-General vs Leveller Magazine Ltd 1979 AC 440, 449F thus summarised the position:

"although criminal contempts of court may take a variety of forms they all share a common charasteristic; they involve an interference with the due administration of justice either in a particular case or more generally as a continuing process. It is justice itself that is flouted by contempt of court."

But I must cite what Holmes Alexander wrote in a frontal attack on the functioning of the Supreme Court of USA in his column,

"9 Men Terror Squad"

"Now can you tell what that black-robed elite are going to do next. Spring more criminals, abolish more protections. Throw down more ultras. Rewrite more laws. Chew more clauses out of the Constitution. May be, as a former Vice-President once said, the American people are too dumb to understand, but I would bet that the outcropping of evidence at the top in testimony before the US Senate says something about the swelling concern among the people themselves."

For such scurrilous remarks against the judges, no contempt proceeding was initiated either by the Supreme Court of USA or the American Bar Association against Mr Holmes Alexander.

Bangladesh

38. As discussed earlier that in our country, laws of contempt of Courts are also broadly of two types, namely, criminal contempt and civil contempt, and based on Common Law. Civil contempt is defined as disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction order, writ or other process of court or wilful breach of an undertaking given to the Court as stated in M Rahman vs Mujibur Rahman, 35 DLR (AD) 203. Where the conduct is an attempt to obstruct the administration of justice or to lower or undermine the dignity or authority of the Court either by writing or publishing or by words spoken or action taken contemptuous in the face of the Court or to bring the Court in contempt is called criminal.

Freedom of Speech vls-a-vis Contempt

<u>39. Article 39 of the Constitution has ordained,</u>

<u>39(1) Freedom of thought and conscience is guaranteed.</u>

<u>(2) Subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interests of the security of State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of Court, defamation or incitement to an offence.</u>

<u>(a) the right of every citizen to freedom of speech and expression; and</u>

<u>(b) freedom of the press, are guaranteed.</u>

<u>So, the right to freedom of speech and expression is guaranteed subject to the limitation as imposed by the Constitution and such limitation is also found necessary in the interest of administration of justice. But it should also be remembered what could readily be read as contemptuous in 1900 or 1912 or 1936 is not so easily read now in the context of expanding rights guaranteed as fundamental to human existence under the Constitution.</u>

Limit of criticism

40. The Court 	must harmonise the Constitutional values of free speech and expression. The balance to be struck between such values vis-a-vis the rights of the people to their lives and properties as guaranteed by the Constitution for strengthening the confidence in respect and dignity and honour of the judiciary. This was aptly stated in Razina vs, Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Ex parte Blackburn. 1968) 2 All ER 319: 1968 CA 150, by Lord Denning.

"All we would ask is that those who criticise us will remember that, from the nature of our office, we cannot reply to their criticisms. We cannot enter into public controversy. Still less into political controversy. We must rely on our conduct itself to be its own vindication.”

Caution of judges

<u>41. In dealing with such proceedings, the judges should keep in mind as was stated in, Asharam M Jain vs AT Gupta, AIR 1983 SC 1151.</u>

<u>"There is never any risk of judicial hypersensitivity. The very nature of the judicial function makes judges sympathetic and responsive. Their very training blesses them with "insensitivity', as opposed to hypersensitivity. Judges always seeking good reasons to explain the wrong conduct. They know there are always two sides to a coin. They neither give nor take offence because they deal with persons and situation impersonally, though with understanding. Judges more than others realise the foibles, the frustrations the undercurrents and the tensions of litigants and litigation but, as elsewhere, lines have to be drawn. The strains and mortification of litigation cannot be allowed to lead litigants to tarnish, terrorise and destroy the system of administration of justice by vilification of judges. It is not that judges need be protected; judges may well take care of themselves. It is the right and interest of the public in the due administration of justice that has to be protected."</u>

<u>The above view finds approval by our Appellate Division in A Karim vs State, 38 DLR (AD) 188.</u>

<u>"So we approach the question not from the point of view of the judge whose honour and dignity require to be vindicated, but from the point of view of the public who have entrusted to us the task of due administration of justice."</u>

Cases cited

42. Let me now discuss some of the cases cited at the Bar. In Andre Paul vs Attorney-General, AIR 1936 PC 141, an appeal from an order of the Supreme Court of Trinidad and Tobago ordering the appellant to pay a fine of £25 or in default to be imprisoned for one month for contempt of Court for publishing an article, and to pay costs. Upholding the conviction, in this most cited case, Lord Atkin observed:

"The path of criticism is a public way the wrongheaded are permitted to err therein, provided that members of the public abstain from imputing improper motives to those taking part in the administration of justice, and are exercising a right of criticism and not acting in malice or attempting to impair the administration of justice, they are immune. Justice is not a cloistered virtue: she must be allowed to suffer the scrutiny and respectful even though outspoken comments of ordinary men."

In Razina vs Metropolitan Police Commissioner; Ex parte Blackburn, Mr Quintin Hogg, a Privy Councillor and former MP and Queen's Counsel, wrote an article in weekly "Punch" entitled "Political Parley" seriously criticising the Court of Appeal and its dicta. Mr Albert Raymond Blackburn, made an application for an order that the writer had been guilty of contempt of court. Rejecting the application, Lord Denning MR observed,

"this is the first case, so far as I know, where this court has been called on to consider an allegation of contempt against itself. It is a jurisdiction which undoubtedly belongs to us but which we will most sparingly exercise: as we ourselves have an interest in the matter as quoted earlier."

In Vishwanath vs ES Venkatramaih, 1990 CrU 2179 (Bombay HC), on 17-12-89 on the eve of his retirement, in an interview to the noted journalist Sree Kuldeep Nayar Mr Justice Venkatramaih, Chief Justice of India, remarked, inter alia,

"The judiciary in India has deteriorated in its standards because such Judges are appointed, as are willing to be 'influenced' by lavish parties and whisky bottles."

"In every High Court, there are at least 4 to 5 judges who are practically out every evening, wining and dining either at a lawyer's house or a foreign embassy'.

He estimated the number of such Judges around 90 and favours transferring them to other High courts.

"Practically in all the 22 High Courts in the country close relations of Judges are thriving."

On the application of Mr Vishwanath, a practicing lawyer of the Court and a former Chairman of Maharashtra Bar Council three newspapers out of several newspapers which published the news item were joined as respondents as contemners along with Mr Justice Venkatrarnaih and Mr Kuldeep Nayar as respondents. The Court held that the former Chief Justice did not commit any contempt. The motion was accordingly dismissed.

43. In PN Duda vs P Shiv Shanker, AIR 1988 (SC) 1208, the Supreme Court of India declined to initiate a proceeding for contempt of court against P Shiv Shanker, the then Minister for Law, Justice and Company Affairs. Mr Shiv Shanker addressed on the occasion of Silver Jubilee Celebration of the Bar Council of Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad. The audience consisted of judges and lawyers. Addressing on the accouritability of the three organs of the State, with scathing reference to some very important decisions of the Supreme Court, he said that

" Anti-social elements i.e. FERA violators, bride burners and a whole horde of reactionaries have found their haven in the Supreme Court"

In Ch Zahur llahi MNA vs Mr Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, PM, PLD 1975 (SC) 383, Mr Bhutto, the Prime Minister of Islamic Republic of Pakistan was arraigned under Article 204 of the Constitution for contempt of court for his certain remarks in respect of a pending proceeding. His speech was directed against lifting ban on the National Awami Party (NAP) to the effect that

"if the Supreme Court in its wisdom or according to its own understanding gives a decision against us then it will not be my decision, or that of the people but will be the decision of the Supreme Court. We will accept this decision but the responsibility for the consequence will be that of the Supreme Court. In spite of this if need be to save Pakistan we will fight in the hills, in the jungles and in the plains."

Mr Bhutto was not found to have committed any contempt of court.

44. In Masroor Ahsan vs Ardeshir Cowasjee, PLD 1998 (SC) 823, the judgment disposed of number of contempt proceedings for punishment of a former PM, a sitting PM, some Members of the Parliament/Senate, Journalists, Editors, Printers and Publishers of some newspapers for their speeches/statements directed against the Supreme Court, its Chief Justice/Judges and some of its judgments.

45. Lastly, Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, 51 DLR (AD) 68. The Prime Minister made certain remarks in respect of the Chief Justice regarding the disposal of bail matters by a Division Bench. On disposing the application, the Mr Justice ATM Afzal, CJ, observed,

"the Court expected more circumspection, understanding, discretion and judgment on the part of the Prime Minister because of the High Office she holds in making off-hand remarks in respect of constitutional functionaries which have been alleged to be contumacious."

Drawing our attention to the above observation, learned Counsels for the motions submitted, even after those observations the Prime Minister was not found to be discreet at all in making her statements in respect of the judiciary. On the other hand, Mr Mahmudul Islam submitted, the observations were uncalled for. The observations were made behind the back of the Prime Minister, not in a legal proceedings and, as such, were not worthy of citation as binding precedent. Be that as it may, at that time, the Prime Minister made the remarks in respect of the Chief Justice, Moreover, in the same order, it was also observed,

"... as the Chief Executive she was entitled to have her own views in the matter having regard to the law and order situation which is the concern of the Executive. The Court is accustomed to such executive chagrin in matters like this."

Now the moot issue

46. As stated earlier, the question precisely is whether the statements of Mrs Hasina, the Prime Minister of the Republic made in the interview amounted to contempt of this Division, essentially criminal contempt or, in other words, such statements have the effect of bringing this Division into disrepute or, the confidence of the people in this Division shattered or interfering with the administration of justice.

47. In view of the above authorities, let me now consider the statements of the Prime Minister. I have gone through the entire interview. On the deterioration of the law and order situation in the country the Prime Minster was asked questions with particular reference to the recent violent incidents involving killings. Most offended statements are to the following effect.

48. She remarked that in a country where the killers get patronisation, the killers are defended, the killers are not put to trial, the killing would continue. The police apprehend the accused, High Court lower Courts enlarge them on bail. High Court or Lower Courts, wherever they go, the Court is as if a safe shelter for the corrupt or accused persons. The lawyer who wants bail should be held responsible or the Court who grants bail should be held accountable. So long it could not be done, the criminals could not be given exemplary punishment, it would be difficult task to improve the situation till then.

49. I have read the above statements in between the lines many a times. The statements are no doubt critical, in general, of the Courts and also of lawyers. The statements are also not accurate, factually. In matters of bail, the weaknesses in the process of investigation by the police, failure of the law officers appearing for the prosecution and the loopholes in the judgment delivery system as were pointed out in the submissions of the learned Counsels on both the sides were not reflected. Failure of the administration in handling the situation was also missing in the statements. But, the statements based on inaccurate assessments of situation, however gross misreading those may be, cannot be tantamount to be contempt of court. Moreover, in the absence of mens rea, no contempt is established.

50. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Republic. She is responsible for the law and order situation in the country. If the questioned statements are read in the context of the entire interview and in the objective reality of the country, those would appear to be nothing but observations of the Prime Minister based on her own understanding and judgment of the situation. The submission that as the statements were coming from the Prime Minister so she should have some restraint or circumspection is a matter completely different from the issue at hand. The judiciary cannot dictate how the executive head should exercise her discretion. We can only desire.

<u>51. Moreover, the statements were not directed against any judgment or order or proceeding of any Court. Nor those were directed against any particular judicial officer or a judge of the Supreme Court. Rather, those appear to be mainly in respect of the judicial system as a whole. I find no justification in the submission that the statements could be read as designed by no other person than the Prime Minister of the Republic to destroy the judiciary in the country Of, intended to bring the judiciary into disrepute or, intended to have the effect of shattering the confidence of the people or to interfere with the administration of justice. Also not directed to scandalise any particular judge or judicial officer of Court or the judiciary. In the first sentence, she referred to the tragic chapter of our national history. In the offended and exasperating part of the statements, the Court, as if, a safe shelter for the corrupt or accused persons in the matter of bails, the words as if in the sentence, have ultimately taken away the sail of the supposed purport of the sentence, the Courts have become a safe shelter for the criminals. Rather, such statements may be the product of distress, frustration and/or helplessness of the Prime, Minster on the basis of her judgment of the situation but without any ill motive or intention to scandalise the judiciary. It is therefore difficult to accept the interpretation of the learned Counsels for the motion.</u>

52. Another pertinent question should be kept in mind the Prime Minister took an oath to defend the Constitution. Her statements on law and order situation vis-a-vis the judiciary should not so readily be read as contumacious in the absence of Clear motive.

Accountability

53. With regard to accountability, I must not miss this opportunity to place the main line of thought of the Judiciary on the subject, Mr Justice Mostafa Kamal, former Chief Justice of Bangladesh, in his reply to the felicitation given by the Supreme Court Bar Association on June 1, 1999 said,

"The legal profession and the judiciary now stand at a cross-road of history. So long the judiciary functioned almost beyond the gaze of public eyes, but with the concept of accountability growing currency by the day, the legal profession and the judiciary can no longer function behind and beyond public scrutiny- The people of this country are alert and watchful of every movement of ours."

(Fulfil the People's expectation" 51 DLR Journal 42)

Mr Justice Latifur Rahman, present Chief Justice, similarly, in reply to his felicitation, also in the same vein said.

“বিচারকগণ কেবল নিজেদের বিবেকের কাছেই নন, সংবিধান এবং সর্বোপরি সংবিধান প্রণেতা জনগণের কাছে দায়বদ্ধ।........

<u>54. After such eloquent statements of the former Chief Justice and present Chief Justice on the Accountability of the Judiciary I may only add that the judiciary is quite alive with the expectations of the people. The conscience of a judge becomes conditioned by the oath he takes to defend the Constitution. We are no doubt holding a public office on oath under the Constitution. A great trust and confidence of the people are reposed in such office. Every day, we are discharging our constitutional duties within the public gaze. Our judgments are the acid test of our accountability. Further, if there is any lapse or failing in the capacity or conduct of a judge, article 96 of the Constitution has ordained the President of the Republic to act and direct the Supreme Judicial Council to inquire into the matter and report its finding to him. Thereupon, the President is empowered to take action under the Constitution. Originally in our Constitution, this power was given to the House of Nations like the parliament in India. So it is' not correct for any body to think that the judges are above law or, there is no accountability of the judges under the Constitution. The sooner it is understood by all and sundry the better for the whole nation.</u>

<u>Opposition MPs came to Court</u>

<u>55. 110 Honourable members of Parliament, all belonging to the main opposition parties came before this Division for an order to punish the Prime Minister for contempt of Court. However, the leader of the Opposition in the Parliament did not join them. The Prime Minister of the Republic is the leader of the House of the Nation. The Parliament comprises of members, both of the ruling party as well as of the Opposition parties. The Constitution ordained the Prime Minister responsible arid accountable before the Parliament for her all actions/omissions and public statements. The aggrieved members of the Parliament could have more opportunities and better scope to hold their leader to account in the Parliament for her statements. But they preferred, to abdicate their constitutional privilege and submitted before us to punish their leader by this Division for infraction of the Constitution. Such novel step unprecedented in the constitutional history, I am afraid, would not create any good precedent.</u>

56. On their behalf, Mr Moudud seriously challenged the locus standi of the intervenors to oppose the motions, As stated above, in case of contempt of court, this Division can suo mota take cognizance. Or anyone can bring the incident of contempt as an information to the notice of this Division. On consideration of the information, if it prima facie appears that there has occasioned a contempt of court, this Division may take cognizance upon such report. The interview of the Prime Minister was reported in the media, both electronic and print, throughout the length and breadth of the country on 27 July, 2000. The Appellate Division as well as this Division did not take any notice of such statements. One month thereafter, three applications, one after another were filed by three sets of people. It seems to me that one application was not thought sufficient to break the slumber of the judiciary. With the equal thrust but in larger number, other two applications were also tabled to reject the motions. In the absence of any law or rule, and in the aforesaid facts and circumstances, we could not refuse to hear the intervenors.

Why so many applications

57. From the making of so many applications, in favour and against the motions, one fact becomes clear that the lawyers are strongly divided on the issue. The intervenors accused the applicants that their motions were politically motivated which they promptly denied. But the question remains, then, what made them so divided on such an important issue. As stated earlier that the judiciary is alive with the concern of the people for the judiciary. But the people are equally and strongly divided like the lawyers. How can I ignore to take into consideration of the perception of the nation of the issue Such division demands serious circumspection from the judiciary. Then the reason for such division is nowhere found except in the politics, the judiciary must guard itself against all chances of the party-politics creeping into the holy precincts of the citadel of justice lest it ultimately fell victim to politics.

For the reasons as stated above, and in greater interest of justice, I also agree with my learned

brother to dispose of all the motions in the line with the desire of Mr ATM. Afzal, CJ as was ordered in the concluding paragraph of his opinion.

End.

full_judgment:
Khademul Islam Chowdhury J: These three Rule Nisi were issued on the application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh filed by one Mr M Mohsin Hossain. Since the facts and question of law involved in all the 3(three) Rules are similar they are heard together and disposed of by this single judgment.

2. In Writ Petition No. 2546 of 1997 the petitioner has challenged impugned notice dated 5- 4-1997 containing Memo No. 13-97 aJ" BTJ"-3/471 fJA 05-04-97 issued to the petitioner under the signature of respondent No.3 Mr SM Shahjahan, Deputy Director Anti-Corruption Bureau, TA/CO-3 section.

3. The gist of the averments are that by the impugned notice annexed to the petition as Annexure-A the petitioner was asked to appear before the respondent No. 4 Anti-corruption Officer. Anti-corruption Bureau, Dhaka on 12-4-1997 with relevant documents relating to the acquired land of the petitioner though no particular of any document was noticed in the impugned notice. The petitioner received the notice on 9-4-1997 at 5 PM and appeared before the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 on 10-4-1997 and informed them that the police have nothing to do with the said documents sought to be produced. The respondent No. 3 fixed further date on 17-5-1997 asking the petitioner to produce the documents; the petitioner was threatened by the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 in that in case he failed to produce unspecified documents of his acquired land he would be compelled to produce documents forcibly. Finding no efficacious remedy the petitioner moved this Court with the Writ Petition.

4. In Writ Petition No. 2519 of 1998 the petitioner challenged the notice contained in সি-আই-ডি অফিস স্মারক নং কেন্দ্রীয় অপরাধ, সি-আই-ডি/২৫-৯৮(বিবিধ)1120 fJA 12-02-98 issued by respondent No. 5 Mr Md Fazlul Karim Khan, PPM Assistant Superintendent of Police CID Bangladesh Dhaka upon the petitioner along with 3 others asking them to appear before him on 27-7-98 at 10 AM in the morning with documents of land relating to CS Plot Nos. 72 and 73 of Mouza Mohakhali for interrogation in connection with application of one Mr Eklasur Rahman, Civilian Staff Officer Rehabilitation Directorate, Army Headquarter Dhaka Cantonment that since the petitioner was not within the country at that. time, an application praying for time on his behalf was filed by the learned Advocate, that the property measuring 1.66 acres in plot No. 87 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 207 and measuring 4.94 acres recorded in plot numbers 40, 72, 73, 74 and 75 of CS Khatian No 174 of Mouza Mohakhali originally belonged to the petitioner. The property was acquisitioned by the Government under Defence of India Rule 75A (2), that Mr ATM Mostafa Kamal recipient of the impugned notice in serial No.1 of the impugned notice along with others filed Writ Petition No. 2536 of 1995 in the High Court Division wherein the Rule was discharged by judgment dated 16th February, 1.998, against the judgment and order the petitioner moved Miscellaneous Petition for leave to Appeal No. 63 of 1998 before the Appellate Division and necessary steps are being taken for filing regular Civil petition, no notice containing the allegations was submitted by Mr Eklasur Rahman and the Miscellaneous petition is pending before the Appellate Division wherein the respondent No. 5 has nothing to do with the aforesaid land, that no criminal case was instituted against the petitioner by the respondent in any police station or court of Bangladesh, that notice issued by the respondent No. 5 is illegal and without jurisdiction. The impugned Notice is violative of the fundamental right of the petitioner and same has been issued only to humiliate and harass the petitioner. The petitioner having no other efficacious remedy moved this Court and obtained the Rule.

5. In Writ Petition No. 1765 of 1998 the petitioner challenged the, impugned action of respondent Nos. 2 to 5 asking the petitioner to appear before the Deputy Police Commissioner, Detective Branch, Dhaka Metropolitan City and produce document at 10 O'clock on 16-6-1998. In the Writ Petition it is alleged that on 14-6-98 at 9-30 AM an Inspector of Police named Md Abdullah, respondent No. 5 herein, accompanied by some police force arrested the petitioner from his residence and produced him before Mr Bazlul Karim. Deputy Commissioner, Detective Branch respondent No. 4 in the Writ Petition. The respondent No.4 asked the petitioner to produce the documents relating to the 15 kathas of land out of 4- 79 acres of land of CS plot Number 25, 26,24, 42 of CS Khatian Nos. 96, 97, 30 of Mouza Samair, Police Station Gulshan, District Dhaka and directed the petitioner to transfer the property to Mr Jamil Akhter and Kazi Nurjahan Alam, respondent Nos. 6 and 7 respectively, the petitioner was tortured mentally and he was directed to refund Taka 74,00,000 to the respondent Nos. 6 and 7, that the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 detained the petitioner in their office up to 4-30 PM and on the prayer of the petitioner he was freed and allowed 2(two) days time, that petitioner was asked by the respondent No.4 about Title Suit No. 290 of 1997 filed in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka for specific performance of contract for sale by Mr Khan Mohammad Ameer as plaintiff against the petitioner and the deed of agreement for sale of 4,79 acres of land to Khan Mohammad Amber. The petitioner was directed to transfer the said land to Khan Mohammad Amber on 16-6-98 when the petitioner again appeared before the respondent No. 4, the petitioner was directed by the respondent No. 4 again to appear on 21-6-96 with the documents of the land and he was threatened that in case he failed to produce the documents and refund the money to respondent Nos. 6 and 7 he would be put to inhuman torture. On 19-6-98 the petitioner filed an application to the Honourable Minister of Home Affairs praying for necessary action against the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 for creating fictitious bainapatra and trying to recover money from the petitioner illegally with the assistance of police of Detective Branch on 21-6-1998 when the petitioner appeared before the respondent No.4 he was again directed by the respondent No. 5 to produce the document and transfer the land to the respondent No.6 and 7 within seven days, but even then on 21-6-98 the petitioner was asked to transfer the land to the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 within 7(seven) days and the respondent No.4 gave threat that if he failed to comply with the verbal order he would be put to torture which might cause his death, that as the respondent Nos. 2-5 chased the petitioner and called him again and again to appear before him in their office and upon coming to know that he may be subjected to inhuman torture, the petitioner stayed out of his residence since 22-6-98. That despite repeated requests made by the petitioner the respondents did not serve any written notice or order upon the petitioner for his appearance and production of document, that no copy of allegation of the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 was served upon the petitioner who collected the copy of the allegation from the office of the Detective Branch, that over the self-same land the maternal uncle of the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 Mr Khan Mohammad Ameer as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 290 of 1997 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka against the petitioner for specific performance of contract and for permanent injunction and obtained order of status quo dated 26-1-98, that against the said order the petitioner filed First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 6 of 1998 before the High Court Division and by an order dated 11-2-98 the Appeal was admitted and record of the case was called for; that no Criminal Case was instituted against the petitioner in respect of alleged deed of agreement for sale by the respondent Nos. 6-7 in any court or in any police station of Bangladesh and that the High Court Division is in seisin of the subject matter in the First Appeal. The respondent No. 5 has no authority to enquire about the land to the petitioner and ask the petitioner to appear and submit document regarding his land. The action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 asking the petitioner to submit document in respect of certain land is illegal and without jurisdiction and it is violative of the fundamental right of the petitioner and the petitioner shall be humiliated and harassed in the hands of the respondents. The petitioner got no other effective and efficacious remedy by law. As such, he moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner in all the three Rules, submitted that the impugned notices by the respondent police officer in Writ Petition No. 2346 of 1997 and Writ Petition No. 2319 of 1998 and action taken by respondent Nos. 3 and 5 in arresting and taking him to DB Office and asking him to produce agreement for sale, sell his land to respondent Nos. 6-7 with threat to compel him to do so are ex facie without lawful authority or any legal basis inasmuch as the same are not intended to be done except for the purpose of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Code of Criminal Procedure as provided in section 94(1) or to require attendance of a witness in course of investigation of a criminal case under section 160 of the Code. Paragraphs 31 and 50 of the Anti- Corruption Manual as referred to in the impugned notice dated 5-4-97 postulate a guideline for the Anti-Corruption officers in dealing with investigation of cases for internal use only and do not apply in respect of property of such person in the absence of any investigation or enquiry of a criminal case. Mr Karim further submitted that the impugned notice issued and action taken are apparently calculated and mischievous acts perpetrated by the high ranking police officers in a most arbitrary and high-handed manner for collateral purpose and, as such, unwarranted and without authority. The learned Advocate submitted that the impugned notice is per se vague in that no particulars of the documents or the information sought to be obtained or given to the respondent having been mentioned in the impugned notice and on all these counts the impugned notices and action are liable to be struck down. The learned Advocate in support of his contentions has drawn our attention to the terminologies, enquiry, investigation as defined in section 4(1) (K)(I) of the Code, placed his reliance in tile case of Mohsin Hossain (Md) (who is also the petitioner in the instant case) vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 2 BLC (1997) 44 wherein it is held that:-

"Section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure authorises a police officer to direct any person to appear before him in connection with investigation of a criminal case. Under clause (1) of the sub-section (I) of section 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure investigation includes all the proceeding under the Code for the collection of evidence conducted by a police officer or by any person (other than a Magistrate) who is authorised by a Magistrate in this behalf. Thus, it appears that investigation under section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure includes also an enquiry directed by a Magistrate. Since there is no reference of any Criminal Case in the notice the same has been issued by the respondent No. 4 in an unauthorised manner."

7. The respondent in this Write Petition did not enter appearance and file any affidavit in opposition. On our query Mr Obaidur Rahman Mostafa the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that neither section 94 nor section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure nor provisions of Anti-Corruption Manual authorises any police officer to issue any notice asking any citizen to attend and produce any document except for the purposes of any investigation, enquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Code before such officer or require the attendance of any person as a witness by order in writing in the absence of criminal case filed against him. The elements of investigation and enquiry are contained in clause (K) and (I) respectively of sub-section (I) of section 4.

8. Such submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General fully support and endorse the submission made by the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner. To examine the validity or otherwise of the impugned notice and action we many refer to the relevant provisions of law contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure.

9. Section 94(1) of Chapter 7 of the Code provides:

"Whenever any court or any officer in charge of a police station considers that the production of any documents or other thing is necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding before such court or officer the court may issue a summons or such officer a written order to the person in whose possession or power such documents or thing is believed to be requiting him to attend and produce it or to produce it at the time and place stated in the summons or order."

10. Under section 3(3) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 (Act. XXVI) an officer of the Bureau may exercise any of the powers of the officer in charge of the police station in the area in which he is for the time being. Both the officer-in-charge of the police station and the officer of the Bureau are thus authorised by law to issue an order for production of a document.

11. Section 160 of the Code in Chapter XIV confers power to any police officer to require attendance of a witness by order in writing at the time of making investigation of a criminal case. In this connection definition of investigation in section 4(I)(a) is also pertinent and quoted below:

"Investigation 	includes also the proceedings under this Code for the collection of evidence conducted by a Police Officer or by any person (other than a Magistrate) who is authorised by, Magistrate in this behalf."

12. The investigation begins on receipt of information relating to commission of cognizable offence and registration of a criminal case at the police station. The crucial test for issuing an order for production of document is that such production is necessary and desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Code. The order itself must indicate the necessity and desirability of the production of a document and the order must contain the description of document so required.

13. In the instant case the impugned notices and the action of the responded apparently do not disclose any valid reason or ground for issuing the notice and also taking action against the petitioner asking him to produce documents. The impugned notice issued by the respondent No.3 in Writ Petition No. 2546 of 1997 and the impugned notice issued by the respondent No.5 in Writ Petition No. 2319 of 1998 appear to be vague and unspecified in the absence of any description of the documents sought to be produced. The action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 calling upon the petitioner to submit documents in respect of certain land which is the subject matter of a contract between the petitioner and the respondent Nos. 6-7 and subject matter of suit for specific performance of contract without serving any notice in writing are prima facie illegal and such action by the concerned police officer is taken by abusing official position in a most high- handed and arbitrary manner for collateral purpose and the impugned notices and action of respondents are not only unauthorised and contrary to the specific provision of section 94(1) read with section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but also they blatantly and flagrantly violated the fundamental right of the petitioner enshrined in Article 31 of the Constitution. We are also of the opinion that the respondent clearly exceeded the limit in issuing impugned notices and taking the impugned action.

<u>14. No police officer can ask any person to attend or to appear before him and no person is required to attend a police officer merely because he is ordered or required verbally or in writing unless his attendance is so required in connection with investigation of a criminal case or any proceeding. Ongoing through the petitions, the annexures thereto and the impugned notices annexed to the Writ Petition No. 2546 of 1997 and Writ Petition No. 2519 of 1998 and the impugned act of the respondent Nos. 2-5 are outside the purview of any of the provisions of sections 94 and 160 of the Code and they do not apply in the instant case.</u>

15. The impugned notices do not answer any of the purposes in law for which they have to be served there being no specific criminal case or proceeding instituted against the petitioner. It appears that the impugned notice in Writ Petition No. 2519 of 1998 no law has been quoted and it related to dispute of landed properties. In Writ Petition No. 1765 of 1998 the petitioner was arrested and confined without any criminal case or any complaint against him recorded at the police station whatsoever and that too relates to a dispute over landed property in respect of which Civil litigation is pending up to the highest court. Thus we find that the impugned notice and the impugned action asking the petitioner to appear before the respondent and to produce document are without any lawful authority. The respondents despite service of notices upon them have not controverted the correctness of the allegation made in the writ petition and also did not contest the Rule at the time of hearing. Since the allegations in the writ petition are not controverted they are deemed to be correct and valid.

16. Accordingly, these Rules are made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned notices issued by the respective respondents in Writ Petition No. 2546 of 1997 and Writ Petition No. 2519 of 1998 and impugned action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 challenged in Writ Petition No. 1765 of 1998 are declared to be illegal and without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.

End.

A Latif & Company Ltd ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant No.2 Executive Engineer LGED at Rangpur presented the appeal against an order dated 16-8-2000 passed by Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 134 of 1997, which refused to set aside the award dated 22-6-2000.

2. The respondent made an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 for filing of the arbitration agreement in Court and for appointment of an Arbitrator to arbitrate on the claims for Taka 65,83,999.60 on account of compensation and interest for cancelling the work order and blacklisting the company. The application was registered as Title Suit No. 134 of 1997.

3. In the application, it is stated that on 6-2-1995 the plaintiff submitted a tender quoting Taka 85,98,775.50 for construction of 124.075 metres pre-stressed bridge on Jumuneshwari River at Shatibari-Balua Bondar road under the police station Mithapukur in the District of Rangpur. On 5-3-1995 defendant No. 1 accepted his tender with the condition for completion of the work within 18 months i.e. 540 days. On 25-3-1995 defendant No. 2 issued the work order.

4. When the defendants were making delay in supplying the layout, on 12-8-1995 the plaintiff wrote to defendant No. 2 with copy to defendant No. 1 requesting for the layout. Defendant No. 2 meanwhile by memo dated 12-4-1995 asked the plaintiff to show cause as to why the work order would not be cancelled.

5. He had to sit idle for about seven months and eighteen days after casting of pre-cast pilings. Defendant No.2 held up the bills of pre-cast pilings and thereby caused monetary loss. The plaintiff could not drive the pilings for want of layout. By onrush of water of the flood the piles went down by erosion and Domar sand of 4000 cubic and middle granulated sand of 3,500 were washed away causing loss of about Taka 3,70,000.

6. After issue of the work order defendants did not supply him any layout within ten months. The plaintiff prayed for extension of time for execution of the work but without any result. By Memo dated 12-4-1997 defendant No.2 let the plaintiff know that his work order was cancelled, as he was already blacklisted by Memo No. 319 dated 3-4-1997.

7. Then, the defendants invited new tender for completion of the work at a cost of Taka 80,80,888 with enhancing the length of bridge to 150 metres. The plaintiff suffered loss of Taka 65,83,669.60 for cancellation of the work order, Hence, the application.

8. By filing a written statement, the defendants denied the claims of the plaintiff. The case of defendants, in short, was that the plaintiff was required to make the pre-cast piles immediately after receipt of the work order. But in spite of repeated demands the plaintiff did not take the work seriously. At last on 22-8-1995 the plaintiff completed casting of the piles. Plaintiff took five months for piles casting. Had the plaintiff commenced the work of the piles driving in time, super structure would have been completed before the flood.

9. Because of slow progress of work, the project faced the flood. Due to flood, surroundings of the bridge loosened and ditch was formed by erosion. Design and alignment needed revision. When the authority was busy in making such design, the work order for construction of a bridge on river Turag at Gazipur was cancelled and the plaintiff was blacklisted for gross violatiori of the contract. After the plaintiff became blacklisted, his work order for the present project was also cancelled.

10. They also contended that before invoking the arbitration clause for appointment of the arbitrator named therein, the application before the Court was not maintainable.

11. On the application first Mr Abdul Jalil, J was appointed as a Arbitrator. As Mr Abdul Jalil, J joined the Labour Appellate. Tribunal the plaintiff made again an application for appointment of fresh Arbitrator. By order dated 12-1-2000 Mr Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J was appointed sole Arbitrator and the plaintiff was asked to pay the entire remuneration of the Arbitrator on his prayer.

12. Before the Arbitrator, the respondent company submitted a statement of claims of Taka 2,21,61,674.99. The appellant opposed the claims by filing a written reply to the claims. They specifically challenged the jurisdiction of Mr Abdul Wadul Chowdhury, J to arbitrate in view of the named-Arbitrator in the Arbitration clause of the contract. It was inter alia, stated that the respondent company on 27-3-1995 received the' work order along with full set of required papers, plans, specifications, layout, etc. so that, the company could perform the work in time, enclosure A Modified design of-pile reinforcement was approved on repeated requests of the company to ease its work. The time of execution of the work as per terms of the contract expired on 1-10-1995. The company prayed for extension of the time on 3-11-1995 i.e. 32 days of the expiry of schedule time. Meanwhile, on 3-4-1997 the licence of the company was cancelled and it was blacklisted for gross violation of the contract for construction of Mouchak Btidge at Gazipur causing huge loss to the public exchequer. In view of such development, the instant contract was rescinded by a letter dated 12- 4-1997.  Thereafter, the company never sought arbitration on any dispute under clause 25 of the contract but went to the Court for seeking appointment of an arbitrator outside the contract, The appointed arbitrator had no jurisdiction to arbitrate on any dispute arising out of the contract.

13. The learned Arbitrator did neither examine any witness nor admitted any evidence. He heard the parties on the statement of claims and reply thereto on the basis of annexures to them. On 20-6-2000 the Arbitrator gave an award of Taka 1,90,47,374.99 in favour of the plaintiff.

14. Against the award, the appellant made an application under section 30 read with section 33 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award. The company opposed the application by filing a written objection. By impugned order the objection was rejected.

15. Mr MA Gaffar, learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the award given by the learned Arbitrator was vitiated for coram non-judice as he had no authority to enter into arbitration in view of the arbitration clause.

16. He submitted that learned Arbitrator acted beyond his jurisdiction in giving the award.

17. Lastly, he submitted that learned Arbitrator misconducted himself as well as the arbitration proceedings by giving the award which on the face of it was perverse.

18. On behalf of the respondent, Mr Shafique Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate, on the other hand, submitted that the very objection filed by appellant does not deserve consideration as no security, was deposited along with the objection.

19. In support he cited the cases of Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim and another, 1988 BLD 369; RAJUK vs MN Alam & others, 54 DLR 161 and Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Progati Prakushali 49 DLR 335.

20. Then, he submitted that as the award was already made Rule of the Court and a decree passed following the judgment, no appeal would lie against such decree except on the ground that it was in access of, or not otherwise in 'accordance with, the award and the appellant failed to make out any case within such limited scope.

21. In support he, cited Abdus Salam and another vs  Osman Gani and another, 1984 BCR (AD) 346 and Dhaka Leather Complex vs Mis Sikder Construction Ltd and another, 12 BLT 17.

22. He submitted that the court cannot sit in appeal and decide the award on merit on facts as well as law.

23. In support, he cited MOL Enterprise Inc. vs Bangladesh, 4 BLC 407 Adamjee Sons Ltd vs Jiban Bima Corporation 45 DLR 89; Province of East Pakistan vs Messrs Architect Engineering Co, 20 DLR (AD) 469; Puri Construction Pvt Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1989 SC 777; Food Corporation of India vs Joginderpal Mohinderpal and another, AIR 1989 SC 1263; Ghulam Abbas vs Trustees of Port of Karachi, PLD 1987 SC 393; Mohammad Eunus & Brothers vs Chittagong University, 44 DLR (AD) 296; KM Shafi Limited vs Government of Bangladesh, 1983 BLD (AD) 109; State of Orissavs Dhandasi Sahu, AIR 1989 SC 1791; Dhandasi Sahu vs State of Orissa, AIR 1987 Orissa 275; IBAD and Co vs Province of Sind, PLD 1980 Karachi 207 and KM Shafi Limited vs Bangladesh, 1983BCR (AD) 155.

24. He also submitted that jurisdiction of the Court to set aside an award is limited to the extent as provided under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. In support, he cited KM Shafi Limited vs Bangladesh, 1983 BCR (AD) 155 and Begum Khadija Akhter Banu and another vs AKM Amanullah and another, 1985 BCR (AD) 8.

25. Admittedly, on 27-3-1995 the respondent company got the work order for construction of a bridge at Taka 85,98,775. In the work order, it was specifically required of the company to commence the work within seven days and complete by 1-10-1996. The work could neither be commenced nor be completed within the stipulated time. On 12-4-1997 the work order was cancelled on the ground that the respondent already became blacklisted hi connection with another work of a bridge at Gazipur. The respondent never invoked the arbitration clause nor' wrote to, the appellant for arbitration. The arbitration clause 25 reads as follows:

"Except where otherwise provided in. the contract all questions and disputes relating to the meaning of the specifications, designs, drawings, and instructions hereinbefore mentioned and so to the quality of workmanship or materials used on the work, or as to any other questions, claim, right, matter or thing whatsoever any way arising out of or relating to the contract, designs, drawings, specifications, estimates, instructions, orders or these conditions, or otherwise concerning the works or the execution or failure to execute the same, whether arising during the progress of the work or after the completion or abandonment thereof shall be referred to the arbitration of the Superintendent Engineer. LGED of the District for the time being in-the manner provided by law relating to arbitration for the time being in force who, after such investigation as he may think proper shall deliver his award which, shall be final, conclusive and binding on all parties to this contract".

26. In the arbitration clause, in the case of any dispute relating to execution or the work, Superintendent Engineer, LGED of the District for the time being was named as the sole arbitrator for arbitration. 'XEN' was wrongly typed in place of Superintendent Engineer, as Mr Shafique Ahmed showed us from printed BD Form No 2911.

27. The respondent, company made - an application under section 20 of-the Arbitration-Act for filing in Court of the arbitration agreement and appoint an arbitrator for an-award on the claims of Taka 65,83,699.60. The Court appointed Mr Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J and referred the Claims as raised in the application for arbitration. But before the arbitrator, the company claimed Taka 2,21,61,474.99 on various beads. Learned Arbitrator entertained such statement of claims and entered into arbitration.

28. Claim No. 1 is for Taka 63,95,919 which was the amount after receipt of part bills of Taka 22,02,856 out of total contract value of Taka  85,98,775.50.

Learned Arbitrator allowed the entire claim on the view,

".....a vested right accrued upon the contractor to complete work and draw the entire contracted value being Taka 85,98,775.50. They had every preparation to complete the work. They also asked the 2nd Party to perform their obligations without killing time but the 2nd Party instead of performing the contract obligations, cancelled the contract illegally basing on a different matter which had no relevancy in the present matter preventing the 1st Party to have the work completed."

29. The learned Arbitrator appears to have allowed the claim for illegal cancellation of the work order as compensation or damages. The contract of the work however, does not provide for any such payment to the contractor on account of compensation or damages. Clause- 3(c) of the contract rather provides that the contractor shall have no claim to compensation, in any case.

30. Mr Shafique Ahmed submitted that the learned Arbitrator is empowered to give compensation or damages for breach of the contract under law of the land even when the contract is silent. Submission may sound appealing but is devoid of any substance. He however, could not show us any authority. The learned Arbitrator neither adjudicates nor sits as a tribunal. His function is like that of a conciliator. He cannot arrogate jurisdiction of a civil Court to decide issues of damages for breach of a Court, particularly when the contract does not give him any such power; Begum Khadija Akhter Banu and another vs AKM Amanullah and another, 1985 BCR (AD) 8. The power and function of an arbitrator is to arbitrate as per terms of the contract. He has got no jurisdiction apart from what the parties have given to him under the contract. An arbitrator who acts in manifest disregard of the contract acts without jurisdiction, Associated Engineers Co vs Government of Andhra Pradesh, (1991) 4 SCC 93. The arbitrator commits misconduct if by his award he decides matters excluded by the contract (Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol IL 4th Edn Para 622).

31. Besides, one is entitled to payment for the work done but we know no law that entitles him to payment for anything not done by him.

32. Claim No.2 is for Taka 98,92,355.49 for business loss and damages for not paying said amount of Taka 63,95,919.50 (under claim No.1) by 31-12-1996 when the contract expired with 16% quarterly business loss up to 22-5-1999 from January, 1997 i.e. 29 months.

33. The learned Arbitrator allowed the entire claim on the ground of illegal detention of Taka 63,95,919.50 again as compensation.

34. When the learned Arbitrator had no jurisdiction to allow claim No.1, allowing of claim No.2 was equally unauthorised and unlawful.

35. Secondly, we find not an iota of evidence in support of the claims for such huge amount. Allowing such claim was based on no evidence at all.

36. Learned Arbitrator also allowed claims No. 10(i), ii(a), iii(a), iv, v, vi(a) and (b) for Taka 23,04,600 for loss and damages for payment on account of the staff and workers' salary for sitting idle.

37. He recorded that he examined the expenses which the contractor had to defray and pay due to default of the 2nd party i.e. the appellant. But we found not an iota of any account either annexed to the application of the company made under section 20 of the Arbitration Act or the statement of claims or exhibited into evidence. So, there is no escape from the conclusion that the award on such claims was also based on no evidence.

38. Secondly, the respondent company received the work order along with plans, specifications, layout, etc. of the work, which was claimed by the appellant but never denied. The company was required to commence the work within seven days of the work order dated 25-3-1995 annexure 1 and complete within 1-10-1996 strictly in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract. The company prayed for extension of the time on 3-11-1996 i.e. after about 32 days of the expiry of the contract time. After lapse of the schedule time, no such claim could validly be made. Lastly, such claims are outside the terms of the, contract.

39. When the Arbitrator was appointed under section 20 of the Arbitration Act by the Court the learned Arbitrator had no authority to travel beyond the reference. He was obliged to arbitrate on the basis of the application in accordance with terms of the contract and the provisions of the Arbitration Act.

40. There cannot be any two opinions on the, authorities cited on the scope of the Court in setting aside an award. Powers of the Court to set aside an award are enumerated by section 30 of the Arbitration Act. Section 30 reads:

"S 30-Grounds for setting aside award- An award shall not be set aside except on one or more of the following grounds, namely,

(a) That an Arbitrator or Umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings;

(b) Than an award has been made after the issue of an order by the Court superseding the arbitration or after arbitration proceedings have become invalid under section 35; and

(c) That an award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid.

41. The apex Courts of the subcontinent are however, of the view that the grounds are not exhaustive. As we have found in the present case that the learned Arbitrator misdirected himself in traveling beyond the reference and gave the award without taking into consideration of the contract at all and against the law. The error is so apparent on the face of the award that there is little difficulty to say that the award was improperly procured which was completely invalid.

42. Now, let us see the scope of the appeal as Mr Shafique Ahmed asked us to. Against the award, the appellant made an application under section 30 read with section 33 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award. By impugned judgment and order said application was rejected. Section 39 (vi) of the Arbitration Act has made such order appealable and the appellant accordingly, presented the appeal. Scope of such appeal is therefore, precisely to see as to whether or not the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in refusing to set aside the award. The appellate Court is equally empowered to set aside the award on any of the grounds under section 30 of the Arbitration Act.

43. It is true a decree was drawn and signed but we could not understand when the award was not made Rule of the Court how a decree could follow such judgment. Be that as it may, the present appeal is preferred against that part of the judgment that rejected the application of the appellant for setting aside the inward. This appeal cannot be termed to be an appeal against the decree. So, the submission of Mr Shafique Ahmed on the scope of the appeal as one against the decree passed under section 17 of the Arbitration Act is wholly misconceived.

44. Mr Shafique Ahmed also submitted that the appeal was not maintainable as the appellant failed to deposit statutory security along with their application for setting aside the award. Proviso to the section 33 reads:

Section 33:

"Provided that no application challenging the existence or validity of an award or for having its effect determined shall be entertained by the Court unless the applicant has deposited in the Court the amount which he is required to pay under the award or has furnished security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum or for the fulfillment of any other obligation by him under the award"

45. Such objection was never raised before the trial Court. The objection for the first time was raised in this appeal.

46. In reply, Mr Gaffar on behalf of the appellant drew our attention to the case of Bangladesh Power Development Board vs The Builders Corporation (2004) 1 LG (HC) 38 and one unreported case of Chief Engineer, Roads and Highways Department vs Messrs Csncord Engineers and Construction Limited decided by a Division Bench of this Division on 4-4-1996.

47. In both cases, no security was deposited. In the former case, a Division Bench relying upon 6 DLR 478 and 8 DLR 305 held, that the award given by an arbitrator not named in the arbitration clause was void ab-initio and a nullity in the eye of law. Upon such view, it allowed the appeal and set aside the award. In similar circumstances, in latter case another Division Bench held the award illegal and without jurisdiction as being Coram non-judice. What they wanted to say is that when the award is void and/or nullity on the face of it, failure of deposit of statutory security could not save such award.

48. In Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim and another, 1988 BLD 369; Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Progati Prakushali and another, 49 DLR 335 and RAJUK vs MN Alam & others, 54 DLR 161 cited by Mr Shafique Ahmed, the objection against the application for setting aside the award was taken at the very first instance before the Court of first instance. Secondly, the present award, on the face of it, appears to be improperly procured from a person who was not appointed arbitrator by the arbitration clause. In the circumstances, we cannot allow such an improper award to be valid to harm the public confidence in the very system of binding arbitration and/or cause loss to the public exchequer.

49. Now, we take up the issue of jurisdiction of the learned Arbitrator to arbitrate and in making the award, As quoted hereinabove that under clause 25 of the contract any dispute in respect of execution of the work shall have to be referred to the Superintendent Engineer of the concerned District. The respondent company did never seek any arbitration as per terms of the contract.

50. The respondent company made an application for appointment of jointly proposed Arbitrator on the claim that there was no Superintendent Engineer in the circle. By order dated 10-6-1998, the application was fixed for hearing on 23-9-1998.. On 23-9-1998 the application was however, rejected as not pressed. Then, the company made another application for appointment of an arbitrator from amongst a list of former Judges. Order dated 28-1-1998 recorded that the company expressed the desire to pay entire fees of the arbitrator. By order dated 24-3-1999 the Court appointed Mr Md Abdul Jalil, J. After he joined the Labour Appellate Tribunal, by order dated 11-10-1999 the Court asked the parties to file names of arbitrators. Then, by order dated 12-1- 2000 the application of the company which was endorsed 'no objection' on behalf of the- appellant was allowed and Mr Abdul Wadud Chowdhury was appointed sole arbitrator and the company was directed to pay the remuneration of the arbitrator.

<u>51. Section 20(4) empowers the Court to make an order of reference to the arbitrator appointed by the parties, whether in the agreement or otherwise. The Court can appoint an arbitrator only when the contract did not name any arbitrator and the parties failed to agree to appoint an arbitrator. Not otherwise. 'No objection' on behalf of a party does not invest the Court with any power which it does not, have under the section. Even when other party did not appear upon notice to an application made under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, the Court is not empowered to supersede the arbitration clause and appoint an arbitrator who is not named in said arbitration clause; of Bangladesh vs Masriki Textile, 35 DLR (AD) 123.</u>

52. Before the learned Arbitrator, the appellant asserted that he had no jurisdiction to arbitrate on the reference. But the learned Arbitrator dismissed the objection on the view that 2nd party did not reply to the legal notice of the 1st party which made the contractor to go to the Court and that 2nd party did not press the issue and declined to argue on the issue before him. He saw clause 25 of the contract. Being fully aware of the arbitration clause, when the learned Arbitrator of his standing and long experience in law could press to go forward with the arbitration, how long the appellant could press the issue is easily understood. Such giving up by the appellant does not vest him with the power which he did not have under the contract.

53. The learned arbitrator found that the cancellation of the contract dated 25-3-1995 was illegal. First, on such date no contract was executed, the work order was issued. Secondly, the work order was cancelled since the company was already blacklisted for gross violation of the terms of the contract for construction of another bridge at Gazipur on 3-4-1997. The company was enlisted. On 11-1-1995 with the office of the appellant. When the company became blacklisted, he ceased to continue any other work of the same authority. Clause 3(a) of the contract gives the authority ample power to rescind the contract and with the rescission of the contract, the security deposit of the contractor shall stand forfeited. The learned Arbitrator therefore arrived at the finding on surmise and conjecture without taking into consideration the terms of the contract.

54. Similarly, he held that the pile construction suffered due to the delay of the 2nd party on annexure 8 and 28 in supplying the layout. But none of the annexures support the learned Arbitrator to arrive at such decision. We have already found that the layout of the pile construction along with other papers was given to the company with the work order which the company did not deny. So, the finding of the learned arbitrator is against the record.

55. Demand for disclosure of remuneration and fees, etc. received by an arbitrator(s) or umpire is getting stronger day by day. In the case of the Bangladesh Power Development Board vs M/s Builders Corporation, (2004) 1 LG 38 a Division Bench of this Division has already held that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in not mentioning in the award what he received as fees and remuneration for the arbitration. We are also of the view that the learned Arbitrator is obliged to state in the award the remuneration and fees received and from which of the parties to ensure fair play and strengthen public confidence in arbitration.

56. In the circumstances, there is no escape from the conclusion that the company improperly procured the award from the learned Arbitrator, which was also invalid. But the learned Subordinate Judge missed the real issues and committed serious error in rejecting the application for setting aside the award and such order cannot be sustained in law. The appeal succeeds, accordingly.

57. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. Impugned order refusing to set aside the award is hereby set aside and the award dated 22-6-2000 is accordingly set aside.' The arbitration agreement now ceases to have any effect.

Communicate at once.

End.

full_judgment:
In this Rule three orders all dated 19-11-200 I passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court,Khulna in Title Suit No. 349 of 2002 are challenged. By the order No. 6 an application under Order VII rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure was rejected. By order No. 7, the defendants were restrained from obstructing the plaintiffs in performing their functions till disposal of the suit. By order No.8, the defendants by an order of ad- interim injunction, are restrained from holding any discussion on agenda No. 6 to the notice of the Annual General Meeting No. BHMMA K (23)/2002-2003/65 dated 13-11-2002.

2. In this matter, the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 instituted the suit praying for a decree for declaration that the letter No. BHMMA- 23/2002/184 dated 19-10-2002, issued by the defendant No. 2 to the plaintiff No. 2 is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs, contending, inter alia, that they are the elected president and vice president of the Khulna Circle of the Bangladesh Hardware Machinery Merchants Association ('Association' in short) for the term 2000 to 2002, that the defendant Nos. 3 to 5 misused power and funds of the organisation, that they tried to victimise the plaintiffs, that the defendants hatched up a conspiracy and managed to issue the letter No. BHMMA-II/02/140 dated 17-8-2002, that in furtherance of their conspiracy the defendants issued the impugned letter dated 19-10- 2002 by which the plaintiffs were suspended from their posts of president and vice president of the Khulna Circle of the aforesaid organisation. On receipt of the notice of the suit the petitioner Nos. 1 and 3 (defendant Nos. 3 and 5) and the petitioner No. 2 (defendant No. 4) filed two separate applications under Order VII rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, contending, inter alia, that the Association is a registered trade organisation and the plaintiff being a member of the said organisation, challenged the decision of the organisation in the suit which is barred under section 12 of the Trade Organisation Ordinance, 1961. The learned Judge in his order No. 6, dated 19-11-2002, observed that under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Civil Court has got jurisdiction to try all kinds of suits of civil nature and since the instant suit is civil in nature, he rejected the said application under Order VII rule 11of the Code of Civil Procedure, relying on the decision of the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Commerce vs Nizamuddin Haider 1985 BLD 57, held that in spite of express ouster of jurisdiction, the Civil Court has got jurisdiction to examine whether the impugned action has been taken illegally or in excess of jurisdiction. The learned Judge further held that the forum of arbitration provided by section 12(2) of the Trade Organisation Ordinance, 1961, is not suitable in the present case. On the same day, by a separate order No. 7 dated 19-11-2002, he granted temporary injunction and restrained the defendants from obstructing the plaintiffs in performing their functions till disposal of the suit.

3. There was another application filed on behalf of the plaintiff praying for ad-interim and temporary injunction to restrain the defendants from holding Annual General Meeting of Khulna Circle of the organisation scheduled to be held on 27-11-2002, in pursuance of the notice dated 13-11-2002. The learned judge after hearing, by his order No.8 allowed ad-interim injunction restraining the defendants from holding any discussion on agenda No. 6 of the notice of the said Annual General Meeting to be held on 27-11-2002.

4. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid orders rejecting the application under Order VII rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and also in respect of the orders of temporary injunction, the petitioners filed the instant revisional application.

5. Mr Quamrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that in view of the bar of suit imposed by section 12 of the Trade Organisation Ordinance of 1961 (Ordinance No. 45 of 1961), the suit is not maintainable and since it is barred under the said provision, the learned Judge erred in law in not rejecting the plaint. So far the orders of injunctions are concerned; the learned Advocate submits he would not press those matters.

6.
