One is the power requiring such person to furnish in the prescribed form and within the prescribed time a statement of his property and the other is the satisfaction that the person co learned has in his possession pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. The first part is the power to act and the second part is the exercise of mental faculty of being satisfied. It is our view that this satisfaction that a person has property in his possession disproportionate to his known sources of income is not derived from or dependent on the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. This satisfaction is not a power or a duty which has been conferred by the Act but is state of mind about a person's properties and assets being disproportionate to his known sources of income. Therefore this satisfaction which may exist in the mind of the Government not being a power or duty conferred by the Act there cannot be any delegation of the pre-condition of satisfaction of the Government to the Director General of Bureau of Anti-Corruption. So in spite of the delegation of power as contained in Memo No. পত্র সংখ্যা জানি (দুদ)। প্রশাসন-29/89-1149 dated 3-10-89, the pre-condition of satisfaction for exercise of power under section 4(1) of the Act remains with the Government. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption can proceed with the power conferred under section 4(1) only if the Government is satisfied. It is therefore not enough if only the Director General of Bureau of Anti-Corruption is satisfied that a person has property disproportionate to his known source of income in order to exercise the power to direct a person to submit list of his wife's and dependent's properties under section 4(1) of the Act. It was argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioners in writ petition No. 5190 of 1996 and writ petition No. 53.84 of 1996 that the mere statement that the Government was satisfied was not enough. The satisfaction had to be objective on the basis of specific material which must be disclosed in the notice under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act. 17. It was submitted in these writ petitions that there was no such objective satisfaction when the impugned orders were issued on the petitioners. They were meant to harass the petitioners. In the affidavit-in-opposition the respondents have denied that the notices were meant to harass the petitioners as the satisfaction of the Government was on the basis of the report of the Central Bank which was placed before us. We are not in a position to go into the question whether the report of the Central Bank was correct or that it was sufficient for the Government to have been satisfied to undertake an enquiry under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act. Such satisfaction is not justiciable as long as there is some material to from an opinion. We cannot question whether there is a prima facie case for satisfaction to carry out an enquiry as long as there is some material. In support he may refer to the case Pearlberg vs Varty reported in 2 All ER (1972) 6 in which there was a reference to the observation made by Lord Ried in the case of Wiseman vs Bormeman. Lord Ried said: "It is, I think, not entirely irrelevant to have in mind that it is very unusual for there to be a judicial determination of the question whether there is a prime facie case. Every public officer who has to decide whether to prosecute or raise proceedings ought first to decide whether there is a prima facie, case but no one supposes that justice requires that he should first seek the comments of the accused or the defendant on the material before him. So there is nothing inherently unjust in reaching such a decision in the absence of the other party." 18. In these cases the petitioners merely have been asked for the statement of their properties and they can always show to the relevant authority that the satisfaction of the Government that they have properties disproportionate to their known sources of income is not correct. 19. The next point was that section 4 is violative of fundamental right guaranteed under Article 35(4) of the Constitution. The Division Bench in the aforementioned case of Mustafiz Rahman has observed as follows: "The petitioner of each of the four writ petitions was asked to submit the statement in the prescribed form giving statements with full particulars of the properties acquired in his name or in the benami the liabilities and the sources of income. On the face of the impugned orders there is nothing to suggest that the respective petitioner was made accused and formal accusation had been made against him and it cannot, also, be said that as accused person he is being compelled to give evidence against himself, Article 35(4) of the Constitution will be attracted only, if the proceedings 'started with the accusation' and the person who seeks its protection is already an accused person and he is being compelled to make the statement. By the respective impugned order, the respective petitioner has been asked to submit statements with full particulars stating the acquisition of properties and the sources of income so that he can satisfy the Government that the properties acquired by him are not disproportionate to his known sources of income. Calling of statements detailing full particulars cannot be characterised as accusation as contemplated under Article 35(4) of the Constitution and the impugned orders do not offend the Fundamental Right guaranteed under Article 35(4) of the Constitution. We are, thus, of this considered view that the impugned orders under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act do not offend the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Article 35(4) of the Constitution." 20. We are in agreement with view held by the Division Bench. By the impugned memos the petitioners have simply been asked to give the statement of their properties, that is, to know the actual fact whether the petitioner has property beyond his known sources of income. There is no fundamental right to privacy or secrecy in respect of property and wealth of a person and therefore calling upon the petitioners to submit statement of their properties does not violate any fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. The petitioners by the impugned notices have not been accused of possessing properties disproportionate to their known sources of income. Therefore they cannot be said to interfere with the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 35(4) of the Constitution. 21. In the case of Abdul Hafiz (Md) and others vs Director General, Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Government of Bangladesh reported in 51 DLR 72 it was observed by the Division Bench of the High Court: “It need be stated further that in the impugned notice, no compulsion is mandated upon the petitioners to give evidence against themselves. In the enquiry before the District Anti-Corruption Officer, the petitioners can very well controvert the allegations made against them in the petition of complaint. It cannot, thus, be suggested that by mere issuance of notices, the petitioners, as accused persons, are compelled to give evidence or to be witnesses against themselves. Article 35(4), therefore, is of no avail to the petitioners." Consequently we do not think that the provision of section 4 of the Anti-Corruption Act is ultra vires of the Constitution. 22. In writ petition No. 5190 of 1996 we find that a reference to the Prime Minister, Secretariat Memo No. 23.40.4.2.0.149.96-461 dated 29-9-96 (Annexure-A). The impugned order also contended that the Government was satisfied that the petitioner has moveable and immovable properties beyond his known sources of income. We have already said that this belief/satisfaction was on the basis of the report of the Central Bank. In such circumstances the requirement of satisfaction as required under the Act has been met and the order under section 4(1) for submitting a statement of moveable and immovable property does not appear to be illegal or without lawful authority. It is merely an order to submit his statement of his property and is not an accusation. The petitioner can always controvert the belief/satisfaction of the Government that he has property beyond his known sources of income. 23. In the result, the Rule issued in this writ petition is discharged. 24. Writ petition No 5384 of 1996- the impugned notice is similar to one Writ petition No. 5190 of 1996 and for the same reason we find no reason to declare the impugned notice in this writ petition to be illegal or without lawful authority . 25. In the result, the Rule in this writ petition is also discharged. 26. In writ petition No. 5382 of 1996 the impugned notice speaks of satisfaction of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. We have already discussed above that the satisfaction of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is not the satisfaction of the Government as required under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act and we therefore find the impugned order to be illegal and without lawful authority. 27. The Rule is therefore made absolute. But so far as the rule relating to section 4 being ultra vires the constitution is concerned it is discharged. 28. In writ petition No. 736 of 1993 the impugned notice under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act refers to a source being Prime Minister Secretariat Memo No. 21.40.4.3.0.12.93-288 dated 11-2-93/29-10-99 (Annexure-A) but the order itself speaks of satisfaction of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. We have already held the view that the satisfaction of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption is not enough to authorise the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to issue notice under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act. In that view of the matter the impugned order must be held to be illegal and without lawful authority. 29. The Rule is therefore made absolute. In writ petition No. 2538 of 1991 the source was President Secretariat's Memo No. 41.20.3.0.9.91-427 dated 19-8-91 (Annexure-A) but the order itself said that the notice under section 4(1) of the Anti-Corruption Act was sent as the Bureau of Anti-Corruption was satisfied from a preliminary investigation that the petitioner had properties beyond his known sources of income. For the same reason as stated in writ petition No. 736 of 1993 we find that the impugned order to be illegal and without lawful authority. The Rule is therefore made absolute. M A Aziz J : I fully agree with the judgment delivered by my learned brother Mr Mainur Reza Chowdhury J but I want to add a few words of my own as regards the "satisfaction aspect" of the impugned notice (in certain cases) under section 4 of the Anti-Corruption Act. Arguments we advanced that the expression satisfaction has no magic in it so that once the Government says that it is satisfaction that someone has amassed wealth and assets disproportionate to his known sources of income he may be subjected to enquiry and investigation simply by serving a notice under section 4 of the Anti-Corruption Act asking him to submit a statement of his properties/assets without disclosing the material basis of such satisfaction. It was also argued that under section 3 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 where the same expression i.e. "satisfaction" has been used, the Government is duty bound to disclose in the grounds of detention the material basis of its satisfaction that the detenu is required to be detained, failing which the order of detention is liable to be declared illegal and not sustainable and the same principle is applicable in a case under section 4 of the Anti-Corruption Act. 32. We are afraid this proposition cannot be accepted because the scheme of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 are widely different. Firstly, under section 3 of the Special Powers Act a person can be put behind the bar without any trial if the Government is satisfied that his detention is necessary in order to prevent him from indulging in prejudicial activities defined under section 2(f) of the said Act and that is why section 8 of the said Act has made it imperative that the detenu must be served with the grounds of detention within 15 days so that the detenu can make an effective representation against the order of detention for the consideration of the detaining authority, whereas there is no such corresponding provision in the Anti-Corruption Act. A notice under section 4 is a mere notice to submit a statement of assets and liabilities for the purpose of preliminary enquiry for ascertaining as to whether there is a prima facie case against the recipient of the notice. If upon such preliminary .enquiry no material to proceed is found out the recipient of the notice is let off and if materials are available, on completion of investigation a charge sheet is submitted and the person is put on trial. At the trial stage a formal charge.is framed and accordingly the accused gets an opportunity to refute the charges i.e. at the time of framing charge as well as at the time of trial. Unlike preventive detention the recipient of the notice under section 4 cannot be confined/detained forthwith. Section 4 relates to preliminary investigation. A notice under prosecution and resultant conviction and as such it is not necessary to divulge the materials which satisfied the Government to issue a notice asking the recipient to submits a statement of his assets and liabilities. 33. In order to prevent the misuse and abuse of the provision of section 4 we however feel that the High Court can see as to whether the said power is exercised in accordance with law and in so doing can look into the material basis of the satisfaction of the Government in view of the fact that section 4 has an inbuilt mechanism to put a person on trial for failure to submit the statements or for submitting a false statement under section 4(1) of the Act. However, the adequacy or otherwise of the material cannot be gone into by the Court. 34. Satisfaction is a state of mind which calls for an exercise of mental faculty. Mental faculty of two persons are never the same. The satisfaction of the highest functionary of the Government as has been held by a Division Bench of the High Court Division to be necessary, cannot be of the quality and standard as that of the Director General of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. 35. Section 9 speaks of delegation of power and duty upon the Director General of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption conferred under section 4 of the said Act and the pre-condition of such satisfaction is the satisfaction of the Government. The satisfaction aspect of section 4 is thus retained by the Government and it cannot be delegated. 36. Section 4 is split up into several parts ie receipt of an information, an enquiry there into, the resultant satisfaction derived therefrom, empowering the Government to ask the recipient of the notice under section 4(1) to submit statements of assets and liabilities. Thus on receipt of information that someone has amassed assets and properties disproportionate to his known source income there has to be an enquiry and upon such enquiry if the Government is satisfied that the said person has in-fact acquired assets beyond his known sources of income, then and only then the Government may exercise the power of asking someone to submit a statement of his assets and liabilities and this power can be delegated under section 9 of the Anti-Corruption Act. Section 9 speaks of delegation of power and duty not of satisfaction and pursuant to section 9, powers and duties mentioned in section 4 have been delegated vide Memo No পত্র সংখ্যা রাস/জানি (দুদ)। প্রশাসন-২৯/৮৯-১১৪৯ dated 3-10-89 So from a reading of section 9 and the aforesaid Memo we find that nowhere in the Act anything but power and duty have been delegated by the Government to the Director General of Bureau of Anti-Corruption because the condition precedent for such delegation is satisfaction of the Government which is incapable of delegation. End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendant appellant-petitioner against the judgment and decree 18-4-1990 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 121 of 1989 affirming those dated 13-4-1989 of the learned Assistant Judge, Naogaon in Other Class Suit No. 194 of 1988 decreeing the suit

2. The facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule, in brief, may be stated as follows:

3. That the opposite party No. 1 being plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 194 of 1988 in the court of the learned Assistant Judge, Naogaon for declaration contending, inter alia, that the defendant No. 1 petitioner herein joined his service of Laskarpur Purbasha Primary School on 3-1-1980 and he was removed from service on 11-2-1986 and the plaintiff was appointed in his place as third teacher of the school on 1-3-1986 but while the school was taken over by the Government with effect from 15-11-1986, the Chairman of the Selection Committee, the opposite party No. 4, collusively omitted the name of the plaintiff from the list of teachers and selected the defendant No. 1 for absorption, which was approved by the defendant No. 3 though at the relevant time the defendant No. 1 was not in service of the school. The plaintiff submitted representation before the defendant No. 3 but without any result The defendant No. 1 was illegally absorbed and was appointed as Assistant Teacher of the aforesaid school, after being taken over by the Government in place of the plaintiff.

4. The case of the defendant-petitioner herein, in short, is that he joined in service of Laskarpur Purbasha Primary School (hereinafter called as the school) when the school was a private school. He was appointed as Assistant Teacher on 3-1-1980 and he had been continuing in service. The school was taken over by the Government with effect from 15-11-1986 while he was duly absorbed as Assistant Teacher of the said school. Thereafter, the opposite party No. 8 being the Chairman of the former Managing Committee, out of personal grudge against the petitioner herein forcibly snatched away the record of the school from the custody of the Head Master and by tampering with the record, particularly the attendance register, the resolution book and visit book removed certain portion of the record and also inserted some portion, writing therein to show that the opposite party No.1 was included as the teacher of the school with effect from 21-3-1986 in place of the petitioner though, in fact, the opposite party No. 1 was never appointed as teacher. He filed the suit at the instance of the opposite party No. 8.

5. The defendant No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 4-6 contested the suit by filing separate written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable and particularly, it is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also the suit was not maintainable in the civil Court as the same was triable by the Administrative Tribunal, since the service matter was involved in the suit and made allegations against the defendant No. 8 as stated above.

6. The learned Assistant Judge, Naogaon tried the suit and on considering the materials and evidence on record decreed the suit.

7. The defendant-petitioner herein preferred Title Appeal No. 121 of 1980 in the court of the learned District Judge, Naogaon against the aforesaid judgment passed by the Assistant Judge, Naogaon. On transfer the learned Subordinate Judge, Naogaon heard the appeal and dismissed the same and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

8. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner and Mr Shahidul Islam, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 appeared at the time of hearing.

<u>9. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the suit was completely barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the suit was filed for declaration simpliciter without any prayer for consequential relief. Moreover, since service matter of a Government employee is involved in this suit the same is not maintainable in the ordinary Civil Court as it is triable by the Administrative Tribunal and there is a complete bar to entertain such suit by the ordinary Civil Court. In spite of clear averment made in the written statement of both the defendant Nos. 1 and 4-6 to the effect that the trial Court did not frame any issue as to whether the suit was maintainable in the ordinary civil Court or the same was triable by the Administrative Tribunal. In support of his submission Mr Halder refers the decisions reported in 35 DLR 224, 49 DLR 38. He has drawn my attention to the prayer portion of the plaint and submits that the first portion of the prayer is as follows: আরজি বর্ণিত যাবতীয় কারনাধীনে ৫ নং বিবাদী কর্��ৃক ১ নং বিবাদী লঙ্করপুর পূর্বাশা প্রাথমিক বিদ্যালয়ে আত্তিকরন জন্য গত ইং ২১-১১-১৯৮৭ তারিখের বাছাই করনের সিদ্ধান্ত ৩ নং বিবাদী গত ইং ২৮-১০-১৯৯৭ তারিখের তাহা অনুমোদন ও ৫ নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক উক্ত বাছাই ও অনুমোদনের পোষকতায় নিয়োগ পত্র বেয়াইনি জগসাজশী, অকার্যকরী ও এক্তিয়ার বহির্ভূত গন্যে বাদীর নালিশী বিদ্যালয়ে শিক্ষক পদে আত্মীকরণ ও নিয়োগ পত্র প্রাপ্তির অধিকার আছে মর্মে বাদী কে বিবাদী গনের বিরুদ্ধে বিজ্ঞাপনী ডিক্রি দিতে মর্জি হয়।This portion of the prayer made in the plaint cannot be declared by the civil Court as because the civil Court cannot declare legal character of the plaintiff.</u>

10. Mr. Shahidul Islam, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1, submits that the defendant No.1, petitioner herein, was appointed as third teacher of the school on 2-1-1986 but he was dismissed on 11-2-1986 as he was suffering from Tuberculosis and he was habituated in remaining absent in the school. The plaintiff was appointed as third teacher of the school in his place on 1-3-1986. In the month of November, 1986 the Government decided to take over the school and the previous Managing Committee was dissolved and fresh committee was constituted, wherein the plaintiff was included as a member of the Managing Committee as teachers representative.

<u>11. The defendant No.5 directed the defendant No. 2 i.e. the Head Master of the school, to send a list of the existing teachers of the school to him. The defendant No.8 forwarded the list being submitted by the defendant No. 2 to the defendant No.5 on 16-7-1986 including the name of the plaintiff. Thereafter, a scrutiny committee (বাছাই কমিটি) was constituted being headed by the defendant No.4, the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon who replaced the name of the plaintiff and included the name of the defendant No. 1 beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff, without giving him any chance of hearing, although the defendant No. 1 was not in service of the school at the relevant time. The Upazila Chairman and the Chairman of the Managing Committee of the school submitted representation to the Director General of Primary Education Department not to accept the list being sent by the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon. The defendant No.7 the Upazila Chairman, also made a prayer to the concerned authority to hold an enquiry but without any result. After filing of the suit on 11-7-1988 the learned Assistant Judge fixed next date on 6-9-1988 for hearing on the point of maintainability and after hearing, the suit was found maintainable vide order dated 17-9-1988. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed written statement on 14-12-1988 and thereafter on 28-12-1988 the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed an application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint and after hearing the parties, the learned Assistant Judge found the suit maintainable and rejected the prayer for rejection of the plaint, against which no relief was sought for in the higher forum by the defendants. In this context Mr. Shahidul Islam submits that after the aforesaid orders being passed by the trial Court and having no relief was sought for against such order by the defendant in the higher forum, they cannot raise this question of maintainability at the revisional stage in this court and the defendants are barred by the principles of estoppel and waiver. Mr. Islam further submits that the suit is maintainable in the present form and the same is not barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In support of his submission he refers to the decisions reported in 45 DLR 375, 1995 BLD 339, 7 BLT (AD) 361, 50 DLR 472 and submits that in the aforesaid reported decisions it has been consistently held that the suit for declaration simpliciter in service matter is maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief.</u>

<u>12. Mr. Islam further submits that the list being forwarded to the defendant No. 5 contained the name of the plaintiff as third teacher of the school and at the same time he was selected as member of the newly constituted Managing Committee of the school as teachers' representative. But the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon being the Chairman of the scrutiny committee most arbitrarily excluded the name of the plaintiff from the list which has been placed for absorption as teacher by substituting the name of the defendant No.1 who was not a teacher of the school at the relevant time. The aforesaid act of the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon is violative of the principles of natural justice in this connection he refers to the decisions reported in 49 DLR 257,50 DLR 472 and 7 BLT (AD) 361.</u>

13. On perusal of the judgment passed by the trial Court it appears that the learned Assistant Judge discussed the evidence on record both oral and documentary elaborately and found that the defendant No.1 was dismissed from service on 11-2-1986 by the Managing Committee of the school for his negligence of duties and as he was suffering from Tuberculosis. On the other hand, the plaintiff was appointed in his place on 29-2-1986 and his name was duly recommended for absorption as teacher by the Government and it was admitted by the District Primary Education Officer and Upazila Education Officer in their testimony that the list containing the name of the plaintiff was forwarded to the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon who himself replaced his name and included the name of the defendant No. 1 and it was held by the trial Court that the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon ignoring the decision of other members of the scrutiny committee most illegally excluded the name of the plaintiff from the list of teachers to be absorbed as the Government teacher and it was not explained by the defendant No. 4 who contested the suit.

<u>14. On proper appreciation of the evidence on record the trial Court decreed the suit. The appellate Court below also rightly considered the evidences on record both oral and documentary and after proper discussion of evidence affirmed the judgment passed by the trial Court and held that the plaintiff is derived from being absorbed as teacher of the school while it was taken over by the Government and he had legal right to be absorbed as teacher of the said school. It appears from the judgments of both the courts below that the defendant No.8, the founder Chairman of the school, supported the plaintiff's case and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 filed written statement supporting the case of the plaintiff' and the defendant Nos. 2, 5 and 6 also supported the case of the plaintiff in their cross-examination. Further, it appears from the attendance register which was exhibited before the trial Court as exhibit "Ka" that the defendant No. 1 was absent for long period but by erasing the relevant column he was allowed to put signature, which was done in collusion with the defendant No.2 to show that at the relevant time he was teacher of the said school. From the resolution book it appears that he was dismissed from service with effect from 11-2-1986 and, on the other hand, the plaintiff was appointed in his place with effect from 11-2-1986.</u>

15. On close scrutiny of the evidence on record it is clearly proved that all the lists contain the name of the plaintiff which was sent to the defendant No. S by the Managing Committee of the school and the documents produced in the trial Court proved. that the plaintiff was a legally appointed teacher in place of the defendant No. 1 who was dismissed for negligence of duties and as being patient of tuberculosis but the defendant No.4, the Deputy Commissioner, Naogaon most illegally and arbitrarily without affording any chance of hearing to the plaintiff excluded his name from the list behind his back and included the name of the defendant No.1 in the list of existing teachers of the school, though he was dismissed earlier from service and he was not at all a teacher of the school.

16. All the above facts are being concurrent findings of fact by the courts below this court should not disturb the concurrent finding of fact in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. Reference may be made to the case of Abdul Quddus Mohammad vs Nizamuddin Ahmed and others: 4 MLR (AD) 129 wherein it has been held that when the findings of the appellate Court are found on correct appreciation on evidences on record and the High Court discharged the Rule there is nothing to interfere with the said judgment. Another decision reported in 3 MLR (AD) 127 may be referred to wherein it has been held that concurrent finding of fact of the trial Court and the court of appeal based on proper appreciation of evidences on record and not vitiated by non-reading or misreading of material evidence on record, such finding cannot be interfered with in exercise of revisional jurisdiction.

17. Before parting with the decision I propose to discuss the decision referred to above by the learned Advocates of both the parties.

18. Mr. Halder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has referred to the case reported in 35 DLR 224 wherein a Single Bench of this court held that "A suit for declaration that the plaintiffs dismissal was illegal and not binding without asking for consequential relief for enforcing the declamatory decree. Omission to pray for consequential relief for enforcing declamatory decree renders it unenforceable in law". This decision was upheld by the Appellate Division in an unreported case being CPSLA No. 299 of 1983. On the other hand, a Division Bench of this court being presided over by his Lordships Mr. Justice Md. Ismailuddin Sarker held that "a suit for declaration that the order of removal of the plaintiff, a bank officer, from service, was void and inoperative and he remained in service, was maintainable without any prayer for further relief'. Both the reported cases were considered by his Lordships Mr. Justice Syed Amirul Islam in a judgment, reported in 49 DLR 38 wherein it has been held that in service matter a suit for simple declaration without any prayer for consequential relief is not maintainable. In this reported case various decisions of this sub- continent were considered and held that since the decision reported in 35 DLR 224 was affirmed by the Appellate Division in CPSLA No. 229 of 1983 (correct number is 299 of 1983) it was binding upon the High Court Division and, as such, the decisions reported in 45 DLR and 11 DLR were found conflicting with the proposition of law as laid down by the Appellate Division.

19. It appears to me that there are conflicting decisions on this point of law as regards interpretation of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. After the aforesaid decisions reported in 35 DLR., 45 DLR and 49 DLR the Appellate Division passed other judgments, one of which was reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 239, the case of Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Syed Moazzem Hossain and others: wherein it has been held that "section 42 Discretion of Court as to declaration of status or right:

"A declamatory suit need not be confined within the terms of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act which is meant for obtaining specific relief. A declaration can be sought for various other matters as well".

<u>20. The Appellate Division held in the case of General Manager (West Zone) Bangladesh Railway and others vs Din Mohmmad and others reported in 7 BLT (AD) 361 that: "Suit for declaration that the plaintiffs are entitled to get appointment on the basis of letter of appointment is maintainable". It has been held in paragraph 5 of this reported case that" it appears from the impugned judgment that the learned Single Judge found that the plaintiffs were listed in the panel at serial Nos. 23 and 24 respectively whereas appointment was given at serial No. 25 in the panel list prepared in this regard. The positive case of the defendants is that after lifting of the Government embargo the plaintiffs would be appointed. All the courts below including the High Court Division having found that the embargo was lifted on 2-2-1989 and thereafter the appointment letter was issued in respect of serial No. 25 without issuing any appointment letter to these plaintiffs. All the courts below having found that the offer letter of appointment has created a right in favour of the plaintiffs, the suit as framed is maintainable and, as such, we do not want to enter into the question, the petition is dismissed."</u>

21. From close reading of the aforesaid decision reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 239, 7 BLT, (AD) 361 it appears that the suit for simple declaration is maintainable in respect of service matter without a prayer for consequential relief.

<u>22. We may profitably refer to a case of Jibon Bima Corporation vs Mustafa Hussain and another reported in 50 DLR 411 wherein it has been held that "A declamatory decree passed in a case without any prayer for consequential relief is an annuity. Such declaration is a gain and its implementation is dependent on as to whom the decree is passed against. In the instant case the defendant being a statutory corporation, there is no reason to believe that such corporation will not implement the decision of the court. In this reported case various decisions including the decision reported in 35 DLR 224, 49 DLR 38, 1948 AIR (PC) 121, 52 CWN 761 (PC), PLD 1949 (Lahore) 219, 22 DLR 589, 45 DLR 375, 1995 BLD (AD) 239, 37 DLR 7, 11 DLR 528 and many other decisions were considered. It has been observed in the aforesaid decisions that while the Appellate Division in deciding the CPSLA No. 299 of 1983 it appears that the relevant decisions as stated above including 35 DLR 24 have not been placed before their Lordships for consideration. But their Lordships in the case reported in 45 DLR considered the aforesaid decisions and also the decision reported in 35 DLR 224 and then held that the suit for simple declaration is maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief</u>

<u>23. On a plain reading of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act it appears that seeking of further relief is made compulsory only when a declaration by itself would not be an effective remedy, for instance where a dismissed government servant filed suit for declaration that he, was dismissed wrongfully but did not ask for further relief by way of arrears of pay. In a suit like the present granting of the declaration would confer a substantive relief on the plaintiff and the relief for arrears of pay is not a further relief but a separate relief and therefore, the suit was competent.</u>

<u>24. It is well settled that a suit for mere declaration that an order of dismissal passed against the Government servant is illegal, inoperative and void without a prayer for consequential relief is maintainable and section 42 of the Specific Relief Act does not bar such a suit.</u>

25. Further reference may be made in 1995 BLD (AD) 239: It has been held therein that "A declamatory suit need not be confined in the terms of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. A declaration may be made for various matters as well" From the discussion made above, I hold that the suit instituted by the plaintiff was maintainable and it was not barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and I am in respectful agreement with the views taken in the decisions reported in 50 DLR 411 passed by his Lordships Mr. Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman and the decision reported in 45 DLR 375 passed by his Lordships Mr. Justice Ismailuddin Sarker (as his Lordship then was) and held that suit for declaration simpliciter was maintainable without any prayer for further relief.

26. As regards the jurisdiction of the civil Court, considering the facts and circumstances of the present suit I hold that the civil Court has jurisdiction to declare any, legal character of a person and the same is not triable by the Administrative Tribunal.

27. During hearing of the Rule the learned Advocate for the petitioner filed some papers namely, photo copy of the circular and office orders of the Government functionaries including photo copy of the service book of the petitioner, which, were filed through supplementary affidavit and the learned Advocate for the opposite party filed counter-affidavit raising objection that since the documents were not filed before the courts below and the same are not authenticated photo copies, they should not be considered by this court at the revisional stage. I find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party. Since the papers and documents were not produced before the courts below and the same were not admitted in evidence this court cannot consider those papers and documents though it is filed through supplementary affidavit at this stage. Let the supplementary affidavit and counter-affidavit thereto be kept in record.

28. In view of the discussion made above, the facts which has been decided with reference to evidences on record by the courts below and arrived at a decision on concurrent findings of fact it is immune from interference by this court unless finding of facts could be proved perverse but the learned Advocate for the petitioner could not point out any such perversity and misreading or non-consideration of evidence by the courts below rather on my careful consideration of the evidences on record and other materials available on record I find that both the courts below, elaborately discussed each and every part of evidence and on proper appreciation of evidence on record, the impugned judgment of affirmance was passed by the appellate Court below and I do not find any error being committed in passing the impugned judgment, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the Rule should be discharged.

29. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

Send down the lower courts record immediately.

End.

lawyer:
Md Altaf Hossain, Advocate ------ For the Applicant. 
No one appears ------ For the Respondent.
parties:
Sogra Begum   ------ Appellant
Vs.
Commissioner of Taxes  ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: This is an application filed under section 5 read with section 14 of the Limitation Act, for condonation of delay of 159 days in filing the reference application under section 160 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984.

2. It is stated that the petitioner is a pardahnashin lady and a housewife and she was assessed to tax under section 82(2)/93 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 on total income of Taka 11,61,555.00 for the assessment year 1987-88 and being aggrieved by the aforesaid assessment order an appeal was preferred before the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) who had granted relief to the petitioner and deleted the addition of Taka 10,07,205.00 against which the department preferred a second appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal which by its order dated 1-8-99 set aside the first appellate order of the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) and restored the order of the DCT. It is further stated that the Tribunal communicated the said order to the petitioner on 29-11-99 when she had a massive heart attack and she was also not keeping good health seeing the murder of her husband and the aforesaid order was misplaced by her which was however re-traced by her subsequently and handed over the same to her lawyer on 26-3-2000. Thereafter, an application was filed before the Tribunal under section 173 of the Ordinance, 1984 for rectification as the order itself was a mistake on the very face of it as the investment in the year 1968 to 1986 cannot be income during the income year 1987-88. So, on the good belief the petitioner preferred to file an application under section 173 of the Ordinance for rectification of the order of the Appellate Tribunal and ultimately, that application being Miscellaneous Application No. 58 of 1999-2000 was dismissed by the Tribunal vide order dated 4-5-2000 and the said order was communicated on 31-5-2000. The petitioner being aggrieved by the said order of Appellate Tribunal passed in the aforesaid Miscellaneous case now intends to file a reference application under section 160 of the Ordinance before this Court against the order dated 1-8-99 passed by the Tribunal in ITA No. 1234 of 1997-98 (Assessment year 1987-88). The assessee received the copy of the order passed in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case on 31-5-2000 and the application for condonation of delay was filed on 1-8-2000.

3. Mr Md Altaf Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the assessee petitioner, submits that the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause in preferring the reference application before this Court under section 160 of the Ordinance against the order passed by the Tribunal in ITA No. 1234 of 1999-2000 on 1-8-99 inasmuch as she was misled by ill advice of her lawyer to file an application for rectification before the Tribunal under section 173 of the Ordinance as the mistake was apparent on the face of the record. The learned Advocate further submits that a litigant should not be punished for the negligence committed by the lawyer or for the ill advice of the Advocate. The learned Advocate further submits that in dealing with a condonation application the principle that substantial justice shall take preponderance over technical consideration should always be kept in view in deciding whether the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause for the delay and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 253 and the decision reported in 167 ITR 471 decision of the Indian Supreme Court. The learned Advocate also submitted that the instant case is covered by the provisions of section 14 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as the application filed under section 173 of the Ordinance was before a wrong forum.

4. Perused the application and considered the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. In this application the clear case that has been made out by the petitioner is that being aggrieved by the assessment order dated 23-11-95 passed by the Assistant Commissioner of Taxes for the assessment year 1987-88 the petitioner preferred an appeal before the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) who allowed the appeal in part and deleted a substantial amount to the tune of Taka 10 lakh and odd but the department being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) took a Second Appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal being ITA No. 1234 of 1997-98 (Assessment year 1987-88) and the Tribunal after hearing the parties allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) and restored the order of the ACT. This order of the Tribunal was duly communicated to the assessee petitioner on 29-11-99 but that was a point of time when she had a massive heart attack and she was also not otherwise keeping good health since the murder of her husband in the heart of the city. Further contention of the petitioner is that the aforesaid order was misplaced by the petitioner and ultimately handed it over to her lawyer on 26-3-2000. It thus appears that the order was retraced by the petitioner but at what point of time that has not been disclosed in this petition but it is clear that on 26-3-2000 that order was handed over to the learned Advocate who on an examination of the same advised her to file an application for rectification of that order under section 173 of the Ordinance instead of filing a reference application under section 160 of the Ordinance before this Court and accordingly, an application was filed under the aforesaid section of the Ordinance which was registered as Miscellaneous Application No. 58 of 1999-2000. The Tribunal after hearing the petitioner dismissed that application on 4-5-2000 and communicated the said order to the petitioner on 31-5-2000 and now having failed before the Tribunal in her application under section 173 of the Ordinance she wants to prefer a reference application under section 160 of the Ordinance against the order of the Tribunal dated 1-8-99 passed in ITA No. 1234 of 97-98. It thus appears that on examination of the Tribunal's order dated 1-8-1999 the petitioner in her wisdom decided to file an application under section 173 of the Ordinance for rectification of the said order of the Tribunal rather than filing the reference application before this Court under section 160 of the Ordinance. It is clear that against that order she had two remedies available to her, i.e. to call in question the legality and propriety of the order of the Tribunal under section 160 of the Ordinance. It is clear that against that order she had two remedies available to her i.e. to call in question the legality and propriety of the order of the Tribunal under section 160 of the Ordinance before this Court by way of reference application or she could file an application before the Tribunal under section 173 of the Ordinance for rectification of the order of the mistake as the mistake was apparent on the face of it.

5. Now the question, that calls for determination in this application is that in view of the admitted facts and circumstances of the case can it be said that the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause in filing this reference application before this Court in time? From the facts noted above it is clear that the application under section 173 of the Ordinance was filed before the correct forum. Thus, the question of getting benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act does not arise at all. Moreover, the instant reference application is not against the order dated 31-5-2000 passed in Miscellaneous Application No. 58 of 1999-2000. Rather, this is against the original order of the Tribunal dated 1-8-99 passed in ITA No. 1234 of 1997/1998 (Assessment year 1987-88).

6. From the statements of facts disclosed in the petition it is obvious that the petitioner after examining the order of the Tribunal thought it wise not to file a reference application before this Court because there was mistake apparent on the face of the record and the necessary relief could be obtained by filing an application under section 173 of the Ordinance and that is why she filed the aforesaid application before the Tribunal for correction of the appellate order dated 1-8-89. It is only when the aforesaid application was rejected by the Tribunal on 8-5-2000 the petitioner now intends to file an application under section 160 of the Ordinance. If the petitioner wanted to call in question the legality and propriety of the Tribunal's order dated 1-8-99 passed in ITA No. 1234 1997/1998 (Assessment year 1987-88), she could file a reference application before this Court when the misplaced order dated 1-8-99 was recovered. But the petitioner after examining the Tribunal's order decided not to file a reference under section 160 of the Ordinance and filed an application under section 173 for rectification of the order. This cause of action was consciously chosen by the petitioner as she thought that she would get the adequate relief under that section. It is therefore, obvious that the petitioner was not prevented by sufficient cause in filing the reference application in time. It is alleged that the order dated 1-8-99 was misplaced. But deliberately the petitioner is silent as to the time when it was misplaced and when it was ultimately found. If the story of misplacement is correct then also the petitioner could not get any benefit on that Court inasmuch as she could obtain certified copy of the order on 4-7-2000 for filing this reference application.

<u>7. In view of these facts and circumstances it cannot be said that the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause in filing the reference application in time. The petitioner voluntarily decided to seek her remedy under section 173 of the Ordinance rather than filing a reference under section 160 of the Ordinance. After failing in her attempt made under section 173 of the Ordinance now the petitioner wants to fall back on section 160 of the Ordinance to attack the order dated 1-8-99 on merit. If now the petitioner is allowed to file a reference application after rejection of the application filed under section 173 of the Ordinance, on 4-5-2000, the petitioner will be given a long latitude, in other words, she will have lots of both the worlds. Such a course is not allowed by the Ordinance. Even in civil Courts if any ex parte decree is passed against a defendant he can either file an application under Order 9 rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree and/or file an appeal before the higher Court. The only limitation is that if the appeal is heard first the Order 9 rule 13 application becomes incompetent i.e. the jurisdiction to pass orders on an application under the Rule subsists only so long as the appellate Court does not decide the appeal. Similarly, in the instant case also the petitioner could resort to both the remedies simultaneously and decision in one would render the other infructuous. But in the present case the assessee giving a go-by to one remedy jumped on the other on her own and when it was proved futile she wants to resort to the other and such course of action is not permissible under the law. In the premises, therefore, the petitioner cannot be allowed to file a reference application now after being unsuccessful in her attempt before the Tribunal under section 173 of the Ordinance.</u>

8. There is another aspect of the case. This is an application for condonation of delay. It is now well settled that each day's delay has to be explained. In this case the petitioner has utterly failed to explain each day's delay satisfactorily inasmuch as the impugned order was communicated to her on 29-11-99 but when it was misplaced is not mentioned. There is no indication when the said order was retraced. It is only stated that the said order was handed over to her lawyer on 26-3-2000. When the Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1999-2000 was filed is also not disclosed. From the records it is found that the said Miscellaneous Case was rejected on 4-5-2000 and the present application was filed on 1-8-2000. It further appears that the result of the Miscellaneous Case was communicated to the petitioner on 31-5-2000 but what happened in between 31-5-2000 and 1-8-2000 is not explained. The petitioner has not made any attempt to explain the delay not to speak of each day's delay. On this score also the application is liable to be rejected.

9. We have gone through the decision relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and we are in respectful agreement with the principles laid down in those decisions. But in the facts and circumstances of the case they have no manner of application. The facts of instant case are quite distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid two cases. In the instant case the petitioner in the garb of filing an application for condonation of delay, in fact, wants to avail of two remedies against the same order. We are of the opinion that the assessee cannot be given two opportunities to assail the self-same order and in that view of the matter we do not find any materials on record to arrive at a finding that the petitioner was, in fact, prevented by sufficient cause in filing the reference application under section 160 of the Ordinance within the prescribed time.

<u>10. The petitioner at her peril had chosen to file an application under section 173 of the Ordinance rather than to file a reference application before this Court under section 160 of the Ordinance. It is now well settled that he who chooses the sword must perish by the sword. In that view of the matter the petitioner must not be allowed to fall back on section 160 of the Ordinance after being unsuccessful in Miscellaneous Application No. 58 of 1998.</u>

11. Accordingly, the application for condonation of delay is rejected.

12. There will be no order as to cost.

At this stage the learned Advocate for the petitioner makes a prayer for giving a certificate under section 162 of the Ordinance for filing an appeal before the Appellate Division. In the judgment we have discussed in detail the facts and circumstances of the case to show how the petitioner has miserably failed to make out a case for condonation of delay. Thus, it does not appear to us to be a fit case for granting a certificate as prayed for. Hence the prayer is rejected.

End.

parties:
Ripon Packaging and Accessories ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Eastern Bank Ltd and another  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Haque J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 12-7-99 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Transfer Miscellaneous Case No. 326 of 1999 rejecting the petitioner's application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure for transferring the Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 pending in the Court of 5th Subordinate Judge, Dhaka to Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka for being heard analogously with Title Suit No. 88 of 1998 pending in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka.

2. Short facts for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are that the present petitioner as plaintiff instituted a Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 in the Court of 5th Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 for a declaration that demand of interest and penal interest by the defendant Bank is illegal, fraudulent, collusive and they further prayed that the plaintiff company is under no obligation to entertain any claim of the defendants and is in no way liable for the dues of the defendant-opposite parties and further that those interest cannot be recovered from the plaintiff-petitioner. The plaintiff has further stated that the plaintiff company opened a CC Account No. 21 with the defendant-opposite party No. 2 subject to the condition that the defendant- opposite parties will extend from time to time credit facilities to the plaintiff-petitioner for their working capital import export credit finance and other normal banking facilities. In the year 1997, the defendant-opposite parties bank arbitrarily discontinued to provide the aforesaid facilities to the petitioner whereby the plaintiff-petitioner suffered a severe loss and damage and that the defendant-opposite parties bank are not entitled to claim the loan money given to the plaintiff-petitioner.

3. The plaintiff-petitioner has stated that the opposite party No. 2 bank as plaintiff also instituted a Title Suit No. 88 of 1998 in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka against the present petitioner impleading them as defendant for a decree of Taka 1,19,01,239.34 alleging inter alia, that the present petitioner availed various credit facilities from the opposite party No.2 bank and they failed to repay the same within the specific time. The present petitioner, in fact, has been contesting the suit.

4. The present-petitioner also filed an application in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure for transferring the Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 pending in the Court of 5th Subordinate Judge to Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.3 so that the said suit No. 153 of 1998 can be heard analogously with Title Suit No. 88 of 1998.

5. The District Judge, Dhaka after hearing the parties and on consideration of the law involved in it rejected the said application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure mainly on the ground that the Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 pending in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka cannot be tagged with the Title Suit No. 88 of 1998 pending in the 3rd Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka since the procedure of disposal of these 2 suits are different.

6. The present petitioner being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 12-7-99 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Transfer Miscellaneous Case No. 326 of 1999 moved this Court in revision and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr M Ziaul Hasan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the Artha Rin Adalat is also a Civil Court and the said Court is vested with the same self-jurisdiction as any other court is having in addition to the jurisdiction vested in it by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of section 5(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain there is no difficulty in disposing of other Civil cases, specifically in view of the fact that common question of law, facts and evidence are involved in both the suits and they should be heard analogously in order to avoid conflicting decisions which may arise.

<u>8. The opposite parties bank have filed counter-affidavit and denied the material facts and law as contended by the present-petitioner. Mr MA Samad, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-opposite parties’ bank, submits that the Artha Rin Adalat has been created by special law to deal with the cases of recovering of loan at the instance of the financial institution. The Artha Rin Adalat has its own certain special procedure, and the Artha Rin Adalat does not have jurisdiction to hear the ordinary civil cases along with the Artha Rin Adalat case. Further, the learned Advocate submits that the parties in both the suits are not the same and the issues are also not the same. The learned Advocate submits that the impugned judgment and order passed by the Court of District Judge is based on law and facts and it is not amenable to revision. Mr MA Samad, the learned Advocate, has placed reliance on a decision (1) in the case of Bangladesh Shilpa Bank vs Bangladesh Hotels Ltd reported in 38 DLR (AD) 70, (2) in the case of Ahmed Silk Mills Ltd vs Bangladesh Shilpa Bank reported in 42 DLR 140 and (3) in the case of Iftekhar Afzal vs Pubali Bank Ltd and others reported in 6 BLT (HCD) 166.</u>

<u>9. We have perused the judgment and order passed by the Court of District Judge, Dhaka and considered the aforesaid decisions and we are of the view that the court below has correctly rejected the application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure since the case pending in the Artha Rin Adalat cannot be heard analogously with any other case filed in any other normal Court created by the Civil Courts Act. The suit No. 153 of 1998 pending in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is a suit under general law, whereas the Title Suit No. 88 of 1998 is a suit filed under special law, and the Artha Rin Adalat has its own certain special procedure than that of the procedure applicable in the suit under general law. Thereafter, the finding of the District Judge that the Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 being the suit under the general law cannot be tagged and .heard analogously with the Title Suit No. 88 of 1998 and a suit filed under special law and the aforesaid finding arrived at by the District Judge is supported by a decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 70.</u>

10. In view of the above decisions we are inclined to hold that the District Judge has correctly rejected the said application and Title Suit No. 153 of 1998 cannot be transferred to the Court of Artha Rin Adalat for hearing analogously with Title Suit No. 88 of 1998. The Court of District Judge has not committed any error of law and warrants no interference by this Court.

11. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Court below is hereby affirmed.

12. The order of stay granted by this Court on 31-10-1999 is hereby vacated.

The suits shall proceed in accordance with the law and both the suits be disposed of as early as possible preferably within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this Judgment.

End.

lawyer:
Fazlul Karim with Mir Hashmat with Razbabul Kabir and Khandakar Aminul Huq, Advocates------For the Petitioner. 
Md Serajul Haque with Md Asrarul Hoque and Abdul Khaleque, Advocates------For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Ziaul Hoque alias Bakul ------ Petitioner
Vs
Md Sirajul Islam and ors ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Abdul Wahhab Miah, J: This Rule issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 26-8-99 passed by the District Judge, and Election Appellate Tribunal, Brahmanbaria in Election Tribunal Appeal No.4 of 1999 reversing the order dated 24-1-99 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal Sadar. Brahmanbaria in Election Tribunal Case No.5 of 1998 should not be set aside and or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The present opposite party No.1 as petitioner filed Election Tribunal Case No.5 of 1998 before the Election Tribunal Sadai, Brahmanbaria for declaration that the election of the present petitioner as the Chairman of No.15 North Ichapur Union Parishad was illegal and to declare him as Chairman of the said Union Parishad. In the election petition the simple case of the election petitioner was that the opposite Party No.1 i.e. the present petitioner, who was declared elected in the election held on 22-12- 97 published in the Gazette on 23-1-98 was disqualified to be a candidate as he did not attain the age of 25 years at the time of filing of the nomination paper.

3. The present petitioner as opposite party No.1 contested the said election petition by filing a written objection. stating, inter alia, that his date of birth is 11-12-69 and he being the eldest son of his parents was admitted at Dalpur Government Primary School, where he completed his education upto Class-V. In 1982 the petitioner was admitted in Class-VI in Doudpur High School and passed Class- VIII in 1984. None raised any objection against his candidature at the time of scrutiny of the nomination paper on 4-11-97, including the election petitioner. The petitioner having attained the age of 25 years as shown in the voter list he was qualified to be a candidate for the post of Chairman and people rightly elected him.

4. The Tribunal by its decision dated 24-1-99 dismissed the election petition on the finding, inter alia, that the petitioner was 25 years of age on the date of filing of the nomination paper and thus he was qualified to be a candidate for the post of Chairman of the said Union Parishad. On appeal, the Appellate-Tribunal considered the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, and came to the definite finding that the petitioner failed to prove that he attained the age of 25 years on the date of filing of the nomination paper and by its decision dated 26-8-99 allowed the appeal, set aside the decision passed by the Tribunal, cancelled the gazette dated 23-1-1998 of the election of the present petitioner and declared the election petitioner namely, the present opposite party No.1, as the Chairman of No.15 Ichapur (Uttar) Union Parishad

<u>5. Mr. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate appearing with Mr. Mir Hashmat Ali, Mr. Rezbabul Kabir and Mr. Khandakar Arninul Huq, learned Advocates for the petitioner submits that the Electoral Rolls Rules, 1982 prepared under the Electoral Ordinance, 1982 has a presumption of correctness in law. He submits that section 17 of the said Ordinance clearly bars the jurisdiction of court to question the validity of the electoral rolls prepared under the Ordinance or the legality or the propriety of any proceedings or action taken thereunder by or under the authority of the commission or the Registration Officer and in the voters list which was prepared under the Electoral Rolls Rules, 1982 and marked as Exhibit 'E', the age of the present petitioner having been shown as 25 years, the said entry could not be challenged and, as such, the Appellate Tribunal committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in holding that the present-petitioner failed to prove that he attained the age of 25 years. In support of his contention Mr. Fazlul Karim has referred the case of Hari Prasad Mulshankar Trivedi vs VB Raju and others reported in AIR 1973 (SC) 2602 and also the case of Kabul Singh Appellant vs Kundan Singh and others reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 340.</u>

<u>6. Mr. Md. Serajul Hoque, learned Advocate appearing for the Election Petitioner (opposite party No. I in this Rule), on the other hand, submits that the entry made in the voters list prepared under the Electoral Rolls Rules is not final and conclusive and there is no presumption of correctness and the same can very much be challenged before the Tribunal. Mr. serajul Haque, in support of his contention, has referred the case of Major Ali Akbar Chowdhury vs Sayeedur Rahman and 4 others reported in 15 DLR 153 and the case of Muhammad Yousuf vs Malik Karam Dad Khan reported in 20 DLR (WP) 33.</u>

<u>7. Mr. Fazlul Karim, in elaborating his submission, has further submitted that although in the case of Shahidullah Kazi vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) and Election Tribunal, Faridpur reported in 20 DLR 633 as referred to by the appellate Tribunal a full bench of this court decided that the election tribunal is competent to enquire as to the age of a person whose name was brought on the electoral roll to entitle him to be elected, yet, the principle of law enunciated in the said case cannot be applied in the instant case as when that decision was given the new law namely, Electoral" Rolls Ordinance, 1982 was not there and in the previous law namely, Electoral College Rules 1964 which was enacted under the provision like section 7 of the present law jurisdiction of court was not ousted. I have considered the submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim and also the provision of section 17 of the Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982. I find that the bar imposed by section 17 is upon the Court and the court mentioned in the section cannot but be construed a Civil Court. The legislature rightly put the embargo upon the Civil Court as because if the Civil Court is given the jurisdiction to sit over the electoral rolls then the very purpose of its preparation will be frustrated as by questioning the validity of the Electoral Roll the whole process of election will be delayed. I am of the opinion that bar imposed on a court cannot be construed to be a bar upon a tribunal, which, when deciding an election dispute can very much see the validity of the entry made in the Electoral Roll as it goes at the very root of the candidature of a candidate. It also does not require any interpretation that the word 'Court' cannot include 'Tribunal' which decides the election dispute and, as such, it cannot be construed that section 17 of the Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982 has ousted the jurisdiction of the Tribunal as submitted by Mr. Karim. The question of qualification and disqualification is very much an election dispute. The principle of law enunciated in the cases referred to by Mr. Fazlul Karim, as mentioned herein above is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as those cases were decided under different laws and under different facts. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case principle of law enunciated in the case reported in 20 DLR 633 is applicable.</u>

<u>8. Mr. Serajul Hoq in reply to the submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim rightly referred the case of Serajul Islam Khan, appellant vs Ahsan ALi Mondal, Provincial Election Authority, Dhaka, Election (Additional Deputy Commissioner), Jess ore, reported in 20 DLR (SC) 336. In the said two decisions it has been clearly held that entry of the electoral roll is not final and disqualification of a candidate, if apparent, can be very much challenged and the Tribunal is competent to enquire the same. The same view has also been expressed in the cases reported in 15 DLR (Dhaka) 153 and 20 DLR (WP) 33. In view of the discussions made above, I do not find any substance in the submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim that the entry made in the Electoral Rolls cannot be challenged. However, I find substances in the submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim to the effect that the Appellate Tribunal while found the present petitioner disqualified to be a candidate ought to have set aside the election of the Chairman of No. 15 North lchapur Union Parishad as a whole and passed order for fresh election. Mr. Fazlul Karim has rightly referred the case of Ahsanur Rahman vs Akkel Malia and others reported in 47 DLR 274. In that case a learned Single Judge of this court has held that the participation of a candidate in the election having been found illegal as he was disqualified to contest the election, the Tribunal was quite competent to declare the election as a whole void as it materially affected the result. I respectfully agree with the principle of law enunciated in the said case.</u>

9. With regard to the finding of the Appellate Tribunal as to the disqualification of the petitioner, I am of the view that the Appellate Tribunal has correctly considered the evidence adduced by the parties both oral and documentary, and it being the final court of fact having come to the definite finding that the present petitioner (opposite party No.1 in the petition) did not attain the age of 25 years on the date of filing of the nomination paper that finding cannot be disturbed in this revisional jurisdiction. Mr. Fazlul Karim tried to argue that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was erroneous but failed to point out any misreading of the evidence or non-consideration of any material evidence. In view of the above, the finding of the Appellate Tribunal as to the disqualification of the present petitioner to be a candidate to contest the election for the post of Chairman of No.15 Uttar Ichapur Union Parishad is hereby affirmed but the declaration of the Appellate Tribunal as. to the election of the Election-Petitioner as Chairman of the said Union Parishad cannot be sustained and the same is set aside.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute. The finding of the Appellate Tribunal about the disqualification of the present petitioner is maintained and the election for the post of Chairman of No.15, North lchapur Union Parishad is declared void. The Election Commission is directed to hold fresh election for the post of Chairman of No.15 North Ichapur Union Parishad immediately in accordance with law. Send down the records at once.

End.
