full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule seeks to review the judgment and order dated 25-7-2001 passed in Writ Petition No. 3962 of 1998 whereby the respondents, the Ministry of Social Welfare and other government functionaries, were directed to give registration to the Samity of the writ petitioners.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the present Rule is that the respondent No. 1 filed Writ Petition No. 3962 of 1998 for a direction on the Secretary, Ministry of Social Welfare and other government functionaries to give registration to the writ petitioner's Samity named Uttara Sarkari Officers Kallyan Samity under Voluntary Social Welfare Agencies (Registration and Control) Ordinance, 1961. The review petitioners were imploded as respondents Nos. 6 and 7 in the aforesaid writ petition but no Rule was prayed against them but Rule was only prayed against the Ministry of Social Welfare and other government functionaries connected with the registration of the Samity. Consequently, no Rule was issued on the respondents Nos. 6 and 7 in the said writ petition. As a result no notice of the Rule was served on the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 to the said writ petition Said respondent Nos. 6 and 7 are now the review petitioners before us. The government servants being allotted of D-type government quarters at Uttara Model Town felt it necessary to form a welfare association for themselves. After several meetings of the said residents a welfare association by the name "Uttara Sarkari Officers Kallyan Samity" was formed on 11-10-96 and the review petitioners, Mr. MA Bari and Mr MA Malek, were elected as the President and General Secretary respectively of the samity. The said samity thereafter started functioning under the leadership of the review petitioners. Meanwhile, some disgruntled members of the said samity having failed to secure desired posts and position in the samity broke away from it and formed another parallel rival samity on 25-8-97 under the same name. The original samity formed under the leadership of the review petitioners applied for the name clearance certificate for registration on 23-8- 97 and thereafter, for registration as a social welfare society on the following day i.e. 24-8-97. The samity subsequently formed on 25-8-97 also applied for name clearance certificate for registration on 27-8- 97 and also for registration on the following day on 28-8-97. Although applications for registration were made for both the samities, Social Welfare Department issued the name clearance certificate on 6-10-97 for registration of the samity which was formed later. Accordingly, the review petitioners (respondent) Nos. 6 and 7 in the writ petition) filed an application before the Private Secretary to the Hon'ble Prime Minister raising objection to the granting of the name clearance certificate in favour of the subsequently formed samity. Thereafter, a letter dated 5-11-97 was written from the Secretariat of the Prime Minister to the Secretary, Ministry of Social Welfare for proper inquiry and report on the objection raised by the review petitioner No. 1 i.e. the President of the original samity. Eventually the Parliamentary Standing Committee for the Ministry of Social Welfare formed a 3(three) member Sub- committee to look into the objection. Convener of the said Sub-committee along with its members held a spot inquiry into the objection and submitted a report to the Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on 6-1-99 recommending registration to the originally formed samity of the review petitioners. In view of the said recommendation the Social Welfare Department of the Government stayed the operation of the name clearance certificate granted in favour of the subsequently formed samity of the writ petitioner. Consequently, the General Secretary of the subsequently formed samity filed the aforesaid writ petition for a direction to give registration to their samity.

3. The Ministry of Social Welfare and other government functionaries contested the Rule in the writ petition. Since no Rule in the aforesaid writ petition was issued on the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 i.e. the review petitioners, they were not aware of the Rule and, as such, they could not contest the Rule. Thereafter the said writ petition was heard and disposed of by the judgment and order dated 25-7-2001, which is now under review. Review of the said judgment and order has been sought mainly on the ground that it was passed and obtained behind the back of the review petitioners and their interest have been adversely affected by the said judgment.

4. Respondent No.1 has filed affidavit-in- opposition and contested the Rule issued in the review petition. It is firstly, contended by the respondent No.1 in its affidavit-in-opposition that since the samity formed earlier in point of time does not have the adequate number of members it is not entitled to be registered under the law; secondly; since the reliefs sought for in the writ petition could only be granted by the Ministry of Social Welfare and the other government functionaries Rule was only prayed against them and no Rule was prayed against the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 in the writ petition who are now the review petitioners. Hence it cannot be said that the judgment and order dated 25-7-2001 passed in the writ petition is hit by the principle of natural justice. It is further contended by the respondent No. 1 i.e. the writ petitioner, that in fact, the review petitioners have suffered no prejudice although the judgment under review was passed in their absence inasmuch as all the points that could reasonably be agitated in the matter on behalf of the rival samity of the review petitioners were adequately placed and agitated by the government and considered by the writ court. The review petitioners have filed affidavit-in-reply reiterating their stand that since they were deprived of the opportunity of being heard in the matter they could not place factual and legal points of their case before the writ court. As a result their interest has been seriously prejudiced by the judgment passed in the writ petition. In short, it is contended that if the review petitioners were before the writ Court, judgment under review would have been different and in their favour.

5. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr. SRM Lutfor Rahman for the review petitioners, has taken us through the review petition, judgment and order passed in the writ petition and the annexures to the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and affidavit-in-reply and submits that although section 114 and Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding review do not apply in terms in writ matters under Article 102 of the Constitution but the principle of review is applicable to the judgment in 'writ as it involves civil proceeding. Mr. Bhuiyan next argues that the review petitioners have been condemned unheard inasmuch as the judgment in the writ petition is passed behind their back adversely affecting their interest in the matter of registration of the samity. It is further contended by him that the writ Court has committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record in coming to a finding on consideration of Articles 75 and 76 of the Constitution and rules 246 and 248 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament that the Parliamentary Standing Committee was not competent to inquire into the objections raised on behalf of the samity formed by the review petitioners without being authorised to do so by the Parliament.

6. Mr. Samsuddin Babul, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1, in reply, submits that since Article 102 of the Constitution has created writ jurisdiction with summary proceeding for a quick remedy, no review lies against the judgment passed in the writ proceeding. Present review' petition is not therefore maintainable. He also submits that since this Bench did not hear and dispose of the writ petition by passing the judgment under review, this Bench is not competent to hear and dispose of the review petition. The learned Advocate further submits that since violation of the principle of natural justice is not a ground for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the judgment and order dated 25-7-2001 passed in the writ petition cannot be interfered with on the plea that the same was passed in their absence and behind their back. The learned Advocate lastly, submits that since all the points were agitated and placed before the writ Court by the concerned Ministry of the government it cannot be said that the interest of the review petitioners has been affected by the judgment under review. It is also contended in the alternative that to allow the review petition would mean to allow another opportunity for rehearing of the matter which is already closed by the final judgment in the matter. In support of the contention the learned Advocate refers to the case of Zobaida Naher @ Jharna vs Khairunnessa, 3 BLC (AD) 170, Nurul Husain (Md) vs Government of Bangladesh, 1 BLC (AD) 219; Chandra Kanta and another vs Sheikh Habib, AIR 1975 SC 1500; Zenith Packages Limited vs Member Labour Appellate Tribunal Dhaka and others, 52 DLR (AD) 160, Bangladesh vs Md.Masder Hossain, 7 BLC (AD) 92

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the review petitioners, while elaborating his argument refers to the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner, Rawalpindi reported in PLD, 1970 SC 1 corresponding to 21 DLR (SC) 356 in support of his contention that the proceeding in the writ petition in the instant case being a civil proceeding this court has power under section 114(b) read with Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure to review the judgment in question. The learned Advocate also refers to the case of Fehmida Khatoon vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Consolidation) Lahore and others reported in PLD 1975 Lahore 942 in support of his contention that a person who was not a party to the writ proceeding can maintain a review petition against the judgment or order which adversely affects his interest inasmuch as the expression "any person" in Order XLVII, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure means any person, whether he has been a party or not, who is aggrieved by the decree or order. Relying on this proposition of law Mr. Bhuiyan submits that even if the review petitioners are not considered to be parties to the writ petition as they were not before the writ court on account of non-issuance and non-service of the Rule on them they are competent to seek review of the judgment in writ all it has adversely affected their right.

8. In the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner, Rawalpindi, PLD, 1970 SC 1 it was held:

"The writ jurisdiction under Article 98 of the Constitution, as already stated, is an original jurisdiction. Obviously, the jurisdiction under that Article pertains to civil as well as other matters. At the moment, I shall consider the nature of the proceeding arising out of a writ petition relating to a civil matter, as in the instant case. A proceeding taken for the enforcement of a civil right is a civil proceeding, whatever may be the source of the Court's jurisdiction invoked for enforcement of such a right. According to Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, "Civil Proceeding" is a process for recovery of individual right or redress of individual wrong, inclusive, in its proper legal sense, of suits by the Crown see. Bradlough V Clarks (2) Whether a proceeding is civil or not depends on the nature of the subject-matter of the proceeding and its object, and not on the mode adopted or' the forum provided for the enforcement of the right. A proceeding which deals with a right of a civil nature does not cease to be so merely because the right is sought to be enforced by having recourse to the writ jurisdiction. Judged from these aspects, a proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution relating to a civil matter is a civil proceeding, although the High Court's jurisdiction in such a proceeding is constitutional jurisdiction of an original kind. A civil proceeding in a Court of civil jurisdiction is government by the Code of Civil Procedure (see its preamble). By virtue of section 117 of the Code, a civil proceeding in a High Court is also governed by the provisions of the Code other than the provisions which are specially excepted A proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution concerning a civil matter being a civil proceeding relating to the High Court's original civil jurisdiction and section 114 of the Code conferring power of review not having been made inapplicable to the High Court in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction, the power to review an order made by the High Court in its writ jurisdiction will be available to it under the said section 114 if that section is otherwise applicable."

9. In the case of Fehmida Khatoon vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Consolidation), Lahore, PLD 1975 Lahore 942, the following observations were made:

"The above discussion raises a question as to why a person, who is not a party to the suit or proceeding as the case may be, cannot file review application against the judgment or order if he feels aggrieved against it on account of his interest having been adversely affected by that. Filing of appeal and review is a substantive right. It has been held clearly in the authorities referred to above that a person, though not a party to the suit or the original proceedings, can be granted leave by the appellate Court to file appeal provided he shows that his interest in the property has been adversely affected. On the same analogy a person who is not a party in the suit or proceeding can file review application against the judgment or order adversely affecting his interest."

10. Mr. Bhuiyan also refers to the case of Moni Begum and others vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha and others, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 and submits that the writ Court in its discretion may apply by analogy the principle of review avoiding technical provisions of review as contained in the Code of Civil Procedure to review the judgment in writ as and when necessary to meet the exigencies of the situation. In this reported case the question arose whether the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure providing that "the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction" was applicable in writ jurisdiction. Justice Mustafa Kamal, as he then was, having delivered the judgment for the Appellate Division observed:

"We would therefore like to answer the question raised in this appeal in the following manner. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not in terms apply to proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. But the Court in its discretion can apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. In what situations the principles of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applied and to what extent may perhaps, be left to the wise discretion of the Court itself. In other words, barring what is specifically provided for in the Rules themselves the Court is themaster of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience."

Mr. Justice Latifur Rahman, as he then was, while agreeing with the judgment delivered by Mr. Justice Mustafa Kamal in the aforecited case made his own comments in paragraphs 26 and 27 thereof as under:

"26. From the Appellate side rules it appears that writ petition in the nature of Habeas Corpus is governed under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Chapter II, as criminal businesses. Hence the writ petitions of other nature such as mandamus, certiorari and quo warranto may be considered as Civil Proceeding."

"27. It is fundamental that the court exists for doing justice and for doing ends of justice such power must exist in every Court, be it a civil Court, criminal Court or a writ Court, Civil cases and criminal cases are governed by the Codes of Civil Procedure and Criminal Procedure. But in writ case there is no such procedure other than the existing rules as mentioned above. Power to do justice is the basic pre-requisite of a court and if a court feels that injustice has been done in a case it can adopt such procedure as it thinks fit."

Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan then refers to and relies on the case of Ram Janam Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh and another. AIR 1994 SC 1722 in support of his contention that the principle of natural justice is also a good ground for interference in review of the judgment passed in the writ jurisdiction. It was held in the aforesaid case:

"The appellant admittedly was not impleaded as a party to the said writ application, but as he is directly affected like many other officers, who had entered into the State Civil Service before the respondent, filed the connected Special Leave Petition, challenging the validity of the judgment aforesaid. In view of the fact that the appellant had entered into Civil Service of the State Government before the respondent, it is not in dispute that he is affected in the matter of seniority by the impugned judgment. It was held by this Court in the case of Prabodh Verma vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1985 SC 167: (1984) 4 SCC 251 that a writ application in which the necessary parties likely to be affected have not been impleaded the High Court should not proceed with such writ application, without insisting, on such persons or some of them in representative capacity being made respondents. It was further held that if petitioner refuses to join them, the High Court ought to dismiss the petition for non-joinder of necessary parties. Admittedly, none was impleaded even in a representative capacity. But, it can be urged on behalf of the respondent that he had not sought any relief against any individual. he had sought the intervention of the High Court to declare Rule 3(1) of 1973 Rules and Rule 3(b) of 1980 Rules ultra vires, so far they made applicable the benefit of those Rules to only specified class of persons and restricted to others who were similarly situated. As such, respondent was not required to implead private respondent, who might be affected by the verdict of the Court. Even if this stand is accepted can it be said that persons who have been affected by the judgment of the High Court in the connected writ application cannot challenge the correctness thereof either by filing a Review Petition before the High Court or by filing a Special Leave Petition before this Court? According to us, the answer is in negative. The appellant has a locus standi to challenge the said judgment although he was not party to the same and the Special Leave Petition filed on his behalf cannot be rejected on that ground. The delay in filing the Special Leave has also been fully explained' in the facts and circumstances of the case, which is condoned." We would not enumerate any other authority on this point.

11. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 i.e. the writ petitioner, has sought to argue, as we have already noted above, that the judgment in writ petition merits no review for .the reason as could be said to have been summarised in the case of Bangladesh vs Masder Hossain, 7 BLC (AD) 92 which runs as follows:

"A review by no means is an appeal in disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected. A review lies where an error apparent on the face of the record exists It is not a re-hearing of the main appeal. Review is not intended to empower the Court to correct a mistaken view of law, if any, taken in the main judgment. It is only a clerical mistake or mistake apparent on the face of the record that can be corrected by the leave but does not include the correction of any erroneous view of law taken by the Court."

12. In view of the accepted position of law on review, as stated above, we hold that the present review application is maintainable. The contention of the learned Advocate for the review petitioners that the writ Court while considering Articles 75 and 76 of the Constitution and Rules 246 and 248 of the Rules of Parliament committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record in holding that the sub-committee had no competence to enquire into the dispute between the two rival samities in the absence of any specific reference of the dispute by the Parliament is not acceptable, because the review is not meant for correcting the mistaken view of law in the judgment.

13. Now with regard to whether principle of natural justice is a good ground for review, we hold that it is a good ground for review in view of the accepted position of law discussed above. The body or the Court with the power to decide cannot lawfully proceed to make a decision until it has afforded to the person affected a proper opportunity to state his case. This principle of natural justice is so fundamental as to require compliance for the ends of justice.

<u>14. The contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 that although the review petitioners was not before the writ Court they were not prejudiced and their interest was not adversely affected as all the points that could reasonably be raised and considered were raised and considered by the writ Court is not acceptable. Admittedly, the government which accorded registration to the samity of the respondent No.1 was present before the writ Court and contested the Rule. But the Government for that matter, in our opinion, could not be taken to be a substitute for the review petitioners in protecting their interest. It is the review petitioners alone who should be considered as the best and competent persons to protect their interest. It is the accepted and settled principle of natural justice that none should be condemned unheard. This settled principle of law in all the cases referred to hereinabove upheld that the aggrieved party could either prefer appeal or review for redress of their grievance. We are in respectful agreement with this proposition of law.</u>

<u>15. The next contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 that since this Bench did not hear and dispose of the writ petition by the judgment under review it has no jurisdiction to entertain and hear this review petition also appears to have no substance. It is noted from the record that the instant review petition was filed and moved and Rule was issued by the same Bench which heard the writ petition and passed the judgment under review. Subsequently, due to the change of constitution of that Bench this matter was referred to this Bench by the learned Chief Justice for disposal. It appears that the learned Chief Justice referred this review petition to this Bench for final disposal under Rule 6, Chapter 10 of the High Court Appellate Side Rules. This Bench is therefore competent to hear and dispose of this review.</u>

<u>16. We find from the record that the other Bench while issuing the Rule in the review petition stayed the operation of the judgment passed in the writ petition. While the said order of stay was in force and continuing the Department of Social Welfare accorded registration on 13-1-2002 in favour of the samity of the writ petitioners. Hence the registration is invalid and a nullity. The case of Md Mojibur Rahman Mia vs Jamini Mosahar and others reported in 7 DLR 82 may be referred to in this connection. Since we have already held that there is a good ground for review in this case the order according registration to the society of the writ petitioner is accordingly set aside.</u>

<u>17. In view of what has been discussed above, since the judgment in the writ petition was obtained by the respondent No. 1 (writ petitioner) behind the back of the review petitioners adversely affecting the interest of the review petitioners the same is set aside on review.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

In short, it is contended that if the review petitioners were before the writ Court, judgment under review would have been different and in their favour.

5. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr. SRM Lutfor Rahman for the review petitioners, has taken us through the review petition, judgment and order passed in the writ petition and the annexures to the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and affidavit-in-reply and submits that although section 114 and Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding review do not apply in terms in writ matters under Article 102 of the Constitution but the principle of review is applicable to the judgment in 'writ as it involves civil proceeding. Mr. Bhuiyan next argues that the review petitioners have been condemned unheard inasmuch as the judgment in the writ petition is passed behind their back adversely affecting their interest in the matter of registration of the samity. It is further contended by him that the writ Court has committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record in coming to a finding on consideration of Articles 75 and 76 of the Constitution and rules 246 and 248 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament that the Parliamentary Standing Committee was not competent to inquire into the objections raised on behalf of the samity formed by the review petitioners without being authorised to do so by the Parliament.

6. Mr. Samsuddin Babul, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1, in reply, submits that since Article 102 of the Constitution has created writ jurisdiction with summary proceeding for a quick remedy, no review lies against the judgment passed in the writ proceeding. Present review' petition is not therefore maintainable. He also submits that since this Bench did not hear and dispose of the writ petition by passing the judgment under review, this Bench is not competent to hear and dispose of the review petition. The learned Advocate further submits that since violation of the principle of natural justice is not a ground for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the judgment and order dated 25-7-2001 passed in the writ petition cannot be interfered with on the plea that the same was passed in their absence and behind their back. The learned Advocate lastly, submits that since all the points were agitated and placed before the writ Court by the concerned Ministry of the government it cannot be said that the interest of the review petitioners has been affected by the judgment under review. It is also contended in the alternative that to allow the review petition would mean to allow another opportunity for rehearing of the matter which is already closed by the final judgment in the matter. In support of the contention the learned Advocate refers to the case of Zobaida Naher@ Jharna vs Khairunnessa, 3 BLC (AD) 170, Nurul Husain (Md) vs Government of Bangladesh, 1 BLC (AD) 219; Chandra Kanta and another vs Sheikh Habib, AIR 1975 SC 1500; Zenith Packages Limited vs Member Labour Appellate Tribunal Dhaka and others, 52 DLR (AD) 160, Bangladesh vs Md. Masder Hossain, 7 BLC (AD) 92

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the review petitioners, while elaborating his argument refers to the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner, Rawalpindi reported in PLD, 1970 SC 1 corresponding to 21 DLR (SC) 356 in support of his contention that the proceeding in the writ petition in the instant case being a civil proceeding this court has power under section 114(b) read with Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure to review the judgment in question. The learned Advocate also refers to the case of Fehmida Khatoon vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Consolidation) Lahore and others reported in PLD 1975 Lahore 942 in support of his contention that a person who was not a party to the writ proceeding can maintain a review petition against the judgment or order which adversely affects his interest inasmuch as the expression "any person" in Order XLVII, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure means any person, whether he has been a party or not, who is aggrieved by the decree or order. Relying on this proposition of law Mr. Bhuiyan submits that even if the review petitioners are not considered to be parties to the writ petition as they were not before the writ court on account of non-issuance and non-service of the Rule on them they are competent to seek review of the judgment in writ all it has adversely affected their right.

8. In the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner, Rawalpindi, PLD, 1970 SC 1 it was held:

"The writ jurisdiction under Article 98 of the Constitution, as already stated, is an original jurisdiction. Obviously, the jurisdiction under that Article pertains to civil as well as other matters. At the moment, I shall consider the nature of the proceeding arising out of a writ petition relating to a civil matter, as in the instant case. A proceeding taken for the enforcement of a civil right is a civil proceeding, whatever may be the source of the Court's jurisdiction invoked for enforcement of such a right. According to Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, "Civil Proceeding" is a process for recovery of individual right or redress of individual wrong, inclusive, in its proper legal sense, of suits by the Crown see. Bradlough V Clarks (2) Whether a proceeding is civil or not depends on the nature of the subject- matter of the proceeding and its object, and not on the mode adopted or' the forum provided for the enforcement of the right. A proceeding which deals with a right of a civil nature does not cease to be so merely because the right is sought to be enforced by having recourse to the writ jurisdiction. Judged from these aspects, a proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution relating to a civil matter is a civil proceeding, although the High Court's jurisdiction in such a proceeding is constitutional jurisdiction of an original kind. A civil proceeding in a Court of civil jurisdiction is government by the Code of Civil Procedure (see its preamble). By virtue of section 117 of the Code, a civil proceeding in a High Court is also governed by the provisions of the Code other than the provisions which are specially excepted A proceeding under Article 98 of the Constitution concerning a civil matter being a civil proceeding relating to the High Court's original civil jurisdiction and section 114 of the Code conferring power of review not having been made inapplicable to the High Court in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction, the power to review an order made by the High Court in its writ jurisdiction will be available to it under the said section 114 if that section is otherwise applicable."

9. In the case of Fehmida Khatoon vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Consolidation), Lahore, PLD 1975 Lahore 942, the following observations were made:

"The above discussion raises a question as to why a person, who is not a party to the suit or proceeding as the case may be cannot file review application against the judgment or order if he feels aggrieved against it on account of his interest having been adversely affected by that. Filing of appeal and review is a substantive right. It has been held clearly in the authorities referred to above that a person, though not a party to the suit or the original proceedings, can be granted leave by the appellate Court to file appeal provided he shows that his interest in the property has been adversely affected. On the same analogy a person who is not a party in the suit or proceeding can file review application against the judgment or order adversely affecting his interest."

10. Mr. Bhuiyan also refers to the case of Moni Begum and others vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha and others, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 and submits that the writ Court in its discretion may apply by analogy the principle of review avoiding technical provisions of review as contained in the Code of Civil Procedure to review the judgment in writ as and when necessary to meet the exigencies of the situation. In this reported case the question arose whether the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure providing that "the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction" was applicable in writ jurisdiction. Justice Mustafa Kamal, as he then was, having delivered the judgment for the Appellate Division observed:

"We would therefore like to answer the question raised in this appeal in the following manner. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not in terms apply to proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. But the Court in its discretion can apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. In what situations the principles of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applied and to what extent may perhaps, be left to the wise discretion of the Court itself. In other words, barring what is specifically provided for in the Rules themselves the Court is themaster of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience."

Mr. Justice Latifur Rahman, as he then was, while agreeing with the judgment delivered by Mr. Justice Mustafa Kamal in the afore-cited case made his own comments in paragraphs 26 and 27 thereof as under:

"26. From the Appellate side rules it appears that writ petition in the nature of Habeas Corpus is governed under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Chapter II, as criminal businesses. Hence the writ petitions of other nature such as mandamus, certiorari and quo warranto may be considered as Civil Proceeding."

"27. It is fundamental that the court exists for doing justice and for doing ends of justice such power must exist in every Court, be it a civil Court, criminal Court or a writ Court, Civil cases and criminal cases are governed by the Codes of Civil Procedure and Criminal Procedure. But in writ case there is no such procedure other than the existing rules as mentioned above. Power to do justice is the basic pre-requisite of a court and if a court feels that injustice has been done in a case it can adopt such procedure as it thinks fit."

Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan then refers to and relies on the case of Ram Janam Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh and another. AIR 1994 SC 1722 in support of his contention that the principle of natural justice is also a good ground for interference in review of the judgment passed in the writ jurisdiction. It was held in the aforesaid case:

"The appellant admittedly was not impleaded as a party to the said writ application, but as he is directly affected like many other officers, who had entered into the State Civil Service before the respondent, filed the connected Special Leave Petition, challenging the validity of the judgment aforesaid. In view of the fact that the appellant had entered into Civil Service of the State Government before the respondent, it is not in dispute that he is affected in the matter of seniority by the impugned judgment. It was held by this Court in the case of Prabodh Verma vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1985 SC 167: (1984) 4 SCC 251 that a writ application in which the necessary parties likely to be affected have not been impleaded the High Court should not proceed with such writ application, without insisting, on such persons or some of them in representative capacity being made respondents. It was further held that if petitioner refuses to join them, the High Court ought to dismiss the petition for non-joinder of necessary parties. Admittedly, none was impleaded even in a representative capacity. But, it can be urged on behalf of the respondent that he had not sought any relief against any individual. he had sought the intervention of the High Court to declare Rule 3(1) of 1973 Rules and Rule 3(b) of 1980 Rules ultra vires, so far they made applicable the benefit of those Rules to only specified class of persons and restricted to others who were similarly situated. As such, respondent was not required to implead private respondent, who might be affected by the verdict of the Court. Even if this stand is accepted can it be said that persons who have been affected by the judgment of the High Court in the connected writ application cannot challenge the correctness thereof either by filing a Review Petition before the High Court or by filing a Special Leave Petition before this Court? According to us, the answer is in negative. The appellant has a locus standi to challenge the said judgment although he was not party to the same and the Special Leave Petition filed on his behalf cannot be rejected on that ground. The delay in filing the Special Leave has also been fully explained' in the facts and circumstances of the case, which is condoned." We would not enumerate any other authority on this point.

11. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 i.e. the writ petitioner, has sought to argue, as we have already noted above, that the judgment in writ petition merits no review for .the reason as could be said to have been summarised in the case of Bangladesh vs Masder Hossain, 7 BLC (AD) 92 which runs as follows:

"A review by no means is an appeal in disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard and corrected. A review lies where an error apparent on the face of the record exists It is not a re-hearing of the main appeal. Review is not intended to empower the Court to correct a mistaken view of law, if any, taken in the main judgment. It is only a clerical mistake or mistake apparent on the face of the record that can be corrected by the leave but does not include the correction of any erroneous view of law taken by the Court."

12. In view of the accepted position of law on review, as stated above, we hold that the present review application is maintainable. The contention of the learned Advocate for the review petitioners that the writ Court while considering Articles 75 and 76 of the Constitution and Rules 246 and 248 of the Rules of Parliament committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record in holding that the sub-committee had no competence to enquire into the dispute between the two rival samities in the absence of any specific reference of the dispute by the Parliament is not acceptable, because the review is not meant for correcting the mistaken view of law in the judgment.

13. Now with regard to whether principle of natural justice is a good ground for review, we hold that it is a good ground for review in view of the accepted position of law discussed above. The body or the Court with the power to decide cannot lawfully proceed to make a decision until it has afforded to the person affected a proper opportunity to state his case. This principle of natural justice is so fundamental as to require compliance for the ends of justice.

<u>14. The contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1 that although the review petitioners was not before the writ Court they were not prejudiced and their interest was not adversely affected as all the points that could reasonably be raised and considered were raised and considered by the writ Court is not acceptable. Admittedly, the government which accorded registration to the samity of the respondent No.1 was present before the writ Court and contested the Rule. But the Government for that matter, in our opinion, could not be taken to be a substitute for the review petitioners in protecting their interest. It is the review petitioners alone who should be considered as the best and competent persons to protect their interest. It is the accepted and settled principle of natural justice that none should be condemned unheard. This settled principle of law in all the cases referred to hereinabove upheld that the aggrieved party could either prefer appeal or review for redress of their grievance. We are in respectful agreement with this proposition of law.</u>

<u>15. The next contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 that since this Bench did not hear and dispose of the writ petition by the judgment under review it has no jurisdiction to entertain and hear this review petition also appears to have no substance. It is noted from the record that the instant review petition was filed and moved and Rule was issued by the same Bench which heard the writ petition and passed the judgment under review. Subsequently, due to the change of constitution of that Bench this matter was referred to this Bench by the learned Chief Justice for disposal. It appears that the learned Chief Justice referred this review petition to this Bench for final disposal under Rule 6, Chapter 10 of the High Court Appellate Side Rules. This Bench is therefore competent to hear and dispose of this review.</u>

<u>16. We find from the record that the other Bench while issuing the Rule in the review petition stayed the operation of the judgment passed in the writ petition. While the said order of stay was in force and continuing the Department of Social Welfare accorded registration on 13-1-2002 in favour of the samity of the writ petitioners. Hence the registration is invalid and a nullity. The case of Md Mojibur Rahman Mia vs Jamini Mosahar and others reported in 7 DLR 82 may be referred to in this connection. Since we have already held that there is a good ground for review in this case the order according registration to the society of the writ petitioner is accordingly set aside.</u>

<u>17. In view of what has been discussed above, since the judgment in the writ petition was obtained by the respondent No. 1 (writ petitioner) behind the back of the review petitioners adversely affecting the interest of the review petitioners the same is set aside on review.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

Md Khalilur Rahman with AQM Shafiulla and Md Ali Jinnah, Advocate------For the Petitioner.
