parties:
Uttara Bank Ltd ------ Petitioner 
Vs
Syed Abidur Reza and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: The Rule was issued by a Single Bench of this Division against judgment and decree dated 22-3-88 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No. 1 at Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 94 of 1987, which set aside judgment and decree dated 25-2-87 passed by Munsif, Additional Court at Sylhet in Title Suit No. 110 of 1986 and decreed the suit.

2. The Rule was heard by a single Bench, who found the matter should be heard by a Division Bench and accordingly, sent the file to the learned Chief Justice. Learned Chief Justice was pleased to direct us to hear and dispose of the matter.

3. Defendant No. 1 Uttara Bank obtained the Rule against aforesaid decree of reversal. Opposite party No. 1, Syed Abidur Reza as plaintiff on 17-3-82 instituted Title Suit No. 97 of 1982 against the petitioner and others for a decree of declaration that termination of his service in the bank by defendant No. 2 by letter dated 19-9-81 dispatched vide memo No. 3392A was illegal, malafide, void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon him and that the plaintiff was still in service. The suit was then renumbered as Title Suit No. 110 of 1986 in the aforesaid Court of Munsif at Sylhet.

4. Plaint case, in short, is that on 19-12-77 the plaintiff joined the office of defendant, Uttara Bank, as a junior assistant and in due course was confirmed. On 30-12-80 he was promoted to the  post of senior assistant and continued as such serving the bank to the satisfaction of all.

5. On 9-9-81 some central leaders of the Bank Employees Federation were arrested at Dhaka pursuant to a nation-wide strike call by the Federation for stopping work from 14-9-81. Against such arrest, the bank employees all over the country went out of their duties as a mark of protest. The plaintiff was then working as a senior assistant in Uttara Bank, Sylhet Branch. The plaintiff had no option but to join other striking employees and did not attend the office since 10-9-81.

6. The plaintiff was a member of the Uttara Bank Karmachari Union. The registration of the union was however, cancelled at the direction of defendant No.6, the Government of Bangladesh, on 19-9-98. Cancellation of registration of the union violated section 15(d)(ii) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance XXIII of 1969).

7. Then, defendant No.6, the Government, announced through radio and television that no action would be taken against those employees who would join their office duties before 9-00 AM on 24-9-81. Responding to the announcement, the plaintiff went to his place of work at Sylhet branch of Uttara Bank at 9-00 AM on 23-9-81 along with others but was not allowed to join. Defendant No.5, manager told him that letter of termination of service was already issued by defendant No.2 and as such, he could not allow them to join. On the following day, on 24-9-81, at 9-00 AM the plaintiff again went to join but was not allowed. On 26-9-81, father of the plaintiff received a letter of termination dated 19-9-81.

8. 	It was further stated that the plaintiff was a confirmed employee. The termination was issued in violation of Clause 18(b) of the Bank Staffs (Service) Rules, 1965. Besides, said service rules was already revised and replaced on 12-9-81 by the Uttara Bank (Employees) Service Regulations, 1981 by the Board of the Uttara Bank. The termination of the plaintiff under the previous and repealed Rules was therefore, illegal and without jurisdiction.

9. Defendant No.2, Assistant General Manager of Uttara Bank, regional office at Sylhet and defendant No.5, Manager, Uttara Bank, Sylhet branch contested the suit by filing two separate written statements.

10. Their common case is that the suit as framed was not maintainable; and also barred by limitation. The suit is hit by sections 6 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act and section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Termination was issued as per requirement of law with all legal dues admissible under the law. The plaintiff was removed by termination simpliciter and such termination has got nothing to do with his trade union activities. After termination, his attempt to join was uncalled for. Such termination gave the plaintiff no cause of action to sue.

On the pleadings following issues were framed-

(a) was the suit maintainable in present form and manner framed?

(b) was the impugned letter of  termination dated 19-9-81 illegal, malafide, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff?

(c) was the plaintiff entitled to get a decree as prayed for? and

(d) what relief, if any, the plaintiff was entitled to?

11. The plaintiff in support of his case examined him. The defendants also examined one witness. Papers and documents adduced by plaintiff were marked as exhibit-1 to exhibit-10 while one power of attorney dated 6-10-86 and another memo dated 10-3-79 adduced by the defendants were marked exhibit-A and exhibit-B.

12. On the aforesaid evidence, oral and documentary, on record the trial Court found the suit not maintainable under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure in view of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (Act VII of 1981) and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877; and, upon such view, dismissed the suit.

13. On appeal therefrom, the appellate Court however, allowed the appeal; set aside the findings of the trial Court and decreed the suit as prayed for.

14. On behalf of the petitioner bank the appellate decree was challenged on several grounds.

15. First, Mr Khalilur Rahman, learned Senior Advocate submitted that the suit, as framed, was not maintainable and the appellate Court by way of mandatory injunction directed the bank to reinstate the plaintiff in violation of section 56(f) of the Specific Relief Act.

16. Secondly, he submitted that the plaintiff was admittedly a worker and his suit before the civil Court was not maintainable and the appellate Court committed serious error in reversing the decree of the trial Court and decreeing the suit in its entirety ..

17. Lastly, he submitted that as the plaintiff was removed from service by termination simpliciter with all benefits that were available so no suit against such termination was maintainable.

18.	Following decisions were cited at the Bar:

1.	BSI Corporation vs Mahbub Hossain, 29 DLR (SC) 41;

2.	New Dacca Industries LId vs Quamrul Huda and others, 31 DLR (AD) 234;

3.	Mobarakganj Sugar Mills Ltd vs ABM Kazi Nazrul Islam, 1987 BLD (AD) 182;

4.	Senior Manager, Dosta Textile Mills Ltd vs Sudhansu Bikash Nath, 40 DLR (AD) 45;

5.	The General Manager, Sonali Bank and others vs Md Nurul Hoque Khan, 8 BCR 44;

6.	Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation vs Md Shahid Hossain Bhuiyan and others, 43 DLR (AD) 154;

7.	Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited and others vs Tafazzal Hossain and others, 44 DLR (AD) 260;

8.	Bangladesh Bank and others vs Mohammad Abdul Mannan, 46 DL R (AD) 1;

9.	Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited vs Md. Nazrul Islam Patwary and others, 48 DLR (AD) 62;

10.	General Manager, Sonali Bank and another vs Md Abul Khayer and others, 2 BLC (AD) 88; and

11.	Rupali Bank Ltd vs Md Arab Ali and others, 7 BLC (AD) 1.

19. The facts of the case are not disputed. On 19-12-77 the plaintiff joined the Uttara Bank, Sylhet branch as ajunior assistant and was then confirmed. On 13-12-80 he was promoted to the post of senior assistant. On 9-9-81 some central leaders of the Bank Employees Federation were arrested at Dhaka for the nation-wide strike call from 14-9-81. Against the arrest, the bank employees all over the country came out of their duties and joined the strike. The plaintiff also stopped attending his duties. Father of plaintiff on 26-9-81 received a letter of termination issued by defendant No.5.

20. Letter dated 19-9-98, Exhibit 5 read as follows:

"The undersigned is directed 	to communicate that the services of Mr Syed Abidur Reza, Senior Assistant of Uttara Bank are hereby terminated under Clause 18(b) of Bank's Staff (Service) Rules, 1965 with immediate effect.

Upon termination of his service as aforesaid, he is entitled to get payment of his legal dues from the Manager, Uttara Bank, Sylhet Branch subject to adjustment of Bank's dues, if any, recoverable from him.

He is requested to collect his dues from the Bank on any working day during office hours. Signed by Assistant General Manager who appeared to be his appointing authority."

21. It is also not disputed that at the time of termination Uttara Bank was one of the six banks constituted by the Bangladesh Banks (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (President Order No. 26 of 1972) by taking over the undertaking of the Eastern Banking Corporation Ltd. The Board of Directors of Uttara Bank in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 29 of said Order and superseding all rules and regulations made or issued in this behalf made the Uttara Bank (Employees) Service Regulations, 1981, which came into force with publication of the notification on 12-9-81.

22. In view of the Regulations, the appellate Court found no difficulty to declare the termination of the plaintiff under the previous Service Rules, namely, the Bank's Staff (Service) Rules, 1965, illegal and of no legal effect.

23. Main thrust of the submissions of Mr Khalilur Rahman appears to be on the relief sought for and the forum for vindication of such relief.

24. It is admitted that the plaintiff was a worker within the meaning of both the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 (Act VIII of 1965), in brief, the Act, and the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance No. XXIII of 1969), briefly, the Ordinance. Mr Khalilur Rahman submitted that the grievance of the plaintiff against the termination, if any, ought to be taken before the statutory Labour Court created by the Ordinance.

25. Proviso to unamended section 25(1)(b) of the Act at the time reads as follows:

"No complaint shall lie against an order of termination of a worker under section 19, unless the worker concerned is an officer of a registered trade union and his employment is alleged to have been terminated for his trade union activities or unless the worker concerned, whether an officer of a registered trade union or not, has been deprived of the benefits specified in that section;"

<u>26. On 19-9-81 the plaintiff was terminated under the superseded and replaced Service Rules of the Bank. The plaintiff was neither terminated under section 19 of the Act nor was he an officer of a registered trade union. As such, the doors of the Labour Court were not open to him to vindicate his grievance under section 25 of the Act against his termination. The relief sought for in the suit could not be prayed before the Labour Court.</u>

27. In GM Sonali Bank v Abul Khayer, 2 BLC (AD) 88 the Appellate Division found the suit of a terminated driver of the bank in Civil Court maintainable. He appears to have been terminated in very similar circumstances of the strike by the bank employees. The Appellate Division also held that the service rules of Sonali Bank and provision of section 19 of the Act for termination were not the same and the termination of the employee under the service rules could not be said to be covered by the Act.

28. It was also contended that during the pendency of the suit, as the Uttara Bank was included in the schedule of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 by the amendment of 1984 the suit before a civil Court was not maintainable. This submission has got no force in view of the fact that the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 came into force on 5-6-81 when Uttara Bank was not a schedule bank under said Administrative Tribunal Act. Uttara Bank was included in the schedule by the Administrative Tribunal (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 on 25-9-84. Neither the amendment was made retrospective to cover the case of the plaintiff nor can such amendment force the plaintiff to bring his grievance before the Administrative Tribunal. Cf: Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Tofazzal Hossain, 44 DLR (AD) 260.

29. Mr Khalilur Rahman also tried to contend though not forcefully that the Government by the time by a vendor's agreement dated 15-3-83 transferred the undertakings of Uttara Bank to the newly constituted Uttara Bank Ltd and after such transfer, the terms and conditions of the plaintiff would be governed by the principle of master and servant. No suit would therefore, lie against termination in a civil Court.

30. Paragraph 6 of the agreement clearly took care of the employees of Uttara Bank in the following terms :

"6. The company shall abide by the provisions of Uttara Bank (Employees) Service Regulations, 1981, in all matters in the terms and conditions of the service of the existing employees of the Uttara Bank and these regulations shall not be varied to the disadvantage of the existing employees without their consent."

31. In view of such clear undertaking by the Uttara Bank Ltd to abide by said regulations in all matters of terms and conditions of the service of existing employees the submission have got no substance. And the terms and conditions of such employees of Uttara Bank as were available to them continued even after the transfer. On the prayer of the Uttara Bank Ltd by order dated 14-2-87 the plaint was amended by adding Ltd after Uttara Bank wherever it was so written. It is needless to say that such transfer of the undertaking did not impact and/or affect the status of the plaintiff as he had in the Uttara Bank vis-a-vis Uttara Bank Ltd, subject however, to the final adjudication in the suit.

32. Lastly, the issue remains for answer as to whether the suit as framed mainly for two declarations (a) that the termination was illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff and (b) that the plaintiff was. still in service is maintainable before a civil Court.

33. In the case of BSIC vs Mahbub Hossain after review of English and Indian decisions on the service conditions of statutory employees, the Supreme Court, as it was then called, formulated the following principles:

(a) If an employee is dismissed or his service is terminated in contravention of a mandatory statutory provision. the employee has a right of action either in a Superior Court in its writ jurisdiction or a Civil Court.

(b) If the service of its employee is terminated in violation of the principle of natural justice. the employee has a similar right to action as in (a).

(c) If the office is a statutory one, the holder of the office has similar right of action as in (a) in case of termination of the said office not in accordance with the law, under which the said office has been created.

(d) In spite of the office being a statutory one or of public character, terms and conditions of the office may be regulated by contract, and termination of service in contravention of such contract, but otherwise than in the manner mentioned in (a) and (b) is not actionable for the purpose of reinstatement in the office.

(e) Terms and conditions of service prescribed by rules, regulations or any other form of delegated legislation made by a body under statutory  statutory force and the dismissal or termination of service in substantial disregard of them will entitle the employee to a right of action as in (a).

34.	The Supreme Court also held that,

"Again, an employee of a statutory corporation of public character, who does not hold any statutory post or status, can nevertheless maintain an action in a Court of law, on a limited ground, that of violation of any mandatory statutory provision as to the kind of contract or the statutory ground of dismissal, or the doctrine of ultra vires or the violation of the rule of natural justice."

(Underlined by us).

35.	In New Dacca Industries Ltd vs Quamrul Huda and others, 31 DLR (AD) 234 a dismissed worker challenged the order of dismissal in writ jurisdiction. The Appellate Division set aside the decision of High Court Division on the view that corporate character of the company with the relationship of master and servant was retained even after nationalisation. Consequently, removal of employee could not be challenged before the writ jurisdiction or civil Court.

36. In the case of Mobarakganj Sugar Mills Ltd vs ABM Kazi NazrulIslam, 1987 BLD (AD) 182 a suit by a dismissed employee of the company for declaring his dismissal a nullity and further declaration that he was still in service was decreed by the trial Court but was dismissed by the appellate Court. A single judge of the High Court Division however restored the decree of the trial Court. The Appellate Division set aside the order of the High Court Division and dismissed the suit, mainly on merit of the case.

37. In Senior Manager, Dosta Textile Mills vs Sudhansu Bikash Nath, 40 DLR (AD) 45 the Appellate Division held that after the company vested in the corporation and corporate character of the company with the relationship of master and servant of the employees and employer continued and the suit by a dismissed employee was therefore, not maintainable. The decision followed Eastern Mercantile Bank Ltd vs Mohammad Shamsuddin, 21 DLR (SC) 365.

38. In General Manager, Sonali Bank vs Md Nurul Haque Khan, 8 BCR (AD) 44 a suit by a dismissed branch manager was dismissed on merit. The decision of BSIC vs Mahbub Hossain was noticed but was distinguished on merit.

39. In the case of Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation vs Shahid Hossain Bhuiyan and others, 43 DLR (AD) 154 some terminated employees of the corporation challenged their termination in writs, the Appellate Division held that no reason is required to be assigned for termination and dismissed the writs.

40. In Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Tajazzal Hossain, 44 DLR (AD) 260 a suit by a cashier of the bank against termination leave was granted on the question of coram non judice. The suit was decreed. The Appellate Division however, set aside the decree on the view that the remedy was available before Labour Court not before a Civil Court.

41. In the case of Bangladesh Bank vs Mohammad Abdul Mannan, 46 DLR (AD) 154 in appeals by the employer and employee against the order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal declaring termination of the employee void, the Appellate Division set aside the order but held that

"We, however, expressed our view that the provision for termination of employees of a statutory Corporation by simply giving him three months' notice or three months' pay is a harsh rule capable of being used indiscriminately and such rule should be re-examined by the authorities concerned, particularly the Corporation and the Government so as to amend the Rules providing for giving at least gratuity to a terminated employee according to the length of service. In the instant case, as we have pointed out, Regulation 12, like its parent law, being protected legislation, the provision for termination by notice is not void though it may be inconsistent with any fundamental right".

42. In the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Md Nazrul Islam Patwary, 48 DLR (AD) 62 a suit by security guard against termination was decreed declaring such termination void and that he was still in service. Appellate Division found the suit maintainable.

43. In the case of General Manager, Sonali Bank vs Abul Khayer, 2 BLC (AD) 88 an application of Sonali Bank for rejecting the plaint of a dismissed driver was rejected. Appellate Division in view of decision in BSIC vs Mahbub Hossain found the suit was maintainable as remedy under section 25 of Standing Orders Act was not available to the plaintiff at that time.

44. In the case of Rupali Bank vs Arab Ali, 7 BLC (AD) 1 a suit by a senior principal officer of the bank against dismissal and for mandatory injunction for reinstatement was found to be not maintainable under section 56(f) of the Specific Relief Act.

45. The principles enunciated in the case of BSIC vs Mahbub Hossain by our apex Court in our view are still shining the path as the polestar to adjudication of the issues regarding terms and conditions of the employees of statutory bodies in midst of various laws prescribing a variety of remedies. The moment we shall take our sight off the polestar we shall miss the course like the sailors in rough seas at dark night. We carefully examined subsequent decisions only to see the development of such service law.

46. Relying upon Rupali Bank vs Arab Ali, 7 BLC (AD) 1 it was contended the appellate Court erred in law in directing reinstatement of the plaintiff. If the decree is examined carefully, there should not be any confusion. The appellate Court decreed the suit to the effect that the termination of the plaintiff was declared to be illegal, malafide, against natural justice, void and not binding upon the plaintiff; and it was also declared that the plaintiff was still in service. The suit was instituted exactly for same relief. In addition, the appellate Court directed the defendants to allow the plaintiff to continue in service in his post with all benefits.

47. Such direction was no doubt, based upon the declarations and in the absence of such direction the effect of the declarations would have the same effect since no one is expected not to carry out the declarations.

48. In English jurisdiction, relief for declarations that order of dismissal and/or termination was nullity and that the employee was still in service was well recognised as back as in 1956 by the House of Lords in Vine vs National Dock Labour Board, [196] 3 ALL E R 939. Similarly, in India such suit is also recognised since 1970 in Executive Committee UP Warehousing Corporation vs Chandro Kiron Tyagi, AIR 1970 SC 1244 and Indian Airlines Corporation vs Sukdeo, AIR 1971 SC 1828.

49. In BISIC vs Mahbub Hossain, 29 DLR SC 41 our apex Court for the first time authoritatively recognised the principles. In its subsequent decisions, no departure was noticed. In Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Nazrul Islam, General Manger, 48 DLR (AD) 62 and General Manager, Sonali Bank vs Abul Khayer, 2 BLC (AD) 88 the Appellate Division found the suits of a removed security guard and driver respectively maintainable for same relief.

50. In view of above legal position and facts and circumstances of the case the appellate decree declaring the termination void and of no legal effect and the plaintiff was still in service must be held to have correctly been arrived at and do not call for any interference. Nor such declaration has resulted in failure of justice.

<u>51. Before parting with the case, we must say few words about the reference. Section 98 of the Code of Civil Procedure conceives of a reference only when the judges of a bench composing of more than two judges differ on point of law. The judges then may state the point of law upon which they differ and the matter shall then be heard upon that point by one or more judges as appointed by the learned Chief Justice.</u>

<u>52. In the case before us learned Single Judge heard and referred the matter for decision by a Division Bench without formulating any point of law. He was however of the view that substantial question of law together with interpretation of statute and relevant provisions of the Constitution were involved. On such assumption we are afraid any matter could be referred. A judge is empowered to decide any matter which comes to him for decision. He must have the courage to decide the matter whatever complications there may be. He must remember that to err is also within his jurisdiction.</u>

53. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 14-7-88 is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the records at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 382 of 1996.
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner. 
Not represented ----- The Respondents.
parties:
Ali Akbar (Md) ------ Petitioner
vs. 
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury J: This petition for leave to appeal is from the judgment and order dated 5 August 1990 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rule issued in Writ Petition No. 27 of 1990 filed by the petitioner. 

2. The subjuct-matter of the writ petition is a fishery known as Kamraghop Beel Fishery which is situated on SA plot No. 1448 of Mouza Athukura within police station Baniachang of Habiganj district. The petitioner's father and 13 others took settlement of the said fishery from Kali Prashad Chakraborty and others, ex-landlords of Nayasarak Sylhet. On the death of his father the petitioner became an owner thereof along with the co-sharers. They had no rent-receiving interest. During the survey settlement made under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the said SA plot No. 1448 was recorded in the khatian No. 1 of respondent No. 1, but its area was wrongly recorded as 0.38 acre in place of the actual area of 65.38 acres.

3. In the year 1989 respondent No.3 the Upazila Nirbahi Officer Baniachang claimed the said fishery as Government fishery and leased it out to one Rajendra Kumar for 3 years from 1396 to 1398 BS The petitioner thereupon filed an application before respondent No.2 the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Habiganj for cancellation of the lease asserting his title to and possession in the fishery. Respondent No.2 found that compensation assessment roll in respect of the concerned village was finally published on 3 March 1962 and accordingly, the fishery in question had vested in the Government under the provision of the said Act. He therefore rejected the prayer by his order dated 26 December 1989. He further directed the district authority to take steps for leasing out the fishery as the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer had no authority to grant lease in respect of such a large fishery. 

4. Since the petitioner did not get any relief he filed the above-mentioned writ petition in the High Court Division to have the said order of respondent No.2 declared to Eave been made without any lawful authority. 

5. It was contended before the High Court Division that no compensation assessment-roll was prepared and finally published in respect of the said fishery and, as such, the fishery in question did not vest in the Government in accordance with the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act Consequently, respondent No.2 acted beyond his authority in directing the district administration to lease out the said fishery. Reliance was placed on the decision of Shah Md. Elias vs. Province 0/ East Pakistan reported in 17 DLR 277 wherein the following view was taken. "A close reading of the provisions points to inevitable conclusions, firstly, that every interest which is liable to be acquired under the Act has to be paid for; and, secondly, that except in the case of acquisition under Chapter II of the Act the interests which are acquirable vest in the Provincial Government only if assessment of compensation in regard to the same has been made and published as provided in the Act. The argument of the learned Advocate General is that, since in respect of the locality in question a notification under sub-section (2) of section 43 has been made and since the Revenue Authority were satisfied that the disputed lands constituted fishery the same have vested in the Provincial Government. We are unable to accept this contention." 

6. The High Court Division did not accept the contention of the petitioner. The said court noticed that the view taken by the High Court in Shah Md. Elias vs. Province of East Pakistan was contrary to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Province of East Pakistan vs. Secretary Muktagacha Abbasia Senior Madrassa, reported in 16 DLR (SC) 281. Then, on consideration of the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the High Court Division held that publication of the compensation assessment-roll relating to a locality would have the effect of vesting a non-retainable property of a tenant irrespective of whether that property was specifically included in the compensation assessment-roll published in the official Gazette under section 43 (2) of the Act and accordingly, discharger the Rule. 

7. The same ground is urged before us as before the High Court Division. It is further urged that the High Court Division was wrong in its view that the decision of the High Court of East Pakistan reported in 17 DLR 277 is contrary to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in 16 DLR (SC) 281. 

8. In the case of Province of East Pakistan vs. Secretary, Muktagacha Abbasia Senior Madrassa, 16 DLR (SC) 281, the writ petitioner who was a tenant having no rent receiving interest challenged the acquisition of a hat which was non-retainable under section 20 (2a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Government resisted the claim mainly on the ground that since there had been a final publication of the compensation assessment-rolls in respect of the concerned Mauzas and the same had been notified in the Gazette on the 27th of March, 1962 the hat had vested in Government and the tenant was no longer entitled to retain possession of it by reason of the combined operation of sub-section (3) of section 44 and section 20 of the said Act. The Supreme Court of Pakistan sustained the objection and observed "Reading the Act as a whole the intention appears to us to be firstly, that all rent- receiving-interest shall disappear, secondly, that so far as tenants are concerned, they will be entitled to retain possession only of certain categories of land which are retainable and thirdly, that even in respect of such retainable lands a maximum ceiling is fixed. So far as rent-receivers are concerned, their interests are to vest either from the date of the notification of acquisition or from the date mentioned in such a notification. But so far as tenants are concerned their interests are to stand acquired and vested in Government on the notification of the final publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll. The scheme of the Act therefore, is that whatever is not retainable vests in the Government by operation of law and that too free from all encumbrances. We are, therefore, of the view that the High Court was not right in holding that the interests of tenants of raiyats in such hats and bazar had not vested in Government." A similar view has been expressed in Province of East Pakistan vs. Haji Abul Hussain & another 22 DLR (Dhaka) 191. In that case a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court held: "In view of the provisions of sections 43 and 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, a tenant's non-retainable land like Bazar vests in the Government on the publication of a Notification in the official Gazette under sub-section(2) of section 43. The Notification referred to hereinbefore is a notification under sub-section (2) of said section 43. This notification relates to a number of villages including Jarulia in which the disputed Bazar situates. Sub-section (2) of section 43 of the said Act provides that Notification under that sub-section shall be a conclusive proof of its publication and its date thereof. Since the Notification relates to a number of villages including the whole of the village Jarulia and as the disputed Bazar lies within that village it should be taken that the Compensation Assessment roll published in this case is also relatable to the disputed Jarulia Bazar. Thus the disputed Jarulia Bazar vested in the Provincial Government during the pendency of this appeal." To the same effect is the decision in Province of East Pakistan vs. Md. Shahabuddin, 25 DLR 248 this decision followed the decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 281. 

9. The consistent view on the point thus seems to be that publication of a notification in the official Gazette declaring that a compensation assessment-roll has been finally published for a village or group of villages or local area as the case may be, specifying in such notification the date of the final publication of the compensation assessment-roll, as required' under section 43(2) is a conclusive proof of such publication and of the date thereof. After the said notification all interests of tenants in respect of their non-retainable property would vest in the Government under section 44(3) of the said Act with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the official gazette. Even if there be any defect in the preparation and publication of the compensation assessment-roll that by itself shall not stand in the way of the vesting. 

10. In the instant case, it is not disputed that notification under se2tion 43(2) of the Act relating to the concerned village was duly published in the official gazette in the year 1962. We therefore find no cogent reason to differ from the view of the High Court Division that the fishery in question has already vested in the Government and the petitioner was not entitled to retain .its possession. 

The petition is therefore dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Golam Mohammad Bhuiyan, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Abul Kalam Chowdhury with ATM Obaidul Hoque, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Jamal Uddin ------ Petitioner
Vs
Mir Kashem Bahumukhi High School and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 28-10-1999 and 4-11-1999 passed by learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court Sadar, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 92 of 1999 reversing the judgment and decree dated 18-7-1999 and 25-7-1999 respectively passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Begumgonj, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 119 of 1996 should not be set aside.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit challenging the dismissal from his service.

3. The plaintiff’s case, in short, is that the plaintiff is the night guard of Mir Kashem Bahumukhi High School of Mirwarishpur, Begumgonj, Noakhali and he joined in the service on 9-6-87 and was discharging his duty most sincerely and efficiently with satisfaction of the authority and the members of the staff. There was no complaint against the plaintiff. There was dissatisfaction amongst the students, teachers and guardians against the Head Master of the School who has influenced the Managing Committee and finally dismissed the plaintiff on the ground that on 24-6-96 the plaintiff entered into the room of the Head Master over the ceiling, that the plaintiff disobeyed the order of the authority, that he removed some valuable records including, the resolution book of the school and also removed the wood, tin and fencing of the school but those allegations against the plaintiff were baseless and without foundation. The plaintiff is a low paid employee and he maintains his family consisting of 9 members and they are suffering during these hard days of economic crisis, The service of the plaintiff though not regulated by the service regulations of the board but is protected by the principle of natural justice and hence the suit for declaration that the order of the principal dated 7-9-96 is illegal, void, inoperative and that he is still in service.

4. The defendants appeared and contested the suit by filing written statements denying the assertion made in the plaint stating that Mir Kashem Bahumukhi High School starts at 7-00 AM and continues till 5-30 PM with morning shift and day shift. The plaintiff being the night guard of the property of the school including the office and other records of the school but on 24-3-1996 he illegally entered into the room of the Head Master through the ceiling of the room and took away resolution book of the school containing the resolution dated 23-4-1996 and 10-5-1996. He disobeyed the order of the Head Master. He misbehaved with Babu Anil Chakraborty on 23-7-1996. Earlier, he took away the wood, tin and fencing of the school for which previously there was proceeding against him and he begged mercy and the authority granted him pardon. Due to his misconduct an inquiry committee was formed to inquire into the allegations made against him and he was directed to appear before the committee on 29-5-1996. The committee conducted the inquiry in presence of the 2 nominated persons of the plaintiffs on 25-6-1996 and the committee by their unanimous report on 5-9-1996 wherein he was found guilty and the committee recommended for disciplinary action against him. Accordingly, the Managing Committee by its resolution dated 7-9-1996 removed him from service. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The suit came up for trial before the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge. Begumgonj, Noakhali and the plaintiff examined 6 witnesses and the defendants examined 7 witnesses to prove their respective cases.

6. After hearing the learned Advocates of the parties and considering the materials on record the learned Senior Assistant Judge decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 18-7-1999 and 25-7-1999 respectively in Title Suit No. 119 of 1999.

7. Against the said judgment and decree the defendant Managing Committee preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Noakhali which was eventually transferred to the court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Noakhali and marked and numbered as Title Appeal No. 92 of 1999.

8. After hearing the learned Advocates of the parties and considering the evidences on record he was pleased to allow the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

9. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff preferred the present civil revision before this court and obtained the present Rule.

10. Mr Golam Mohammad Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, appeared for the petitioner and Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury with Mr ATM Obaidul Hoque appeared for the opposite parties.

11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the court of appeal before erred in law failing to appreciate the findings arrived at by the trial Court. He further submits that the allegations against the plaintiffs have not been proved in accordance with the evidences on record, rather PW 5 Ali Akbar stated that he was present at the time of inquiry but the Managing Committee could not prove the allegations satisfactorily before the Inquiry Committee. He further submits that though the service of the plaintiff is not regulated according to the service regulations of the Board but the service of the plaintiff is governed under Master and Servant Rules and it is protected under the principle of natural justice. He further submits that the plaintiff is a low-paid night guard of the school and he has a poor family consisting of 9 members and they are suffering during these hard days of economic crisis and that the plaintiff has already suffered for about 8 years.

12. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1, on the other hand, submits that the plaintiff petitioner obtained the Rule only against opposite party No. 1 not against the members of the Managing Committee and, as such, the decree, if any, obtained by the plaintiff-petitioner will be a non executable decree and it will not be binding upon the Managing Committee and the Court should not pass a non executable decree. He further submits that in the present civil revision there is no law point involved nor the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner could agitate any law point. He further submits that the appellate Court being the last court of fact, the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner are relating to the facts and revisional Court should not enter upon and assess such evidences relating to the facts. He further submits that the plaintiff in his deposition admitted that he has entered into the room of the Head Master without any permission at night. He also admitted that he had taken away wood tin and fencing of the school and the authority pardoned him. He also admitted that he filed false voucher of Taka 2,940. He also admitted that he supplied script (nakal) at the time of examination of his wife. He also admitted that he has refused to accept the letter issued by the authority against him. The learned Advocate further submits that all the allegations admitted by the plaintiff prove the misconduct of the plaintiff-petitioner. He further submits that the authority and inquiry committee served notices against him and the inquiry was made by properly constituted committee wherein 2 persons including the plaintiff petitioner were also present and the inquiry committee unanimously submitted their report. The authority issued 2nd show cause notice against the delinquent plaintiff-petitioner but he did not reply. There is no illegality or miscarriage of justice. The trial Court decreed the suit only on the basis of some points, on the evidences of some witnesses without considering the whole evidences but the trial Court found him guilty and he pointed out the finding of the trial Court which runs thus:

‘বিবাদী মূলের বিভিন্ন সময়ের রেজুলেশণ বই প্রযালোচনা দেখা যায় যে,প্রধান শিক্ষকের আনুকূল্য পাইয়া বাদী স্কুলের কোন কোন শিক্ষকের প্রতি তাচ্ছিল্য প্রদর্শন করিয়াছে ও ঔদ্ধত্যপুর্ন আচারনও করিয়াছে যাহা একজন নৈশ প্রহরী হইতে কোন ভাবেই কাম্য হইতে পারে না। এইজন্য বাদীকে সতর্ক করিয়া দেওয়া আবশ্যক।’

<u>13. He further submits that the activities of the plaintiffs and the findings made by the trial Court as well as the findings of the appellate Court confirm the misconduct of the plaintiff-petitioner. He further submits since the service of the plaintiff petitioner is not regulated by the Service Rules of the Board the provisions of the Master and Servant Rules will apply. He further submits that since there is no statutory provisions regulating the service of the plaintiff-petitioner a decree for reinstatement against an unwilling Master should not be granted. In support of his contention he cited that case of SE kabir vs Spencer & Co (Pak) Ltd and others reported in 21 DLR 581 wherein it has been held that in, the absence of any statutory provision protecting the servant, which have the impact of Keeping the servant in service to grant to the servant a decree against an unwilling Master. In support of his contention he has cited the case of Abdul Majid vs Bata Shoe Company 'through its Provincial Controller reported in 30 DLR 262 where it has been held that the defendant company, cannot be forced to reinstate the plaintiff since the parties are governed by the ordinary law of Master and Servant. He also cited the case of Messrs, Malik and Haq and another  vs Muhammad Shamsul Islam Chowdhury and two others reported  in 13 DLR (SC) 228 where it has been held that in, the absence of any statutory provisions, protecting the servant, it is not possible in law to grant to him a decree against an unwilling Master that he is still his servant. A servant cannot be forced upon his Master. He also referred the case of Azizur Rahman vs Burmah Oil Co. (Pak) Trading Ltd reported in 13 DLR 458.</u>

<u>14. He also pointed out that except a suit for damages or for compensation no other suit would lie, nor the servant is entitled to any other relief such as his reinstatement to service or a mere declaration that his service was wrongly terminated by Master . In support of his above contention he cited the case of case of Hasan Ali vs Manager, Amin Match Works reported in 19 DLR 307.</u>

<u>15. In reply to the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Golam Mohammad Bhuiyan submits and cited the case of Nazir Ahmed, vs Bangladesh Jute Industries reported in 31 DLR 196 where it has been held that where the authority passed the order of termination of an employee's service without applying its mind such order calls for court's scrutiny, but the learned Advocate could not point out in this case where the authority did not apply their mind, rather in the said cited decision it has been held that the employers power to discharge an employee from service cannot be questioned. He also cited the case of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation vs Mahbub Hossain Chowdhury reported in 29 DLR (SC) 41 pointing out the principle of natural justice, where it has been held that the essential requirement of natural justice must at least include that before someone is to be condemned he should be given an opportunity to defend himself and, that in order that he may do so, he is to be made aware of the charges of allegations or suggestions which he has to meet.</u>

<u>16. In this case the charges were framed by the authority and an inquiry committee was formed and 2 persons along with the plaintiff-petitioner defended himself before the inquiry committee and there was an unanimous report against the plaintiff-petitioner and the authority issued 2nd show cause notice upon the plaintiff-petitioner, even the plaintiff-petitioner admitted his guilt before the trial Court in his cross examination that he has entered into the room of the Head Master without permission, he took away materials of school, he submitted false voucher, supplied script in the examination of his wife, etc., and, as such, the reported cases are not much helpful for the petitioner.</u>

<u>17. It appears hat the trial Court decreed the suit though he was found guilty of misbehaviour and misconduct but the appellate Court reversed the said decision and dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff-petitioner is guilty of misconduct. The finding of facts arrived at by both courts below that the plaintiff-petitioner is guilty of misconduct does not call for interference. According to the decisions reported in 13 DLR 458. 13 DLR (AD) 228, 19 DLR 307, 21 DLR 581 and 30 DLR 262 the service of a servant cannot be enforced against an unwilling master as the service of the plaintiff-petitioner is governed by the rules of Master and Servant. The plaintiff-petitioner in his plaint stated that his service is not regulated by regulations of the Board and his service was protected by the principle of Natural Justice. The learned Advocate for the petitioner does not deny that the relationship of the plaintiff-petitioner between the management is master and servant. Considering the decisions, the master cannot be forced to accept the service of the servant. In the facts and circumstances and materials on record, I do not find any substance in the Rule.</u>

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Ismail, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Harendra Nath Nondy, Advocate ----- For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Abdul Mannan (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Swaraj Roy and ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the plaintiff upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order dated 8-5-2000 passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court at Noakhali in Title Suit No. 2 of 2000 which allowed the prayer of opposite party No. 1 for addition as a defendant in the suit.

2. Short facts for disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff on 11-1-2000 instituted the suit for specific performance of contract. His case is that opposite party No. 2 entered into a contract with him for sale of 3.315 acres of land at a consideration of Taka 2,37,000 and on receipt of Taka 2,00,000 opposite party No. 2 executed a Bainapatra on 12-6-1995. As the opposite party No. 2 avoided receiving the balance and executing and registering necessary sale deed the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

3. On 21-3-2000 opposite party No.1 made an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code for addition. His case, in short, is that neither the plaintiff nor opposite party No. 2 has any right, title or possession in the suit land. Moreover, opposite party No. 2 migrated to India long ago and died there. By way of pattan and purchase his grandfather and father acquired the suit land at various times from 1925 and possessed. Lastly, the suit land was recorded in the name of his father during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and they have been in possession on payment of rents. In the present revenue survey also, his name was correctly recorded. In order to grab the suit land the plaintiff created the Bainapatra. He accordingly, prayed that for disposal of such suit, his presence is necessary.

3. Plaintiff opposed the application by filing a written objection mainly raising objection on the scope of inquiry in a suit for specific performance and denied that opposite party No. 1 has got any possession on homestead on the suit land. It is also claimed that the story of settlement and sale deeds were created for the purpose of the application.

4. Hearing the application and considering the papers produced, the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the same by the impugned order.

<u>5. Mr Md Ismail, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract only question for inquiry is whether the contract in question is genuine or not and whether the plaintiff is entitled to a decree upon such contract. In such a suit of the petitioner, opposite party No. 1 has got no locus standi to be added or his presence is necessary. In support he relied upon the decision in the case of Golam Kader vs Abdul Khaleque Choukder and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 107 and that of Muzaffar Ali and another vs Monwara Hospital and others reported in 1999 BLD 484 = 51 DLR 341.</u>

<u>6. Mr Harendra Nath Nondy, learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, submits that opposite party No. 1 is on the land as a successive owner in possession. His father's name was recorded in the SA Khatian and they have been possessing the suit land all along on payment of rents. Opposite Party No. 1 has also got his homestead on the land. Having come to know that the alleged vendor opposite party No. 2 migrated to India long ago and died the petitioner instituted the suit and if a decree is obtained, naturally ex parte, in such suit it will be very difficult for opposite party No. 1 to protect his possession in the land. He, therefore, submits that in order to avoid multiplicity of the proceedings and also for ends of justice presence of opposite party No. 1 is necessary at least to prove that the vendor of the petitioner migrated to India long ago and died there long before the execution of Bainapatra on 12-6-1995. In support he cites decisions in the case of Muhammad lshaq vs Jamila Begum and others reported in PLD 1955 Lahore 644, in the case of Surjya Kanta Majhi and another vs Aswini Kumar Debnath and others, 16 DLR 238 and that of Barjang Lal Agarwala vs Aksed Ali Shaikh & others, 35 DLR 110 and that of Md Toafazzal Hossain vs Sunil Kumar Basak & ors 7 BLT (AD) 103.</u>

We have perused the plaint, the application for addition and the objection thereto, and heard the learned Advocates. We have also closely read the decisions relied upon by the learned Advocates.

7. Let us first see the decisions cited at the Bar. In the case of Golam Kader, an application for addition was made in respect of a small fraction of the total land involved in the suit. They also claimed the land independently as their own. Appellate Division thereupon held the averments in the application for addition of party disentitle them to be included within the framework of the present suit. That will convert the present suit for specific performance of contract into a suit for determination of title which is not permissible in law.

8. In the case of Muzaffar Ali, a Division Bench relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division found the applicant in similar circumstances was not a necessary party.

9. In the case of Mohammad Ishaq, Mr Kaikaus, J as his Lordship then was, in a suit for specific performance allowed the application for addition of a 3rd party, saying,

"In the view that I take, namely, that a person who claims adversely to the vendor and vendee can be impleaded in a suit for specific performance, I am supported by a number of authorities."

<u>10. In the case of Mir Hasmat Ali vs Birendra Kumar Ghosh, 16 DLR 239 a Division Bench of this Court in a similar suit for specific performance of contract on consideration of numerous authorities has come to the following view:</u>

<u>"If the contract is of a collusive nature (and circumstances mentioned above makes it probable that it may be so) as alleged by the province of East Pakistan then material facts in this behalf will not be placed before the Court by the parties, namely, the plaintiff and the defendants. The presence of the Province of East Pakistan thus becomes necessary for the purpose of enabling the Court to receive all relevant information’s which will give guidance as to appropriate principles applicable to the case."</u>

11. In the case of Bajrang Lal Agarwala, ATM Afzal J, as his Lordship then was, sitting in a Division Bench delivered a judgment in a suit for specific performance of contract on consideration of authorities, holding.

"There is no doubt that generally in suits for specific performance only the parties to the contract or those against whom the contract can to any extent be enforced should be impleaded as defendants. That is the ordinary rule but it is subject to exceptions and does not debar the impleading of a person claiming an interest adversely to the vendor and the vendee when the circumstances of a case so require."

12. In the case of Md Toafazzal Hossain, the Appellate Division in a suit for specific performance confirmed the decision allowing the addition being of the view,

"the case of respondent No. 1 clearly comes within the exception of the general principle of addition of party in a suit for specific performance of contract and that he is a proper party to be added as a defendant in the suit for proper adjudication of the real dispute as to whether the Bainapatra in question is a fake one and as to whether there was any family settlement as alleged in the plaint by the plaintiff on the basis of which the contract in question with defendant Nos. 1 to 3 entered into"

<u>13. Law therefore appears to be settled that in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land, the moot issues to be decided is, whether the contract is genuine, and whether a decree for specific performance can be granted to the plaintiff in the facts and circumstances of the case. In such suit, the parties and their successors are the only necessary parties. There may be exceptions to such general principles. If somebody comes before the court with an application for addition contending that the whole transaction was forged fraudulent and cooked up for the suit with a view to grab the suit property and that the alleged vendor died long before the contract, his presence, it is difficult to say, would not be of any assistance to the court for adjudication of the above issues, Of course, there is no scope in such suit to raise and decide the title of such third party and therefore, there is no chance to convert the suit into a suit for declaration of title.</u>

<u>14. Moreover, when such third party claims to be in possession, the Court is also under an obligation to see if by rejecting the prayer of such third party and pushing the parties to multiplicity of proceedings would not result in injustice.</u>

15. As stated above that the opposite party No. 1 claims that opposite party No. 2, alleged vendor of the plaintiff, migrated to India long ago and died there and that the Bainapatra dated 12-6-1995 was created for the purpose of the suit. He also claims that for generations opposite party No. 1 has been living in the suit land on payment of rent on the basis of record of rights. Opposite party No. 2 has not yet appeared in the suit. According to opposite party No. 1, there is no chance of any appearance on behalf of said opposite party No. 2. In such circumstances, appearance of opposite party No. 1 in the suit at least to see whether the 'Bainapatra' of the plaintiff is genuine or not will be an invaluable assistance to the Court. On the facts and in view of the ratio of above decisions, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error or illegality in the exercise of his discretion in allowing the application for addition. No failure of justice has occasioned thereby.

In the result, this Rule is discharged and the impugned order is affirmed. No order as to costs. The order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby re-called and vacated. Communicate.

End.
