lawyer:
Ajmalul Hossain, QC with Iftekhar Ahmed Advocates ----- For the Petitioner (In both Rules). 
M Moniruzzaman Khan with Mokunda Chandra Debnath, Advocates ----- For Opposite Party No.8 (in both Rules).
parties:
Standard Bank Ltd ------ Petitioner
Vs
Tripos Engineering & Trading Company (GO) ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant No.5, the Standard Bank, obtained the Rules against similar orders, by which applications of the plaintiffs for temporary injunction were rejected and earlier order of status quo vacated. As the issues raised in both the Rules are the same and contesting parties are common, both the Rules were heard together and now disposed of by this order.

2. On 8-11-2001 opposite party No. 1, Tripos Engineering & Trading Company in former Rule as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 337 of 2001 in the Sixth Court of Assistant Judge at Dhaka against the petitioner, the Standard Bank and others for a decree of declaration that any payment by virtue of back to back letters of credit as described in the schedule to the plaint to be made by defendant Nos. 4 and 5, ie the Standard Bank to defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3, the beneficiaries thereunder, is illegal.

3. In the plaint, it is averred that defendant No.6, Vitessee Trading (LLC) placed a purchase order for supply of ready-made garments for an amount of US$ 1,00,000 vide a letter of credit dated 6-2-200 I. After said letter of credit was transferred to the plaintiff, the plaintiff opened number of back to back letters of credit for different amounts in favour of defendant No.1, Modem Textile Mills and defendant No, 2, Global Textile Mills for supply of yams against the lien of said master letter of credit. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2, in order to make wrongful gain intentionally supplied fabrics and yams of inferior quality and thereby, committed fraud.

Upon such averments, on 9-11-2001 said plaintiff made an application under Order XXIX rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction for restraining defendant Nos. 4 and 5 ie the petitioner Bank, from making any payment to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 against the back to back letters of credit.

4. Same date the trial Court issued notice upon the defendants asking them to show cause within seven days as to why they should not be so restrained as prayed for and also directed the petitioner Bank to maintain status quo in respect of any payment to defendant Nos. 1 to 3.

5. Then, opposite party No.8, the Premier Bank Ltd, got it added as defendant No. 9 by an order dated 31-10-2002. On 2-2-2003 the Premier Bank made an application under Order XXXIX rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the order of status quo.

6. By impugned order, the Court rejected the application for temporary injunction and vacated its order of status quo dated 9-11-2001. Against this order, the petitioner Bank obtained former Rule.

7. Just in similar circumstances, in latter Rule Amitex Knitting and Dyeing as plaintiff on 8-11-2001 instituted Title Suit No. 338 of 2001 in the same Court against the petitioner Bank and others for a decree of declaration that any payment by virtue of back to back letters of credit by the petitioner Bank to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is illegal.

8. This plaintiff got two letters of credit dated 18-1-2001 and 18-4-2001 for US$ 192,000 and US$ 160,006 respectively for supply of ready-made garments. Against the letters of credit, the plaintiff opened number of letters of credit in favour of said Modem Textiles and Global Textiles for supply of yams. But said defendants supplied inferior quality of fabrics and yam and thereby committed fraud.

9. On the following day, the plaintiff Amitex also made an application under Order XXIX rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction for restraining defendant Nos. 3 and 4 ie the Standard Bank from making any payment against the back to back letters of credit.

10. Upon hearing of the application, the Court was pleased to issue notice upon the defendants asking them to show cause within seven days as to why they should not be so restrained by an order of temporary injunction till disposal of the suit as prayed for. Meanwhile, the Court directed defendant Nos. 3 and 4, the petitioner Bank to maintain status quo in respect of any payment to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by its order dated 9-11-2001.

11. The Premier Bank similarly, got it added by making an application under Order I rule 10(2) of Code of Civil Procedure as defendant No.9. On 2-2-2003 the Premier Bank made an application under Order XXIX rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the order of status quo. By impugned order, the Court rejected the application for temporary injunction and vacated its order of status quo dated 9-11-2001. Against this order, the Petitioner Bank obtained latter Rule.

12. Taking us through the records, Mr Ajmalul Hossain, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner Bank, submitted that the trial Court committed an error of law in rejecting the application for temporary injunction and vacating its earlier order of status quo without considering the facts evidencing clear fraud perpetrated by the plaintiff and opposite party No.9, the Premier Bank, which has resulted in serious miscarriage of justice.

13. Secondly, he submitted that in the course of a local inquiry held by the bank, existence of the beneficiary of the back to back letters of credit could not be found and hence, the plaintiff, beneficiary and the Premier Bank colluded with each other to defraud the petitioner Bank is established.

14. Lastly, he submitted that when there was a clear case of fraud established, the issuing bank cannot be asked to make any payment under the letters of credit.

15. Opposing the application, affidavits-in-opposition were filed on behalf of opposite party No.8, the Premier Bank, in both Rules.

16. In the affidavits, it is stated that as the impugned order is appealable, the revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable.

17. It is further stated that the suit was valued at Taka 1,00,000. But the petitioner Bank falsely wrote the valuation of both the suits as well as the revision applications as US$ 3,14,431 and obtained the Rules from a Division Bench by such misrepresentation.

18. It is stated that the plaintiffs opened back to back letters of credits in question for purchase of 100% cotton yam for making readymade garments. The plaintiffs already admitted to have received the yam under the letters of credit and used those in making garments, After the beneficiary, Modem Textiles tendered the shipping documents in the petitioner Bank through the Premier Bank, both the plaintiffs duly accepted the documents on full satisfaction and authorised the petitioner Bank to issue acceptance. Accordingly, the petitioner Bank accepted the documents and communicated its acceptance of the bills with confirmation of payment to the Premier Bank on the date of maturity. Acting upon such communication, the Premier Bank already negotiated the bills and effected payment to the beneficiary, Modern Textiles.

19. Mr M Moniruzzaman Khan, learned Counsel for the opposite party No.8, submitted that after acceptance of the bills/documents and communication of the confirmed date of payment, the petitioner bank could not now refuse payment under the letters of credit in question.

20. Secondly, he submitted that after the order of status quo was vacated, the petitioner bank already paid two-thirds of the proceeds under the letters of credit. Now they could not take shelter under any supposed case of fraud to avoid payment of the rest of the proceeds.

21. He also took us through Articles 3, 4 and 9 of the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit, ICC 500 as of January 1, 1994 and submitted that after acceptance of the documents and communicating its decision to pay on the date of maturity, the petitioner bank was obliged to pay.

<u>22. In support, he cited the decisions in Zyta Garments Limited vs Union Bank Limited, 55 DLR (AD) 56; Gooryolny (Bd) Textile Limited vs Chartkan Information Textile Limited and others, 54 DLR (AD) 70; Training Knit Wear Limited vs DGM. Sonali Bank and others, (1997) 2 MLR (AD) 396, Comforts Apparels (Pvt) Ltd vs Imperial Knitting Industries Ltd, 53 DLR 350; SM Fazlul Huque vs Salauddin Ahmed and another, 1992 BLD 155: Janata Bank vs Ahmedia Garments, 40 DLR 72; Sarhind Garments Ltd vs Glory Truth Industries, 49 DLR 260; Uttara Bank vs Macneill and Kilburn Limited and others. 33 DLR (AD) 298; and United Commercial Bank Limited vs Synthetic Textile Limited and others (1937) Company Cases 245.</u>

23. Affidavits-in-reply on behalf of the petitioner Bank were also filed. In the affidavits, it is stated that after the Accepted Bills for Payment (ABP) became matured, the petitioner Bank extended the maturity date several times informing the Premier Bank that Modem Textile Mills would not have any objection to such extensions. The Premier Bank also did not object to such extensions for payment of the ABPS. It is further stated that when the plaintiffs Tripos and Amitex failed to produce export documents in respect of the master letters of credit the petitioner Bank became suspicious and inquired into the matter. In the course of inquiry, Mr Mamun, Mr Nairn and Mr Hasan, officers of the petitioner Bank, in July, 2002 went to the address where the Modem Textiles Office was supposed to be situated. In spite of their best efforts, they could not find any office of Modem Textiles there.

24. Mr Ajmal submitted that as the impugned order-was not appealable to this Division, revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not barred.

<u>25. In support he cited the authorities in S Zafar vs Abdul Khalique, PLD 1964 Karachi 1964 (FB); Arts Council of Pakistan vs Reazuddin Pirzada, PLD 1969 Karachi 349; Wahid Sadek vs Mozibur Rahman, 42 DLR 220; Rupban Bibi vs Aynal Kha and others, 44 DLR (AD) 144; Hajee Nurul Alam vs Abdus Subhan Sawdagar Waqf Estate, 45 DLR (AD) 168 and Shahidul Islam vs Md Sayedur Rahman, 47 DLR (AD) 70.</u>

26. With regard to subsequent discovery of fraud after part payment against the letters of credit, Mr Ajmal took us through the book of Documentary Credit by Raymond, Ali Malek and David Quest, 2nd Edition and read Paragraphs 9.42, 9.43 and 9.44 therefrom, and submitted that as the entire payment under the letters of credit was not yet made, so the petitioner Bank was still entitled to refuse payment of the rest of the proceeds under such letters of credit on the ground of fraud, non-existence of the beneficiary, Modem Textile.

<u>27. In support, he cited the decisions in the cases of Edward Owen Engineering Ltd vs Barclays Bank International Ltd and another, (1978) 1 QB 159; United City Merchants vs Glass Fabrics and Equipment’s Ltd, (1983) AC 168 and Volyvinter Oil SA vs Chase Manhattan Bank, (1984) Lloyds Law Report 251.</u>

28. We have perused the record as placed before us.

The issues facing us are mainly,

(1) whether or not the applications made under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure for revision against impugned orders are maintainable; and

(2) whether or not in the facts and circumstances of the case, the issuing Bank, Standard Bank, is entitled to withhold payment under the letters of credit in question to negotiating bank, Premier Bank.

29. Facts are not disputed. In both the suits, as transferees of the master letters of credit, the Modem Textiles Mills and the Tripos Engineering and Trading Company (GD) as plaintiffs opened back to back letters of credit through the Standard Bank in favour of the Modern Textiles Mills Limited for supply of cotton yarn. In matter of establishing the letters of credit, the Premier Bank advised said issuing bank. After the shipment and acceptance of the yam, said beneficiary, Modem Textiles, submitted drafts and necessary documents for payment and on full satisfaction of the terms and conditions of the letters of credit the plaintiffs, in their turn, instructed the issuing bank for payment. Accordingly, the issuing bank accepted the drafts and documents and communicated its decision to pay on the date of maturity to the negotiating Bank. The date of maturity was however extended with the concurrence of all the parties more than once. In due course, acting upon such communication of the issuing bank, the Premier Bank already paid off the beneficiaries.

30. Then, the plaintiffs instituted the suits and prayed for temporary injunction for restraining their bank, the Standard Bank, from making any payment till disposal of the suits. The Court also granted an order directing the Standard Bank to maintain status quo in respect of payment till disposal of the application. Then, the Premier Bank got it added as defendant and made application for vacating the order of status quo. The application was heard on 3-2-2002. The plaintiffs never opposed the application. The Standard Bank prayed for time for filing a written statement but did not oppose the application.

31. In the circumstances, the Court by impugned order rejected the application of the plaintiffs for temporary injunction and vacated its earlier orders of status quo. After the order of status quo was vacated, the Standard Bank paid the bulk of the proceeds under the letters of credits in question to the negotiating Bank. Then, the issuing Bank obtained above Rules on 3-5-2003. The plaintiffs never challenged the orders nor appeared in the Rules.

<u>32. Now, let us take up the first issue first Conflict in the decisions of the High Courts of the Sub-continent continued for a long time over their powers in the exercise of discretion under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It appears, the matter was raised as an issue before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Municipal Committee, Bahawalpur vs Sh. Azizi Elahi, 22 DLR (SC) 389. Against a decree the appellant did not prefer any appeal and after three months came up with an application under section 115 of the Code for revision. High Court held that revision was not maintainable. In affirming the decision of the High Court, the Supreme Court held that,</u>

<u>".... If a decree or an order, which is in the nature of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure, has been passed by the Court of first instance, and it is appealable under the Code, then, whether the appeal lies immediately to the High Court or only after another appeal has been taken before the District Judge, the revision would not be competent."</u>

<u>It further held that,</u>

<u>"The words 'no appeal lies thereto' are words of general import and there is nothing in the section to confine their operation only to first appeals. If this is not done, and an 'appeal' is held to include a second appeal then no difficulty is created by the word 'thereto'."</u>

33. At the time of decision, provisions under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure were the same in Pakistan, India and here in Bangladesh. The High Courts in such countries were empowered to exercise the discretion of revision power under the section only to correct the jurisdictional errors committed by the Courts subordinate to it.

<u>34. Only condition imposed in the exercise of the discretion is in the catch phrases "any case which has been decided" and "in which case no appeal lies thereto". Case has not been defined in the Code. In the case of SS Khanna vs FJ Dillon. AIR 1964 SC 497, tracing the historical evolution of the powers of diverse High Court's supervisory jurisdiction the Supreme Court of India held,</u>

<u>"The expression 'case' includes a suit, but in ascertaining the limits of the jurisdiction of the High Court, there would no warrant of equating it with a suit alone... .... .. ..</u>

<u>To interpret the expression 'case' as an entire proceeding only and not a part of a proceeding would be to impose a restriction upon the exercise of powers of superintendence which the jurisdiction to issue writs, and the supervisory jurisdiction are not subject, and may result in certain cases in denying relief to an aggrieved litigant where it is most needed, and may result in the perpetration of gross injustice.</u>

<u>In considering whether the revisional jurisdiction of a High Court was intended to cover decisions, which did not dispose of the suit or proceeding, possibility of delay arising in the disposal of some cases because of investigation commenced by the High Court is not, in our judgment, a sound ground for presuming that the jurisdiction was to be limited to those matters which were finally disposed of."</u>

35. This case was not brought to the notice of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Nor the Supreme Court of Pakistan thought fit to inquire into the purport of the phrase, "any case which has been decided" in the facts of the case.

<u>36. Following the above decision, the Supreme Court of lndia in Vidya Vati vs Devi Das, AIR 1997 SC 397 again held,</u>

<u>"Now, there can be no doubt that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure a revision application can lie before the High Court from an order made by a Subordinate Court only if no appeal lies from that order to the High Court. The words of limitation used in section 1 15 are 'in which case no appeal lies thereto' and these words clearly mean that no appeal must lie to High Court from the order sought to be revised, because an appeal is much larger remedy than a revision application, and if an appeal lies that would afford sufficient relief and there would be no reason or justification for invoking revisional jurisdiction. "</u>

37. In our jurisdiction, under changed provisions of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, exercise of the discretion is now made limited to "if such subordinate Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice."

<u>38. Power under the section is revisional in nature. This power is quite distinct and different from the powers to be exercised in appeal and review. This extraordinary power vests in the High Court to correct error of law of the Subordinate Court which results in failure of justice. Such power therefore cannot be exercised when an appeal shall lie to it.</u>

39. As the orders passed by an Assistant Judge in suits valued at Taka 1,00,000 only in rejecting applications for temporary injunction and vacating its earlier orders of status quo were not appealable before this Division, revision applications under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure made against such orders cannot be said to be not maintainable.

40. So far the customers rushed to this Division for order preventing their banks from paying under letters of credit. Nowadays, the banks which issued irrevocable letters of credits and confirmed its obligation to pay are coming for similar order against negotiating banks to withhold payment. This is definitely not good instance to the reputation of the banking system of the nation in commercial and trading transactions. The issue raised is already settled in various ways in number of decisions in our jurisdiction and beyond.

41. Settled principle is that when an irrevocable letter of credit is issued/opened and confirmed by a bank, such bank is left with no option but to respect its obligation under the letter of credit and pay if the drafts anti documents are found to be in order and the terms and conditions of such letter of credit satisfied. Customer cannot instruct the bank not to pay and the bank cannot act upon such instruction, if any, for withholding the payment. Any dispute between the buyer and seller has to be settled between them in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract of sale. If the buyer suffered, in any way, he can sue the seller for damages.

42. Only exception to such general statement of principle that is recognised by a Court of law is an obvious and clear fraud brought to the knowledge of the issuing bank. However, mere allegation of fraud is not sufficient to entitle the issuing bank to withhold payment. The drafts/documents submitted for payment must be tainted by real fraud. Before acceptance of the drafts and documents submitted, issuing bank is however entitled to refuse payment under the letter of credit and return the drafts and documents on the ground of discrepancy and/or fraud.

43. In UCM vs Royal Bank of Canada, 1983 HL 168 the House of Lords held in a case of a bill of lading with wrong date of loading placed on it by the carrier's agent was far from being a nullity and allowed the appeal of the seller against the bank. It reasoned, inter alia.

"The whole commercial purpose for which the system of confirmed irrevocable documentary credits has been developed in the international trade is to give to the seller assured right to be paid before he parts with control of the goods that does not permit any dispute with the buyer as to the performance of the contract of sale being used as a ground for non payment or reduction or deferment of payment. .....

To this general statement of principle as to the contractual obligations of the confirming bank to the seller, there is one established exception: that is, where the seller for the purpose of drawing on the credit, fraudulently presents to the confirming bank documents that contain, expressly or by implication, material representation of fact that to his knowledge are untrue."

44. Question raised herein upto what point of time the bank will be entitled to refuse payment on the ground of fraud? In other words, what is the extent of such time the issuing bank would be entitled to refuse payment.

45. In Documentary Credit referred and relied upon by Mr Ajmal,

Paragraph 9.42 writes, the question may arise in two situations: first, if the bank has already paid on the credit and the applicant (or other instructing party) is resisting reimbursement; secondly, if the bank has not paid and is resisting proceedings by the beneficiary for payment under the credit.

9.34 In the first situation, if the bank pays in accordance with the terms of the credit, then it is entitled to reimbursement unless there was clear evidence of fraud at the time of payment. The bank has strictly limited period to consider the documents and cannot, and should not, engage in prolonged enquiries of the sort which might be carried out at a full trial between beneficiary and applicant. It is not open to the applicant objecting to the bank's decision to rely on evidence not made available to the bank at the time of payment.

<u>46. United Trading Corporation SA vs Allied Arab Bank Ltd, (1985) 2 Lloyd's Law Report 554 at page 556,</u>

<u>"It seems to us clear that, where payment has, in fact, been made, the bank's knowledge that the demand made by the beneficiary on the performance bond was fraudulent must exist prior to the actual payment to the beneficiary and that its knowledge at that date must be proved. Accordingly, if all a plaintiff can establish is such knowledge after payment, then he has failed to establish his course of action. The bank would not have been in breach of any duty in making the payment without the requisite knowledge. We doubt that this is really open to contest."</u>

<u>47. When an irrevocable letter of credit is opened and confirmed by a bank, such bank is left with no option but to honour its obligation under the letter of credit and pay. After the acceptance of the Accepted Bills for Payment (ABPs) and communication of its decision to pay on the due date, a new contract takes effect between the advising/negotiating bank and issuing bank, and such contract is independent of and separate from the contract of sale, neither the seller nor the buyer has any privy to such contract [Zyta Garments Ltd vs Union Bank Ltd and another. 55 DLR (AD) 56]</u>

48. Mr Ajmal asked us to take notice that after part payment, the bank came to know in the course of an inquiry that there was no existence of the beneficiary, and the buyer, seller and the negotiating bank all colluded with each other to defraud the bank. He submits that when the entire payment under the letter of credit was not complete, the bank was still entitled to withhold payment. Submission may be ingenious but is of no substance. We know no law that supports him.

49. The petitioner bank did not oppose the application of its customer, the plaintiff, for temporary injunction against payment under the letter of credit. Order of status quo was vacated at the instance of the negotiating bank, defendant No.9, by the impugned order. The plaintiff did not challenge the impugned order. The petitioner bank has already made payment of bulk of the proceeds under the letters of credit. Now after obtaining the Rule and by filing an affidavit-in-reply sworn on 11-11-2003 the petitioner bank claims that it came to know in July 2002 in the course of an inquiry by its official that there was no existence of the beneficiary. In the circumstances, such claim is nothing but an allegation (not proved) must be held to have been resorted to avoid payment. Such belated claim/assertion cannot be entertained because that goes against the public policy.

50. In view of above authorities, we are more fortified in our view that once the drafts and documents submitted for payment under a letter of credit are accepted and the date of payment is communicated in case of a deferred credit, and bulk of the proceeds is already paid, the issuing bank has got no right to withhold the payment notwithstanding the fact that the payment was not complete.

51. In such view of legal position, ultimate decision of the trial Court in rejecting the application for temporary injunction and vacating its earlier order of status quo did not result in any failure of justice, and therefore, does not call for any interference.

52. In the result, both the Rules are discharged with cost. The trial Court is directed to proceed with the suit expeditiously.

53. Orders of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rules are hereby recalled and vacated. The Standard Bank is directed to make the payment under the letters of credit in question to the Premier Bank without any further delay.

Communicate at once.

End.

lawyer:
AFM Shahid, Mehir Kanti Mazumder with Nahid Yeasmin, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
KZ Alam with Shariful Islam Khan and AHM Mashfiqur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Shishir Kanti Pal and others  ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Nur Muhammad and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by the heirs of deceased defendant Nos. 7, 8 and other defendants against the Judgment and decree dated 31st October, 1993, passed by the District Judge, Lakshimpur in Title Appeal No. 44 of 1989 reversing those dated 30-4-1981 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali in Other Class Suit No. 85 of 1967.

2. The opposite party Nos. 1-4 as plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 85 of 1967 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali for declaration that the suit property as described in Schedule A to the plaint measuring an area of 29.41 acres was never treated as enemy property and that notification No. 6330 EPMC dated 31-7-1965 published in Dhaka Gazette dated 4-11-1965 was illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that previously they were the inhabitants of village Amarpur under police station Birganj of Tripura State within Indian Dominion having their ownership and possession in 'B' scheduled land in India. The 'A' scheduled land to the plaint belonged to Sree Gopal Chandra Pal and 10 others who intended to migrate to Tripura state from their home District Noakhali and upon their approach to exchange their' 'A' .scheduled land with the 'B' scheduled to. the plaint which belonged to the plaintiffs they agreed to the proposal and accordingly, on 24-5-1963 the owners of the 'A' scheduled properties Gopal Chandra Pal. and 10 others executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 to effect a deed of exchange and the said power of Attorney was duly registered in the office of a Magistrate, 1st Class, Udaypur, Tripura on 24-5-1963 which was also duly restamped in the then Pakistan and the parties to the said exchange got possession of their properies under the said deed and the plaintiffs migrated to Pakistan in the month of August, 1963 and since then they have been possessing the 'A' scheduled properties and made improvement of the same. Some interested persons after the departure of its Hindu owners managed to publish the. notification in question in respect of the 'A' scheduled properties naming the same as evacuee properties in the Dhaka Gazette vide Notification No. 6330 EPMC dated 31-7-65 which was illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs in respect of 'A' schedule properties and those interested persons were trying to take lease of the 'A' scheduled properties on the basis of said illegal notification and hence the plaintiffs were, compelled to file the suit.

4. The opposite party No. 5 the Government of Bangladesh as defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement stating, inter alia, that the 'A' scheduled properties belonged to the recorded Hindu owners and the same according to the provisions of East Bengal Act XXIV of 1965 became enemy properties and the same vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Properties. There was no deed of exchange in respect of the A Scheduled properties in favour of the plaintiffs by the Hindu owners and the plaintiffs had no ownership in the 'B' scheduled properties to get exchange of the 'A' scheduled properties and the alleged exchange by way of power of attorney was fraudulent, forged and fabricated. The plaintiffs were never the inhabitants of Tripura state and now on the departure of the Hindu owners they have created fabricated and forged exchange documents to grab the suit 'A' scheduled properties without having any right, title and possession in the land in either of scheduled properties to the plaint.

5. The petitioner No. 6 defendant No. 5 and the opposite party No. 7 as defendant No. 6 and the predecessor of the petitioner Nos. 1 to 3 Gouranga Chandra Pal and the predecessor of the petitioner Nos. 4 and 5 Nityananda Pal, the petitioner No. 7, the petitioner No. 8, the Petitioner No. 9 and the petitioner No. 10 as defendants No. 7 to 12 filed three Sets of written statements in the suit after being added as defendants denying the plaintiffs case of title and possession by virtue of exchange thereof:

6. In the written statement filed by defendant No. 5 (petitioner No. 6 in this Rule) it was contended that his father Chandra Kumar Pal had ownership and possession in 11.77 acres of land of khatian Nos. 30 and 32 of the' A' scheduled properties to the plaint who died leaving behind him and his brother Sarbananda Pal as sons, Sarbananda Pal had to go to Calcutta in the year 1358 BS when he sold all his inherited properties to the defendant No. 5 at a consideration of Taka 6,500 out of which 5,000 on being paid possession of the share was delivered to him and before that transfer the defendant No. 5 and his brother jointly sold 1.26 acres of land to others. The defendant and his brother Sarbananda never executed any power of attorney in favour of the plaintiffs and that the alleged power of attorney is a forged, fraudulent and fabricated one and the plaintiffs created the said power of attorney forging their names which was earlier seized by the local chairman of the Union Parishad and thereafter the plaintiffs have created a new forged power of attorney with help of some veteran forgers of Comilla and Chittagong Districts. The plaintiffs are inhabitants of Noakhali District who used to go to Tripura state for seasonal employment in agricultural firm and they had no title and possession in '8' scheduled properties to the plaint and the defendants never exchanged the '8' schedule properties with the "A' scheduled properties. The suit property of khatian Nos. 30 and 32 cannot be treated as enemy property, which exclusively belong to the defendant No.5.

7. The defendant No. 6 in his written statement contended, inter alia, that his father Purna Chandra Pal was the owner of land of Khatian Nos. 29/94/94/100 and 255 of the schedule 'A' to the plaint and died leaving behind three sons namely, the defendant Jashoda Kumar Pal and Kali Kumar Pal. About 15 to 16 years before Kali Kumar and Joshoda left this country by transferring the lands of their share to the defendant No. 6 and had been living in West Bengal but they never had gone to Tripura and the defendant No. 6 or his two other brothers never executed any power of attorney purporting alleged exchange of the 'A' scheduled property with the '8' scheduled property to the plaint. His brother Joshoda Kumar Pal died before the alleged execution of Power of Attorney and on the basis of forged document, the plaintiffs cannot get any decree in the suit. The properties belong to the defendant No. 6 and the same cannot be treated as enemy property.

8. In the written statement filed by the predecessors of the present petitioner Nos. 1 to 3 as defendant No. 7, predecessor of the petitioner No. 4 and 5 as defendant No. 8 and the petitioners Nos. 7 to 10 as defendants No.9 to 12 contended inter alia, that in part of land of khatian No. 33/5b/ 52/53/55/95/94 Raj Kumar Pal, Rajani Kumar Pal, Chandra Kumar Pal and Ram Sundar Pal, were the owners and had been in possession thereof. On the death of Raj Kumar Pal his three sons defendant No. 9 (petitioner No. 7), defendant No. 10 (petition No. 8) and Anukul Chandra Pal became the owners thereof. Anukul Chandra after transferring his share in favour of defendant Nos. 9 and 10 went to India about 15/16 years before Rajani Kumar died leaving behind two sons defendant No. 7 (the predecessor of petitioner Nos. 1 to 3) and Gopal Pal as his heirs. Gopal Pal transferred his share to the defendant No. 7, Chandra Kumar Pal died leaving behind three sons’ defendant No. 8 (predecessor of petitioner Nos. 4 and 5) Chitta Ranjan Pal and Sushil Pal as his heirs and thereafter Chitta Ranjan and Sushil transferred their shares to the defendant No. 8 and left for India. Ram Kumar Pal died leaving behind four sons defendant No. 11 (petitioner No.9), defendant No. 12 (petitioner No. 10), Harihar and Fani Bhusion Pal as his heirs, Harihar and Fani Bhusion Pal after transferring their share in favour of the defendant Nos. 11 and 12 left for India and, as such, the property in their possession and title in respect of the lands as described in 'A' schedule cannot be treated as enemy or evacuee property. None of the owners of the 'A' scheduled property ever executed any power of attorney in favour of the plaintiffs and the signatures appearing in the said power of attorney are all forged and the initials in the names of the Government officials in the said documents are also created with the help of veteran forgers with purpose to file this false suit.

9. During the trial the plaintiffs examined two Witnesses- PW 1 being the plaintiff No. 1 and PW 2 being one Loketullah. On behalf of the Government of Bangladesh Tahashilder was examined as DW 1 and defendant No.5 himself was examined as DW 2. The learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali by his Judgment and decree dated 30-4-1981 dismissed the suit. Against the said Judgment and decree the plaintiff-opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 44 of 1989 before the District Judge, Lakshimpur. The learned District Judge after hearing the said appeal by the impugned Judgment and decree allowed the appeal and decreed the suit after setting aside the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Being aggrieved by the said Judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the petitioners obtained this Rule.

<u>10. Mr AFM Shahid, learned Advocate appearing with Mr Mehir Kanti Mazumder and Mrs Nahid Yeasmin for the petitioners-submits that to maintain a suit for declaratory decree under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiffs must have clear title to the suit property and no suit can be filed or maintained on the basis of a so-called power of attorney executed in India without being authenticated by the then Embassy of Pakistan. Mr Shahid submits that the appellate Court while decreeing the suit failed to consider this legal position of the case occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit. Mr AFM Shahid in support of his contention has referred the case of Sahera Khatun and another vs Anwara Khatun and ors reported in 1 BCR 126 = 33 DLR 442. the case of Hasmat Ali vs Mofizuddin Majhi and others reported in 37 DLR 231. Mr Shahid further submits that from the 'B' schedule to the plaint it appears the properties of India have not been described which prima facie shows that the alleged property in India has not been exchanged with the 'A' scheduled property in Bangladesh and the power of attorney having not been authenticated by the then Pakistan Embassy was not admissible in evidence as per provision of section 85 of the Evidence Act. In support of the contention he has referred the case of Nurunnesa and ors vs Babar Ali Bepari reported in 33 DLR (AD) 124. Mr Shahid lastly, submits that the appellate Court passed the impugned Judgment and decree without the consideration of these legal aspects of the case and thus committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice and, as such, the same calls for interference by this court.</u>

11. Mr KZ Alam learned Advocate appearing with Mr Shariful Islam and AHM Mashfiqur Rahman, learned Advocates for the plaintiffs-opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the plaintiffs in support of their case that the properties as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint which belonged to Hindu owners were exchanged with the properties in India as described in schedule 'B' to the plaint have produced power of attorney duly authenticated by the learned Munsif, Uddayapur in the state of Tripura and the same has been re-stamped in Comilla it cannot be said that the plaintiffs had/have no semblance of title to maintain a suit of the instant nature and as per provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act the plaintiffs have right to protect their possession. He submits that as the property was notified as a vested property the plaintiffs had no other alternative but to file the suit to protect their possession. Mr KZ Alam submits, that in the facts and circumstances of the present case the plaintiffs might not have acquired title to maintain a suit for declaration of title under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but the suit of the instant nature by virtue of the registered power of attorney with condition of exchanging the properties in India with the owners of the then East Pakistan is maintainable in law and the Court below rightly decreed the suit.

12. From the Judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial Court disbelieved Exhibit 1 namely, the Power of Attorney, on the ground that PW 1 Nur Mohammad stated in his deposition that he has no paper to show that he had any property in India although the trial Court noted that PW 1 stated in his evidence that he gave all the paper of their ownership to the exchanges and his exchanges did not give any paper except the power of Attorney. The trial Court disbelieved the power of Attorney for the further reason that there is no legible date in the official seal of the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla as affixed on the special adhesive stamp appearing on the first page of Ext 1. The trial Court also found that there is no mention of any reference of any case in the power of Attorney in connection with which it was restampted and revalidated. The appellate Court being the final court of fact considering the evidence on record both oral and documentary and on examination of the power of Attorney came to the definite, finding that the same was registered on 24-5-1963 in the Court of, Munsif/Magistrate, Uddayapur and is a genuine one and not collusive and reversed each and every finding of the trial Court in this regard. In considering the genuineness of the power of Attorney the appellate Court considered the question of possession of the suit property by the plaintiffs with reference to the pleading of the parties and the evidence of the PWs and the DWs and came to the definite finding that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit property since 1963. The appellate Court also found that in the written statements filed by the defendant Nos. 5-12 they did not deny the specific assertion of possession of the suit property by the plaintiffs since 1963 and did not say that the plaintiffs entered into their homestead by force. It appears that the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration that the suit property was never treated as enemy property and Gazette Notification published in that respect was illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them. It is interesting to note that the defendant No. 5 who contested the suit never took any step challenging the Notification by which the property was treated as enemy property. It also appears that the defendant No. 5 who deposed in the suit in the month of February 1971 came from India with Pakistan passport which was marked as Ext A-11 and subsequently, he took it back with the condition that he will refile the same but did not refile the same. An application was filed in this court stating that either he lost the passport or misplaced it but no document has been filed to show that the same was lost. The very fact that the defendant No. 5 came in 1971 in the month of February with Pakistani passport shows that he was in India and he exchanged his property along with other brothers with those of the plaintiffs in India which have been fully described in schedule 'B' to the plaint. The trial Court itself observed to the effect:

"The passport marked Exhibit A 11 as filed on behalf of Rashamoy Paul shows that he remained as Citizen of Pakistan at the relevant time though it is found in the deposition of this witness that his all other relations including his family members are inhabitants of India. So, it has now got to be ascertained whether DW 2 came over here at the instance of certain interest persons to depose in this suit

but did not decide the matter. It is also to be noted that although the other defendants filed written statement but except the defendant No. 5 none deposed in support of their respective case, It is true that it is the plaintiffs who are to prove their case and they cannot succeed .on the weakness of the defendant's case" but when the plaintiffs filed the registered power of Attorney as the basis of' their possession in the suit land and when the contesting defendant challenged the said power of Attorney, and the exchange in pursuant he had some onus to prove assertions to his case of living in Bangladesh and possession in the suit land which he has failed to prove. Similar is the case with the defendant No. 1 namely, the Government. Although the Government of Bangladesh published notification treating the suit property as evacuee property yet the government did not assert that they took possession of the suit property namely, the 'B' schedule property after its owners left this country and have been possessing the same through the lessees. The trial Court observed to the effect.

" ....DW 1 Shamsul Haque was examined on the side of the defendant No. 1. He is a Tahsilder of the enemy property department. He does not appear to have any personal knowledge as regards the alleged possession of any persons in the suit land"

<u>13. The trial Court, in fact, did not come to any finding as to the factum of possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs which is very crucial in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and discarded the evidence of PW 2 on the ground that he was the solitary witness as in the possession of the suit land in support of the plaintiffs case of possession since 1963, completely overlooking the provision of section 134 of the Evidence Act and the further fact that the plaintiffs possession was never denied by the contesting defendants herein as discussed above. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and the particular fact that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land since 1963 by virtue of the registered power of Attorney. I am of the view that the plaintiffs have acquired a right to the 'A' scheduled property at least to protect their possession to maintain a suit within the meaning of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and their suit is maintainable. The principle of law enunciated in the cited Cases as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners have got no manner of application in the facts and circumstance in the instant Case and accordingly, I do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. The registered power of Attorney was taken aback by the plaintiffs from the record. Mr KZ Alam produced the same before me and I have also examined the same and from a mere look with the eye it appears that the same was registered in the Court of Munsif, Uddaypur and was validated by the Deputy Commissioner. The appellate Court has rightly' observed that no step was taken on behalf of the contesting defendants to prove forgery and fraud in creating the power of Attorney.</u>

14. For the reasons stated hereinabove, I do not find any error committed by the appellate Court in passing the impugned Judgment and decree calling for interference by the Court.

In the result, this Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
